@@118558839 <h> LATEST EDITORIAL <h> Books Capitalism and the planet -- analysis reqd . <h> RICHARD MURGATROYD is disappointed by an ambitious survey that fails to get to grips with the relationship between human consciousness and nature <p> PROFIT BEFORE HUMANITY : Female pigs used for breeding - ' breeding sows ' are confined most of their lives in ' gestation crates ' which are so small that they can not even turn around . The pigs ' basic needs are denied , and they experience severe physical and psychological disorders Photo : Farm Sanctuary/flickr/CC <p> ? <h> This is the last article you can read this month <h> You can read more article this month <h> You can read more articles this month <h> Sorry your limit is up for this month <h> Living on Earth : Life , Consciousness and The Making of the Natural WorldPeter Godfrey-Smith <p> A CLIMATE emergency , species extinction , habitat destruction ... all largely driven by human actions and choices . Why has our impact become so destructive ? Logically , consciousness -- whether human or animal -- plays an important part . <p> The author begins with fundamentals . He charts the rise of life from the simplest chemical processes 3.8 billion years ago to the present . The emphasis is on the role evolution played within a unified , complex , ever-changing ecosystem . Shifts in climate are decisive , but living creatures also change their environments simply by living . No species in the long history of life on Earth has proved so dynamic as us . <p> Humans also belong in the web of life . The experience of living on this riotous , diverse , colourful planet , with all its joys and challenges , evokes deep feelings . Godfrey-Smith gives plenty of examples , and we are reminded of the sheer wonder of life . <p> So far so good . His account sets the scene for the main question : what part does human consciousness play in all this ? <p> The short answer is almost everything . The scale of humanity 's impact can be measured in biomass -- the actual material of life . Human biomass is now nine times that of all wild mammals . Now add the animals and birds we farm . Livestock comes in at 14 times the biomass of wild animals and farmed birds more than twice that of wild birds . <p> This startling material dominance has arisen because of conscious choices made by billions of people over millennia . The consequences for nature are vast and the author rightly seeks to drill down into some key issues , including climate change , factory farming , habitat preservation and the use of animals in experiments . <p> Sadly , at this point he starts to lose his way . To be fair , it 's hard to get to grips with the reasons why humans do what we do to the natural world . His explanation revolves around a vague take on " human nature , " that flags up our capacity for analysis , co-operation , sociability and ability to develop technology . All these qualities mean that we are uniquely able to shape the natural environment . But why and how ? Godfrey-Smith generally falls back on the idea that we do what we do because we can . <p> But generalised abstractions do n't really explain humanity 's relationship with nature , past or present . Ultimately , as a species we deploy our enhanced mental and physical capacity to adapt and consume natural resources and then transform them into something else . This process of creative destruction is one of relatively peaceful co-existence and conflict . <p> However , once we moved past the primitive hunter/gatherer stage and developed mass agriculture and later industry , a new dynamic kicked in . The growth of hierarchical class-based societies based on private property fundamentally changed the way we interact with nature . This experience also decisively shaped our consciousness . <p> Godfrey-Smith is an academic philosophy professor , and it soon shows . He tends to swerve away from this essential materialistic point and instead focus on moral , quasi-religious or philosophical issues . Although we are generally spared the God part , the Gaia theory which casts the Earth as a semi-conscious entity able to protect itself from threats ( like us ) predictably gets a good airing . The ensuing discussion meanders through thickets of speculation , ethical debates and digressions . <p> To be fair , he tries hard to explain the competing ideas put forward by his fellow academics in accessible ways , and often succeeds . But after struggling through hundreds of pages of dense verbiage this reader at least suspected he could n't see the trees for the wood . <p> Take the case of factory farming , surely the ultimate example of big business commodifying nature ? Clearly , the " choices " made here by both capitalist owners and consumers are rooted in a market system of mass production for profit . But amazingly , the word " capitalism " does n't appear once . <p> Equally disappointing is the discussion of climate change . After ritually denouncing fossil fuels -- but not the companies and governments that produce or enable them -- he seems to mentally shrug . Yes , we should be doing something to stop global warming , but probably wo n't . <p> Maybe , we should accept the inevitable and create special environmental zones instead ? Then again , are there ethical problems with that too ? Choices . Tricky things choices , especially in the absence of a clear analysis of the dominant class interests and ideas that are shaping them . <p> So ultimately the author fails to really get to grips with the current relationship between human consciousness and nature . Late capitalism leaves nothing untouched , whether human or non-human . Living fruitfully on Earth therefore requires system-change as well as a deeper understanding of our place on the planet . That will be a choice , but one that also requires class consciousness to achieve it . 
@@118561942 <h> Get the latest Plymouth Live breaking news on WhatsApp <p> More than 2,000 new trees are set to be planted in Plymouth over the winter months . The trees will be planted all over the city in parks , public spaces , residential streets and outside housing developments . <p> The planting will include more than 1,500 whips , over 70 maiden fruit trees , and 450 standards . Whips are young and slender trees which are often just a few feet tall at the time of planting . <p> A maiden is a smaller tree , usually three to five foot tall while a standard is a large tree that at the time of planting is already six to ten feet tall , having been grown in a nursery for several years . Standards are usually the preferred choice for planting in urban areas such as streets and parks . <p> Plymouth City Council says this season 's schedule includes planting fewer whips , but more fruit trees and standards . Locations for the trees include : <p> Collings Park -- a scheme designed by the Forest Rising youth programme alongside community groups , residents and primary schools to plant trees and other landscape enhancements to provide a more nature rich and accessible green space for the local community <p> Central Park Golf Course -- Working with the Central Park Golf Hut , this will include an edible hedge , orchard , high density woodland and avenue trees across the site . Other enhancements include additional seating areas , interpretation boards , and over 1,000m2 of cut and bail wildflower meadow . <p> Southway -- More than 100 large trees including a new community orchard are to be planted on verges and in residential pocket green spaces <p> Hoe Park -- Working with local stakeholders , a mixture of 15 fruit trees will be planted next to the existing orchard , behind the Hoe Clock Garden . <p> Councillor Tom Briars-Delve , cabinet member for the environment and climate change , said : " Another year , another bumper tree planting programme . I ca n't wait to get started ! Our tree planting record over the last few years speaks for itself . <p> " Thanks to our involvement in the funding and running of the Plymouth and South Devon Community Forest , we have been able to significantly improve the tree coverage across our city . I look forward to planting a few of the 2,000 myself . " <p> The planting is funded and supported by Plymouth and South Devon Community Forest ( PSDCF ) , a partnership between Plymouth City Council , National Trust , Woodland Trust , South Hams District Council and West Devon Borough Council , Dartmoor National Park Authority , Devon County Council , West Devon Borough Council . It is funded through the DEFRA Nature for Climate fund . <p> Launched in September 2020 , PSDCF has overseen the planting of over 180,000 trees across 155 sites , stretching from the South Devon coast to Dartmoor National Park . @@118571044 <h> Are these the most fantastic forests from across the globe ? <p> Covering over 31% of Earth 's land area , forests can be a restorative and peaceful haven for nature lovers . Not only do they possess a wealth of environmental benefits , but they can be good for our mental health too . A 2019 study found that spending two hours a week in nature can help improve our health and wellbeing . But there 's more , a separate research study has shown that even looking at an image of nature can be great way to boost your mood while at home . So what are you waiting for ? <p> From the mountainous terrains of China to the underwater jungles of North America , BBC Bitesize takes a look at some of the most magical forests from across the world . <p> Image caption , <p> The Jiuzhaigou Valley is recognised for its colourful waterscapes , wild forests and layered waterfalls <h> Jiuzhaigou National Park - China <p> Renowned for its scenic views and majestic landscapes , Jiuzhaigou National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage site that sits along the edge of the Tibetan Plateau in China . <p> Jiuzhaigou , which translates to " Nine Settlement Valley " , refers to the nine Tibetan settlements along its length . <p> Amidst approximately 280 square miles ( 725 sq km ) of forest , it hosts many waterfalls , caves , lakes and snow-topped mountain peaks . There is a current human population of 1,000 people , with evidence showing that people have been living in the national park for up to 3,000 years . <p> According to UNESCO , the reserve is home to 140 bird species . It also hosts a number of endangered animal species , such as the giant panda and the Sichuan takin . <p> Image caption , <p> There are around 400 billion trees standing in the Amazon and these trees influence rainfall cycles throughout South America <h> The Amazon Rainforest - South America <p> Spanning eight countries and encompassing around 40% of Brazil 's total land area , the mighty Amazon Rainforest is often described as the lungs of the planet . By far the largest forest in the world , it covers 2.3 million square miles ( 5.9 million sq km ) , stretching from the Atlantic Ocean in the east to the tree line of the Andes in the west . <p> Approximately 47 million people live in the Amazon region . This includes over 400 different indigenous groups , more than anywhere else on Earth , and an estimated 300 indigenous languages are spoken across the rainforest . <p> As one of the world 's richest and diverse habitats , it is home to several million species of insects plants and birds . It also boasts major wildlife such as jaguars , capybaras , sloths , red howler monkeys and pink river dolphins . In fact , it is thought to be home to 10% of the known species on Earth . <p> Image caption , <p> These giant kelp can grow up to 18 inches per day <h> Channel Islands National Park - North America <p> This is n't your typical land forest ! On Anacapa Island , a small volcanic island off the coast of California , US , is the Channel Islands National Park , host to a number of underwater kelp forests . <p> Giant kelp is a type of large , brown seaweed that can be found along the US 's west coast , especially in southern California . One third of southern California 's kelp forests can be found within the Channel Islands National Park . <p> This kelp grows into forests at depths of nearly 100ft ( 30m ) . Its blades provide refuge for over 1,000 types of marine plants and animals that can be found within the Channel Islands kelp forests . <p> Image caption , <p> Before World War I , Hallerbos was part of the Sonian Forest , Europe 's largest beech forest <h> Hallerbos Forest , Belgium <p> Ever wanted to wander in a real-life enchanted forest ? He has seven Baftas and enough Golden Globes ( four ) that he uses one as a doorstop . Armageddon , his most recent Netflix stand-up show , went straight to No 1 on the streaming service . Mortality , which just added seven shows to its UK tour , is likely to be just as popular . Andy was wary of triggering a fight . <h> Advertisement <p> What was mildly offensive about Gervais in the Noughties has become more controversial in the hysterically partisan 2020s . The comedian , who has often told interviewers of his wish to " polarise " audiences , has achieved exactly that . While many mainstream comedians have attacked Donald Trump on their late-night shows , Gervais has spent the culture wars mocking liberals . LGBTQ rights groups in particular have condemned his jokes about trans people and accused him of spreading misinformation . <p> None of this has put a dent in Gervais . At the end of Mortality he tells his audience that culture is " coming out of a weird five-year period when you could n't say anything " . The unsayable was sayable again . <p> " They 're only jokes , " Andy said with a sigh , quoting a Gervais line : " And we 'll all be dead soon , wo n't we ? " Was Andy right to be nervous about the woke brigade ? We were in Brighton after all , a town where you could wrap a trans flag around a passing seagull and expect it to find a seat in the House of Commons . <p> In 2020 the comedian Frankie Boyle launched a broadside at Gervais . " <p> Gervais with his partner , Jane Fallon <p> KARWAI TANG/GETTY IMAGES <p> And it 's true that Gervais has ended up in a strange place . Enormously popular with his public , he is no longer the toast of fellow comedians and comedy writers . When the UK comedy listings bible Chortle called him a " bold free speech warrior saying what he wants in the face of the censorious left " in November , they did n't mean it as a compliment . Reviews for his live stand-up shows have been patchy for years , with critics irritated by Gervais 's rotating stock of Twitter-influenced culture wars jokes -- but it has not stopped audiences coming out to enjoy them . <h> Advertisement <p> At the Brighton Centre in late November there were thousands of Gervais fans . The long lines testify to a cultural truth of the moment : pissing off liberals is popular and lucrative . Mortality 's next ten shows , stretching into 2025 , are already sold out . <p> " He says what he wants to say , " says Mark , a 38-year-old engineer . " People care too much about what other people think . " As Gary Neville , Jamie Carragher and Ian Wright nodded along , Gervais parsed the working-class roots of his comedy : " It 's funny because I think comedy , particularly British stand-up is traditionally -- you 're a jester , down with the people , making fun of the bosses . " <p> Whether you can be a " jester " while being a millionaire who fronts a new line of premium vodka is something that clearly troubles Gervais . His dad was a labourer who worked for petty cash . His mum was a housewife who , he has said , swore a lot . Cemetery Junction , the 2010 film that is easily Gervais 's most personal work , is about young men escaping these roots , just as he did when he became the first person in his family to go to university ( he studied philosophy at UCL ) in the early 1980s . <h> Advertisement <p> He has never really shed his blue collar , or a sense of disgust at being thought of as a rich celebrity . Much of the laughter in Gervais 's work finds these men falling over the connotative tripwires and exploding the linguistic landmines of political correctness . Not only are they downwardly mobile , they 're also desperately uncool . These are the people who trouble Gervais 's conscience in his stand-up , and it is their side he has taken in the culture wars . <p> With Ashley Jensen in After Life <p> **28;383;TOOLONG <p> In Brighton his fans resembled his characters . It may not be pleasant or polite , but millions of people are likely to agree with Gervais , or , at the very least , find that idea very funny . <p> Gervais has promised that Mortality would be his most " confessional " show yet . It 's not really . Rather than being personal and intimate , Mortality tells us more about the state of the country where Gervais is so successful : angry , bitter and polarised , with its patience wearing thinner every day . Gervais sounded less like a comedian and more like a spokesman for a furious , gathering backlash to liberalism . " All the high-spilling assets are being looked at . " <p> Stay updated with the latest Swansea news by signing up for our newsletter here . <p> Swansea beach 's bathing water quality near the Tawe often achieves a " good " rating , not quite reaching the " excellent " standard seen at Langland and Caswell further west . However , concerns were raised during the climate change and nature scrutiny panel meeting about Welsh Water 's pumping station activities at Langland , reports Wales Online . <p> It was revealed to councillors that the station 's emergency overflow system had been discharged 12 times throughout 2023 , with five instances occurring within the May to September bathing season , each lasting around 30 minutes on average . Mr Osborn suggested that some spills might have arisen from a blockage in the outfall pipe , prompting stormwater to back up . <p> Welsh Water has since cleared this blockage , which should mean problems only arise if there is a pump failure . Further issues noted by Mr Osborn include the potential for stormwater infiltrating beach-side showers at Langland , connected to the sewage system , indicating possible future remedial work . <p> During a meeting , it was reported that the sewage treatment plant in Caswell has had permission to discharge under certain conditions , leading to three spills in 2023 , with one potentially caused by maintenance . Mr Osborn noted an improvement over previous years , citing diversions of some surface water sources . <p> Mumbles councillor Will Thomas revealed he and his colleagues have been gathering data from Welsh Water and urging action , though he acknowledged the costs involved due to Gower and Swansea 's network layout could reach " tens of millions of pounds " . Cllr Thomas also highlighted that spill data at Knab Rock pumping station in Mumbles was " exceptionally high " and expressed concern over the lack of authority intervention despite Welsh Water 's plans to install three new pumps . <p> Mr Osborn has labelled the number of spills at Knab Rock as " excessive " and in need of attention . However , he clarified that these spills were into underground tanks rather than from the tanks into the sea , which " confuses the issue somewhat " . <p> His colleague at NRW , Sarah Bennett , stated that they are regulating the situation through a recently modified permit for the Knab Rock pumping station , which obliges Welsh Water to investigate when a certain number of spills occur . Mr Osborne emphasised that NRW is pressuring Welsh Water to make improvements . <p> " We do regulate this problem - it bothers us , we expect action , " he declared . These problems are n't new . <p> Three years ago , a scrutiny meeting raised concerns about large numbers of spills from combined sewer overflows in the Tawe . One councillor reported that a combined sewer overflow in Clydach had discharged into the river 154 times in 2020 , totalling 1,166 hours . <p> At the same meeting , Mr Osborn admitted that NRW had " certain issues with " Langland pumping station 's emergency overflow system . A report presented at the most recent meeting this month revealed that NRW conducts bathing water samples at various beaches , while the council does so at non-designated spots at Broughton and Rhossili , Gower . <p> The report concluded that , generally , coastal waters have been " hugely improved by large and sophisticated treatment schemes " . <p> Following a meeting where Welsh Water was notably absent , a spokesperson commented on the ongoing situation regarding the pumping stations at Langland and Knab Rock . @@118573117 <h> Plans submitted for multimillion-pound flood defence scheme in Poole <h> Plans submitted for a multi million pound flood defence in Poole <p> PLANS for a multimillion-pound flood defence scheme in Poole have been submitted . <p> The project , set out from Poole Bridge to Hunger Hill , plans to reduce tidal flood risk in Poole town centre , the Old Town and surrounding areas for the next 100 years . <p> The proposed project , led by the BCP Council in collaboration with the Environment Agency and other organisations , will create a permanent flood defence along 1.5km of Holes Bay 's eastern side , between Poole Bridge and Hunger Hill . <p> The scheme is divided into five zones , with interventions planned for 2025 , 2071 , and 2105 to address the impacts of climate change and sea level rise . <p> If the plans are approved , BCP Council will take ownership and maintenance responsibility for the defences . <p> Ringwood-based Knights Brown Construction has been selected to build the defences . <p> Nick Gib , senior design manager for Knights Brown , said : " Historically , we have completed numerous projects in and around the Poole area . <p> " We 've been involved in this project providing early contractor involvement , considering the buildability to minimise cost while reducing disruption and environmental impacts . " <p> Matt Hosey , BCP Council 's head of flood and coastal erosion risk management , said that Poole is one of the highest-risk areas in the Wessex region for flooding . <p> He previously told the Daily Echo : " There is definitely a significant flood risk . That is reflected in the fact that the Environment Agency has its own temporary defence plan for Poole town centre as well . <p> " We work in partnership with the Environment Agency . They have got priority sites nationally , and Poole town centre is one of those . If we had extreme events forecast , they would put temporary defences down West Quay Road instead , for example . <p> " The preference is for us to crack on and deliver this defence because that would negate the need for them to put the barriers down the highway . " <p> The 2014 Poole Harbour and Wareham Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management Strategy identified 573 properties in Central Poole at high flood risk , a figure expected to rise to more than 2,000 by 2110 . <p> With regeneration unable to provide adequate defences , the BCP Council proposed a Council-led scheme , approved in 2020 . @@118573537 <h> Review : How good is That Christmas and how Suffolk is it ? <p> Suffolk is , of course , the best and only place to spend Christmas , so it was lovely to see it depicted in the new Richard Curtis film , That Christmas . <p> Directed by Simon Otto and based on That Christmas and other stories by Suffolk resident , Curtis , the film tells the story of a fictional seaside town , Wellington-on-Sea , and how the residents there cope with a massive snowstorm as the big day approaches . <p> Southwold lighthouse ? Surely it is indeed our lighthouse in That Christmas ( Image : Netflix ) Even though the film is an animation , Suffolk is happily very recognisable . The Southwold lighthouse , the beach and the dunes -- it could n't be anywhere else - and having spent my life trying to explain to people where Suffolk actually is , I 'm always delighted when we make it onto the cultural map . <p> That amount of snow just before Christmas would be unusual of course but in movieland we can happily believe such a sumptuous white Christmas possible , and sitting down with my mulled wine in my pyjamas to watch the film on Netflix last night , I felt the same glow I used to get as a child when it was time for The Wizard of Oz . <p> This looks familiar ... ( Image : Netflix ) This film is n't as smart as The Wizard . It brickbats its climate change and diversity agenda very firmly indeed - it took me years to work out what The Wizard was all about but That Christmas told me what I should be thinking in the first scene . <p> Richard Curtis ' genius has always been his ability to make you laugh and cry within the same minute . There was n't quite enough of that here for me and the little nods to Love Actually were a reminder that the now much maligned Christmas classic was far less heavy handed than this new advocate for decency and kindness . <p> I also struggled to make out a genuine Suffolk accent -- although there was quite a bit of Yeovil thrown in as usual . But we ca n't all be Ralph Fiennes in The Dig , can we ? <p> Danny and ' good twin ' Sam were charming ( Image : Netflix ) On the plus side , there were some lovely characters , particularly the little boy , Danny , ( Jack Wisniewski ) and his single mum ( Jodie Whittaker ) -- a nurse who works all hours and struggles through the snow on Christmas Day to make sure Bill Nighy 's Lighthouse Keeper gets to spend one last festive season with his mum . <p> Fiona Shaw 's Ms Trapper won my vote for best character -- a lonely teacher whose grief for her lost love is covered by outward grumpiness . When she shows Danny what Christmas might be like through his exhausted mother 's eyes , as an exhausted mother myself , my own eyes , I must admit , teared up . <p> And then of course there is Brian Cox 's brilliant Scottish Father Christmas whose interactions with his reindeer , Dasher , ( Guz Khan ) , are a highlight , as is the storyline of the good twin ( Zazie Hayhurst ) and the naughty twin ( Sienna Sayer ) , which was quite touching in its examination of what it means to be misunderstood . <p> To cap it all , there 's a charming new Ed Sheeran Christmas song , Under The Tree , and you ca n't get much more Suffolk , festive or delightful than that . <p> So , all in all , if you want to get yourself in the festive mood and revel in seeing Suffolk on the telly , give this film a go . By the end , I was feeling fully Christmassed up and confident that this would be far from the last time I watched That Christmas . <h> Comments : Our rules <p> We want our comments to be a lively and valuable part of our community - a place where readers can debate and engage with the most important local issues . @@118587924 <p> From facing deadly conflicts and humanitarian crises in Gaza , Lebanon , Ukraine and Sudan , to witnessing the polarisation in societies that followed a record number of elections around the world , women have had to dig deep and find new levels of resilience . <p> BBC 100 Women acknowledges the toll this year has taken on women by celebrating those who -- through their resilience -- are pushing for change , as the world changes around them . The list also remains committed to exploring the impact of the climate emergency , highlighting climate pioneers who work to help their communities tackle its impacts . <h> Culture &amp; Education <h> Plestia Alaqad , Palestinian Territories <p> Journalist and writer <p> Twenty-two-year-old Plestia Alaqad had recently graduated from university when the war in Gaza began . In the earliest days of the war , she posted a video of herself in her apartment during intense Israeli airstrikes . <p> It went viral , and she amassed four million followers on Instagram with subsequent Gaza updates , poems and diary entries . Her memoir based on these reports , Eyes of Gaza , will be published soon . <p> Alaqad is One Young World 's Journalist of the Year 2024 . She has also campaigned for Palestinians at high-profile forums like the World Government Summit . <p> Alaqad left Gaza in November 2023 . She has been awarded a scholarship for a master 's in media studies in Beirut . <h> Hamida Aman , Afghanistan <p> Media and education entrepreneur <p> When Afghan girls were denied access to secondary education by the Taliban , media entrepreneur Hamida Aman decided to launch the Begum Academy , an online space offering free multimedia courses for students who were not able to attend school . <p> In the last year , the educational platform has provided more than 8,500 videos in Dari and Pashto , covering school curricula for grades seven to 12 . <p> The service followed her Radio Begum project , a station made by women and for women , which was created after the Taliban takeover in 2021 . <h> Svetlana Anokhina , Russia <p> Human rights campaigner <p> Svetlana Anokhina has spent years helping victims of domestic violence escape from Russia 's North Caucasus , a Muslim-majority region straddling Eastern Europe and Asia . <p> Along with other volunteers , she founded the Marem project in 2020 . The initiative helps women at risk from Dagestan , Chechnya and other North Caucasus republics organise evacuations and find temporary accommodation , as well as providing them with legal and psychological support . <p> Last year , the authorities opened a criminal investigation against her on charges of discrediting the Russian Armed Forces . <h> Christina Assi , Lebanon <p> Photojournalist <p> Photojournalist Christina Assi grew up in 1990s Lebanon - a time of constant instability in the aftermath of civil war - and this fuelled her drive to document conflict and cover the untold stories of war . <p> Her life took a tragic turn in October 2023 , when she was severely injured in an Israeli strike in southern Lebanon while reporting . <p> The blast killed fellow journalist Issam Abdallah , five other colleagues were wounded and Assi would later have a leg amputated . <p> The experience led her to campaign for journalists ' safety , and she dedicated her participation in the 2024 Olympic torch relay in Paris to all the journalists who have died in the line of duty . <h> Eugenia Bonetti , Italy <p> Nun <p> Sister Eugenia Bonetti has helped manage more than 100 shelters and establish a network with nuns in Africa to support migrant women victims of human trafficking and exploitation . <p> She spent many nights assisting women who had been forced into the sex trade in Rome and became the president of Slaves No More , an organisation that raised awareness of human trafficking . <p> Bonetti was a missionary in Kenya for more than 24 years and helped train officials in various countries to develop anti-trafficking initiatives . <p> Before retiring , she was asked by Pope Francis to write the 2019 Way of the Cross , a key annual devotion for Catholics marking Good Friday at the Colosseum . <h> Shin Daewe , Myanmar <p> Film-maker <p> Award-winning documentary maker Shin Daewe was arrested when found with a drone in her luggage . <p> She was put on trial this year in military-ruled Myanmar , accused of violating counter-terrorism laws . At a closed court , she was denied legal representation and sentenced to life imprisonment . <p> The film-maker has opposed military rule since 1988 and is no stranger to detention . <p> She has directed a dozen short documentaries , many of which have attracted international attention , including her film about the 2007 pro-democracy protests , where thousands of Buddhist monks joined the demonstrations against the junta . <h> Tracey Emin , UK <p> Artist <p> In the 1990s , Tracey Emin rose to prominence for provocative pieces such as My Bed and Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963-1995 , also known as The Tent , which invite people to reflect on their sexual experiences . <p> She has since become an instantly recognisable name in the art world , celebrated for her confessional and autobiographical style . <p> It 's now 25 years since My Bed was first exhibited in London , sparking much media debate . Once portrayed as the enfant terrible of British art , this year Emin has been made a dame for her contributions to the visual arts . <p> The artist has set up the Tracey Emin Foundation in Margate , UK , to nurture upcoming talent . <p> Being a woman right now , I think we need as much resilience as we can have . I think now is a time when there has to be greater unity and a greater fight for women . <p> Tracey Emin <h> Cristina Rivera Garza , Mexico/US <p> Writer <p> Prolific author Cristina Rivera Garza has been recognised with many awards over the years , including the 2024 Pulitzer Prize in the memoir category for her book Liliana 's Invincible Summer , which shines a light on the issue of femicide . <p> Through the story of her sister Liliana -- murdered in 1990s Mexico by a former boyfriend who fled and was never brought to trial -- the writer confronts the trauma of losing a loved-one and embarks on a quest for justice in a country with one of the highest femicide rates in the world . <p> Rivera Garza is also the founder and chair of the PhD programme in creative writing in Spanish at the University of Houston . <p> Messing with language continuously and thoroughly so that language may finally convey women 's side of the story may well lay the foundation for any kind of resilience . <p> Cristina Rivera Garza <h> Linda Dr ? fn Gunnarsd ? ttir , Iceland <p> Women 's shelter manager <p> At the Icelandic Women 's Shelter , Linda Dr ? fn Gunnarsd ? ttir helps those who are forced to leave their homes due to domestic violence . <p> Iceland is a country that often tops the rankings as the " best place to be a woman " , but where gender-based violence rates remain persistently high . <p> As the centre 's general manager , she leads the project to open a new space that would be Iceland 's first purpose-built shelter for women . <p> Gunnarsd ? ttir says that 20 years ago , 64% of women who stayed at the shelter eventually went back to their abusers , but that figure is now down to 11% as a result of improved support and services . <h> Maheder Haileselassie , Ethiopia <p> Photographer <p> Working in a landscape of dried rivers and decimated crops , Ethiopian photographer Maheder Haileselassie documents how severe drought has pushed families in her country to give their daughters up to child marriage . Her work Between Yesterday and Tomorrow won her the 2023 Contemporary African Photography Prize . <p> Human rights organisations anticipate that the number of girls at risk of child marriage as a result of the climate crisis will increase globally by a third by 2050 . <p> Haileselassie 's photography is informed by the history and experiences of the people she engages with every day , as well as her own . <p> Her work has been exhibited at many prestigious venues , including this year 's African Biennale of Photography . <h> Harbia Al Himiary , Yemen <p> Heritage conservation engineer <p> With many buildings of historical importance damaged after years of war in Yemen , engineer Harbia Al Himiary embarked on a mission to give them a new lease of life . <p> Working with other organisations such as the UN 's cultural agency , Unesco , she has restored dozens of residential and heritage buildings in Old Sana'a and across the country . Unesco has surveyed damage at more than 16,000 sites . <p> Her work in the field of heritage conservation has not only preserved historic sites but also improved the quality of life of many . <p> Al Himiary has also trained local residents in traditional building crafts and inspired young girls to get into the industry . <h> Anat Hoffman , Israel <p> She is a founding member of the Women of the Wall group , which seeks equal prayer rights for Jewish women at the Western Wall in Jerusalem 's Old City . Over the years , she has fought against rules barring women from wearing prayer shawls and reading from the Torah collectively . <p> Hoffman also served for 20 years as the executive director of the Israel Religious Action Center , the legal and advocacy arm of the Reform Movement that works to promote equality and social justice . <p> Prior to that , she held a seat on the Jerusalem City Council , where she challenged ultra-Orthodox policies . <h> Maria Teresa Horta , Portugal <p> Poet <p> Writer and journalist Maria Teresa Horta is one of Portugal 's most prominent feminists and author of many award-winning books , but she is perhaps best known as co-author of the internationally acclaimed Novas Cartas Portuguesas ( New Portuguese Letters ) , written with Maria Isabel Barreno and Maria Velho da Costa . <p> The collection of fiction , poetry , and erotica was quickly banned in 1972 by Portugal 's authoritarian government and Horta and her fellow co-authors stood trial for obscenity and " abusing the freedom of the press " . <p> The case of the Three Marias , as they became known , made headlines and inspired protests worldwide . <p> Their trial ended after the 1974 Carnation Revolution brought down the regime - and this year marks the 50th anniversary of that historic moment . <h> Johana Baham ? n , Colombia <p> Social activist <p> A visit to a Colombian prison transformed the life of actress Johana Baham ? n , inspiring her to work for those who needed a " second chance " . <p> In 2012 , she shifted her career from acting to advocating prison reform and founded Fundaci ? @@118605520 <h> If you take the train , stay somewhere low-impact , eat low-food-miles fare and avoid the ski lifts , can you still have fun ? Our writer finds out in La Plagne <p> High on a glacier above La Plagne in France , Max Silvin explains the dilemma facing modern ski resorts . " Of course , we want skiers to come here , " says the 74-year-old mountain guide . " Our local economy needs them . But now we are losing snow because the climate is changing and temperatures are rising . Look . " And with that , he gestures across the snowy valley in front of us , streaked with boulders and mud . <p> For the best part of half a century the Bellec ? te glacier , beyond the " piste closed " signs where Silvin and I are standing , was a popular summer playground and a favourite of high-altitude skiers in winter . Now rocks and hidden crevasses make it unsafe . Human-driven climate change is to blame -- and by extension , so , in part , is tourism . At the peak of its popularity , ten years ago , the Tarentaise Valley resort , part of the Paradiski ski area and linked to Les Arcs , was attracting 2.5 million visitors a year . <p> " I first came here in 1968 when I was 18 years old , " Silvin says , wistfully . " Back then it was possible to ski all the area we can see , in winter and summer . But in the last 25 years , the glacier has almost gone . " It 's not the only sign of climate change up here . An even earlier victim of the thaw was the Bellec ? te chairlift that served the glacier . The melting permafrost meant that its towers were becoming unsafe and last year they were stripped away . <p> Now , La Plagne is fighting back . It 's at the forefront of a campaign to make skiing more eco-friendly . Compagnie des Alpes , which manages the ski area here , along with other large French resorts , has converted piste-bashing machines from diesel to a synthetic fuel made from waste fats and vegetable oils that produces 90 per cent less carbon dioxide . In various shops throughout La Plagne 's sprawling , 11-village resort you can buy reconditioned skis and second-hand ski jackets , and various accommodation touts its eco-credentials . <p> For me that journey begins with a single step -- uphill . Silvin teaches the " old ways " of skiing , from the time before mass tourism brought high-speed lifts , spa hotels and budget air travel . This means skiing down mountains only after walking up them , otherwise known as ski-touring . <h> Advertisement <p> " When I was young we would come to La Roche de Mio , below the summit , then climb up here with skins every morning before skiing down . There were no lifts or mountain restaurants up here . " <p> La Plagne is a large resort made up of 11 villages <p> My skis are fitted on the underside with skins , strips of synthetic fur that are slippery as I slide the skis forwards , then grip the snow to resist backsliding , allowing me to hike up the slopes at miraculously steep angles . The only greenhouse gas is my panting breath . <p> That 's not all I 'm doing to reduce my carbon footprint . Rather than staying in a centrally heated hotel , I 've opted for a cheaper , well-insulated self-catering apartment , Residence Le Phoenix , in my chosen village of Belle Plagne . Perhaps alarmingly , it is equipped with disposable paper bed linen and bath towels , supposedly greener than the washable variety , according to the rental agency . <p> To stick to my low-carbon plan , my daily diet will not be an all-you-can-eat buffet , where food waste is likely . Instead , I 'm sticking to homemade food , no meat -- mainly tinned , eaten cold , because according to several environmental websites canned food has a lower carbon footprint as it uses less energy than the transportation and refrigeration required for fresh produce . There will be those who disagree , of course , and after a week existing on mainly vegetables in brine plus a few sardines and local goods , I 'm happy not to put up a fight . <h> Advertisement <p> More appealing is that at the end of the week I 'll be heading not for the airport but the railway station . <p> Some of these measures may sound extreme , but taken together I 've calculated that I 'll produce about a tenth of the carbon of a " normal " ski holiday -- ie one which involves jetting to a resort , maxing out an access-all-areas lift pass and staying half-board . <p> Nick Rufford embarked on an environmentally-friendly diet on his trip <p> Low-carbon skiing is taking hold as a trend . Many European resorts are attempting to reduce their footprint . SkiWelt Wilder Kaiser-Brixental leads the way in renewable hydroelectricity generation in the Austrian Tyrol . It has installed what it claims is the world 's first solar-powered lift , an eight-seater chairlift at SkiWelt S ? ll . Meanwhile , the Ischgl-Samnaun region in Austria has switched to 100 per cent renewable electricity and subsidises ski buses to reduce traffic . <p> US resorts including Wild Mountain in Minnesota and Taos Ski Valley in New Mexico have declared themselves carbon neutral , while Laax in Switzerland is aiming to go one step further and be " carbon-zero " by 2030 . <h> Advertisement <p> It all sounds worthy , but is it worth it ? Maybe tinned food is going too far , but if you get to ski on crisp snow in early light , and silence , with hardly anyone else around , you 'll have no complaints . <p> Low-impact skiing does have its drawbacks . Trudging up steep slopes on skins is a novelty on the first morning but it 's time-consuming and arduous . <p> You can count on completing only a couple of long runs in a day . And with no lift ride between descents , your legs do n't get much chance to recover . Where you 're climbing , off-piste , the snow is n't groomed and can change abruptly in texture from deep powder to icy ridges , making it hard to set a rhythm . In order to make a sharp turn while skinning uphill you need to master the kick turn . Done properly , this is an efficient and elegant way to change direction but to reach that degree of proficiency means a trial-and-error phase involving crossed skis and faceplants . <p> On the plus side , when I find myself on a secluded side of the mountain , there 's a great sense of isolation . The views are spectacular and when I reach the summit there 's a rewarding glow . As Abraham Lincoln might have said , climbing warms you twice : once through physical exertion and once with the knowledge you 're doing your bit . <h> Advertisement <p> Piste-basher machines can run on synthetic fuel made from waste fats and vegetable oils <p> GETTY IMAGES <p> As for my other attempts to cut my carbon footprint : the tinned food diet did n't last the week . As my resolve weakened , I topped up first on locally sourced baguette , then supermarket jam , then , dammit , Swiss chocolate . As for the paper bed linen and towels in my apartment -- forget it . They were shredded after two days of normal use and by the fifth day had disintegrated . It 'd have been better to bring my own sleeping bag . After a week I was dreaming of soft cotton towels and freshly laundered sheets , and a plate of steaming raclette . <p> After five days of putting Silvin 's techniques into practice , I 'm proud to report my thighs had developed a hitherto unfamiliar tautness and I had become a kick-turn ninja . But had I helped save the planet ? <p> The good news for anyone following in my tracks is that the least hair-shirtist of my eco-sacrifices was also the most effective.After waving goodbye to Silvin and handing back my skis and skins I boarded an SNCF Grand-Vitesse train at Aime La Plagne station , which whisked me smoothly to Paris Gare de Lyon in six hours without the misery of long transfers and airport chaos . <p> So , the reckoning . First , other heavily promoted " eco " ski trips -- the kind that promise organic menus , electric taxis and recycled ski goggles -- are probably just window dressing . They may be planet-friendly in other ways , but not in terms of net-carbon saving . Ski lifts do n't move the dial much , either . It 's hard to estimate their impact -- one internet source suggests an average ski lift uses as much electricity in a month as 3.8 domestic dwellings use in a year , but that may be referring to a drag lift rather than , say , a gondola . What is certain is that more than 80 per cent of France 's electricity comes from nuclear or hydro , so its carbon score is near zero . The share of clean electricity is even higher in the Alps , and that 's not counting solar lifts . In other words , clambering up mountains , as I did , does n't cut much ice , or save it from melting . <h> Advertisement <p> Travelling by train is one the biggest steps you can take to reduce your carbon footprint <p> Not flying is what really makes a difference . A single passenger on a return flight from London to Geneva ( 1,600km ) creates 400kg of CO2 , or four tenths of a tonne , according to the Department for Business , Energy and Industrial Strategy , based on an estimate of 250g of carbon dioxide per passenger per kilometre . By contrast , travel by train or coach reduces carbon emissions to about an eighth of that , ie 50kg , according to EcoSki , a ski tour operator with a focus on environmental responsibility ( ecoski.co.uk ) . <p> There 's another option that allows you to travel with a clearer conscience . You can offset your journey and any other carbon you produce during your holiday by purchasing carbon credits relatively cheaply through websites such as clear.eco , terrapass.co.uk or mycarbonplan.org . The cost of carbon offset through My Carbon Plan is ? 10 a tonne . According to ecollective , a carbon consultancy , this is enough to offset a typical ski trip for a family of four to the French Alps for seven days producing 1.04 tonnes in total . <p> So , if someone offers you disposable sheets to sleep on , you could take the paper out onto the piste and burn them . Well , that 's what I 'll be doing in future . Likewise paper bath towels . I wo n't be ending the week with a pile of empty tuna tins either . In the big scheme of things , it 's pointless . Comfy rail travel is not . So I 'll see you on the platform at St Pancras . Nick Rufford was a guest of La Plagne , which has seven nights ' self-catering for six from ? 758 ( en.la-plagne.com ) . @@118605530 <h> One couple 's dream house dangles precariously over the sea , but they 're confident it will stand the test of time and gravity <p> When Jane Ramsay was a child , she never went abroad on holiday . " <p> Buying a house so close to the river should involve detailed checks , not only on riparian rights , but to assess flood risk . <p> " Buyers should consider the likelihood of flooding when purchasing a property near water , as it can significantly impact both insurance costs and mortgage eligibility , " says Matt Joy , chief growth officer at eConveyancer . " When it comes to selling a property , sellers must be aware that flooding is a key question in the TA6 property information form , part of the conveyancing process . Additionally , any flood risk will be revealed in the environmental report that buyers will receive during due diligence . " <p> In comparison to coastal locations , it 's generally easier to obtain information on inland waterways , Joy adds : " Buyers can typically access details about riverbank and canal ownership , responsibility for repairs and maintenance , fishing rights , water abstraction licenses , drainage rights , liability for river flooding , and rights of way along towpaths . " <h> Advertisement <p> Obtaining buildings and contents insurance is a big worry . " You can look into insurance in advance of buying a property , so you have time to compare quotes and the level of cover , " says a spokesman for the Association of British Insurers ( ABI ) . " Insurers have different ways of assessing risk , and this may be based on their appetite for risk . Some will use sophisticated flood mapping to understand the various levels of risk that there might be from coastal , river or surface water flooding . This mapping can give an indication of the likelihood of your property flooding and how serious the level of flooding may be . " <p> Previous flood claims are a good indication of future flood risk ; but just because a property has n't flooded recently does n't mean that it is not at risk of flooding in the future . " Climate change leading to more frequent , severe and widespread flooding events is also changing the nature of flood risk , " the ABI confirms . <p> Flood Re , a joint initiative between the government and insurers , was established in 2016 to make buildings and contents insurance -- including re-insurance -- for flood-prone or afflicted homes available and more affordable . <p> To qualify for Flood Re the homeowner or their immediate family must live in the property -- the policy is not available to landlords -- and it must have been built before January 2009 . <p> Flood Re will end in 2039 ; industry experts speculate that insurers may not be keen to renew their participation given that weather-related home insurance claims reached a record ? 573 million last year , up 36 per cent in 12 months . <h> Advertisement <p> The view from Melsom 's home at sunset <p> DANIEL BURDETT &amp;AMP ; CHARLOTTE ROSE MELSOM <p> Aaron Jones , a specialist flood risk surveyor from Ashfield Solutions in Wales , says homebuyers are rapidly becoming aware of the need to assess the likelihood of flooding : " What we 've seen in the last six months is a vast advance in interest from people thinking of buying homes near water and wanting to know the risk themselves , rather than waiting for conveyancing . " <p> His company 's flood reports , compiled " by a human " , he emphasises , cost from a couple of hundred pounds , depending on the size of the property . They pull together data from bodies including the Environmental Agency and local authority , topographical information , any previous flood claims and other relevant details . <p> " If the house is located on Watery Lane or Mill Close , that 's a sure indication it 's going to be near water somehow , " he adds . " The amount of properties with water names in the UK is nobody 's business . " <p> He echoes the added-value view : " This desirability to live by a river means that such properties are often of a higher worth . The types of people who buy those properties might be better able to afford the hit should flood damage occur . " <p> Mary Long-Dhonau , property flood resilience champion <p> Jones and Long-Dhonau are involved with the development of flood performance certificates ( FPCs ) . Bringing together partners including the Flood Hazard Research Centre at Middlesex University and Flood Re , the idea is to provide homeowners -- and buyers -- with an invaluable assessment of how individual properties would fare in the event of flooding , and what flood resilience measures have been installed . <p> The ultimate aim is to make an FPC part of the sales pack when a property is sold , like with energy performance certificates ( EPCs ) . The first pilot project has been completed at East Peckham in Kent ; a second pilot , backed by government funding , will take place in Northamptonshire . <p> Such information is becoming ever more urgent . As The Times reported in May , banks have quietly been changing their lending policies on flood-vulnerable properties after a report from the Bank of England in 2021 warned that they should act to limit the financial impact of climate change . <p> Buyers may find it difficult to secure borrowing , and homeowners find mortgage payments massively increasing , or even lending not being renewed when deals come to an end . <p> Since the Bank of England report , lenders have been using a hotchpotch of mapping technology to gather data on the homes of their customers , ascertaining whether they are susceptible to flooding . <p> " In general , lenders tend to be cautious about properties exposed to any environmental risks , including flooding , " Joy says . " As a result they may require more detailed investigations than usual if the property falls into a high-risk category . This can involve additional surveys , insurance requirements or stricter lending terms to ensure the property is adequately protected against potential risks . " <p> Meanwhile , a bigger recognition of the risks has led to a more proactive response towards flood protection , Long-Dhonau says . " We tell people how to plan in case of a flood , with flood doors , anti-flood airbricks , " she explains . " But there is also far more knowledge about how to make a house recover after a flood . There are beautiful flood-recoverable kitchens that can get wet and be washed down again , plasterboard that does n't crumble , glossy plastic skirting boards . People are thinking , ' If we 're at flood risk , what can we do to adapt our homes ? ' . " <p> Flood Re offers its Build Back Better scheme , which enables homeowners to invest in flood resilience measures as part of a claim , over and above work to repair damage and loss caused by a flood . Launched in 2022 , Build Back Better allows homeowners to claim up to ? 10,000 through their insurer to cover the costs . 
@@118605533 <p> Garden pests and diseases are n't limited to spring and summer ; several remain active in autumn , winter , or even all year round . " We 've always had pests and diseases . Gardening is one of those hobbies where something is always trying to eat or destroy your beloved crop , " says Raoul Curtis-Machin , the director of horticulture at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh ( RBGE ) . <p> The danger now is that , as our changing climate brings us wetter and milder winters , pathogens and critters that in the past would have been destroyed or driven into hibernation by the cold hang around for longer . In addition to long-established enemies such as slugs and snails , vine weevil bugs and downy mildew , we now have non-native newcomers to contend with . These include the cold-hardy golden root mealybug and the Asian hornet , which preys on pollinators like bees . <p> " As the weather warms up you ca n't stop these bugs flying across the Channel . Before it was too cold and they were n't spreading , " Curtis-Machin says . <p> First , to minimise risk , buy your plants carefully from a reputable retailer , preferably one that is a member of Plant Healthy , a voluntary biosecurity certification scheme . Before purchasing , inspect the plant 's foliage and if possible its roots , for signs of infestation or fungal disease . <p> Second , in the garden , your best defence against most pests is to encourage in predators . Provide habitats for amphibians , birds , bats , hedgehogs and insects such as ladybirds , beetles and solitary bees , and they will repay you by eating your pests . <h> Advertisement <p> You should also avoid blitzing your plants with chemicals . Pesticides and herbicides kill the good guys along with the bad by poisoning them or destroying their food chain . They also infect the soil , damaging its web of mycorrhizal fungi and microbes essential for plant health . <p> Beer traps can drown slugs who dive in for a bevvy <p> ALAMY <p> If your garden wildlife is n't keeping pests in check , try to tolerate a few and control the rest with natural or chemical-free methods , such as biological controls that rely on natural predators to kill pests . RBGE has been gradually replacing pesticides with natural deterrents . A common complaint among gardeners is that such methods often do not work , but Curtis-Machin insists they will help if used efficiently . <p> For this year 's abundance of slugs and snails , RBGE has been using garlic spray and coffee grounds around plants , which are replenished every three days or after rain . Beer traps -- beer-filled containers placed at surface level -- can drown slugs who dive in for a bevvy . But not always , he admits : " I 've had some luck but not with the bigger , roughty-toughty slugs . I 've actually watched a slug go in , have a damned good drink then come out again and go back onto my hosta leaves . It was one of those giant , brown slugs . There 's no one size fits all . " <p> For potted plants , placing a copper ring around the pot gives off a tiny electrical charge that repels gastropods . " I 've used that myself and it 's worked for years . Every now and again you 'll find it 's been breached ; there might be a crack in the pot or moss or something 's grown over the copper that might deactivate the charge , " says Curtis-Machin . <p> Throw beer-drowned slugs away or on a compost heap . Slugs are nocturnal so another option is to pick them off at night with a torch . Then , as with snails , caterpillars and vine weevil grubs , leave them out for predators in a spot away from your plants . With aphids , you could squash them by hand or spray them with water , but it is better to leave them to be eaten . <h> Advertisement <p> " If you get an explosion of aphids , be patient -- it wo n't be long before ladybirds come along or possibly a blue tit or some of the small birds will come and have a go , " Curtis-Machin says . <p> There are diseases to watch out for too . Phytophthora species cause roots and stem base decay in trees and shrubs , herbaceous perennials , bedding plants and pot plants . Caused by microscopic fungus-like ( oomycete ) organisms , can strike at any time of the year , but is especially prevalent in heavy , waterlogged soils . Unfortunately , symptoms such as wilting , yellowing or sparse foliage , and branch dieback often do n't appear until the decay is well advanced . <p> Confusingly , symptoms can resemble those caused by other issues , such as honey fungus -- the UK 's most destructive fungal disease . Honey fungus attacks the roots of woody and perennial plants , spreading underground through roots and by root rhizomorphs ( commonly known as bootlaces ) that can extend up to 30m . Other symptoms include white fungal growth beneath dead bark , and in some cases , mushrooms sprouting in the autumn . For both diseases , you must dig up and destroy the affected material and soil . If you suspect you have phytophthora , it is important to report it to your local plant health inspector . <p> To minimise the risk of pests and diseases , practise good husbandry . Vigorous plants with enough space , water , nutrients , requisite light and shelter , are better equipped to fight off attacks . Vigilance and prompt action are key . To prevent the spread of disease , immediately remove infected foliage , or in the case of heavy infestations , destroy the plant . Buying pest- and disease-resistant cultivars is also a good idea . <h> Advertisement <p> The UK is under constant threat from potentially devastating non-native nasties -- such as bacterial disease Xylella fastidiosa -- being imported on infected plants and packaging . <p> " It 's crazy that we import so many plants . Growing everything in Britain is the best way of keeping all this stuff at bay , " Curtis-Machin says . <p> One way to do this he suggests , would be to give nurseries that are signed up to Plant Healthy the same tax incentive given to the UK film industry : " So if you expand your nursery you get a tax break . " <p> In return , we gardeners must play our part , he says -- not clamouring about climate change and pollution while simultaneously expecting to snap up imported plants for peanuts . <p> " Plants are ridiculously cheap , grown for three years and only ? 8 or ? 9 . You can get a cheese for that which has taken six months to grow . " <h> Pests to look out for in autumn and winter <p> Controlling pests is a balancing act between protecting plants and preserving a food chain for wildlife . The best approach is to practise good husbandry and vigilance , buy pest- and disease-resistant cultivars , and encourage natural predators into your garden : birds , amphibians , insects and invertebrates , hedgehogs , bats and shrews . If you need to take action , use natural or biological controls rather than pesticides . However , be aware that biological controls are not always risk-free and only work under specific conditions . <p> ALAMY <p> Slugs and snails : To deter them try using copper rings on pots , beer traps , regularly replenished crushed garlic or coffee grounds on soil , or picking them off by hand and leaving out for predators . <p> ALAMY <p> Vine weevil grub : C-shaped , white with a brown head , they feed on the roots , causing plants to wilt eventually die . Regularly check the soil in pot plants , shake out infected roots and leave grubs out for predators . Biological nematodes only work in specific temperatures . Adult vine weevils lay hundreds of eggs during spring and summer . To minimise this , pick the adults off by hand at night or use biological nematodes . <h> Advertisement <p> ALAMY <p> Golden root mealybugs : Cold-hardy and small with yellow waxy body . These suck the sap from the roots of outdoor plants causing them to wilt . Regularly check pot plants and discard heavily infested plants . <p> ALAMY <p> Aphids : These sap suckers can weaken plants and transmit viruses . Encourage predators such as ladybirds and beetles , but first remove any ants as they protect aphids by squashing predators . Otherwise , remove aphids by hand or by spraying them with water . <p> ALAMY <p> Winter moth caterpillars : These feed off foliage and fruitlets in spring , but are vital food for birds . To control bad outbreaks , prevent wingless females from laying eggs in fruit trees in autumn by placing a greasy or glue band round the trunk . Be sure to remove it in the spring . <p> ALAMY <p> Asian hornets : These have a black body with one yellow/orange stripe , yellow legs , and are 2.5-3cm long . They kill bees and other pollinators . If spotted , report them immediately to : alertnonnative@ceh.ac.uk with a photo .

Despite the controversy , Labour MPs voted through the inheritance tax raid on farms this week . <p> While the petrolhead TV star turned celebrity farmer might have been at the forefront of protests hitting the streets of London , by his own admission it is not the genuinely wealthy like Clarkson who would prove to be the ones truly losing out to the tax changes . <p> Instead , it is cash-poor but asset rich farming families who fall through the cracks of the new rules that may be forced to sell off parts or all of their farm in order to fund inheritance tax charges . <p> The changes were intended to close a loophole for wealthy investors buying up farmland , and yet it is not these people that will face the greatest impact of the new rules . <p> Critics say investors may opt to sell farmland and move money elsewhere , or hold onto it , as it still benefits from a 50 per cent discount on inheritance tax . In contrast , for farmers land is an essential ingredient of their business and way of life , which in many cases has been passed down the generations . <p> Those affected have gone from a long-running inheritance tax exemption to facing big bills for death duties , so the move has been hugely controversial . <p> Meanwhile , the government 's figures on the impact have been called into question . We take a look at what the inheritance tax changes mean for farmers , what they can do - and whether there is any chance the new rules might change ? <p> Clarkson 's Harm : TV star Jeremy Clarkson speaks out against the damage of the inheritance tax changes during the farmers ' demonstration <h> Inheritance tax and farmland - the new rules <p> Under the new rules , farmers will lose 100 per cent relief on inheritance tax on agricultural property and business assets . <p> From April 2026 , agricultural and business inheritance tax reliefs will be restricted . Estates will only get full inheritance tax relief on the first ? 1million of combined business and agricultural assets . Above that they will get a 50 per cent relief on the tax rate , meaning inheritance tax will effectively be charged at 20 per cent on assets above the ? 1million threshold . <p> This is still beneficial compared to the 40 per cent rate charged elsewhere . Farmers and landowners will also get the standard inheritance tax-free allowance of ? 325,000 for an individual plus an extra ? 175,000 if their own residence is passed on to a child or grandchild . <p> The ? 1million agricultural relief is per farm owner , so could be doubled up by a married couple , but only if both are still alive and those whose partner is already deceased can not use any of their unused amount , as with standard IHT allowances . <p> In order to qualify for this agricultural property relief , farms must have been owned and used for agricultural purposes for two years if farmed by the owner , or for seven years if rented to a farmer . <p> The eventual inheritance tax bill is payable over a 10-year period , without interest accruing on the outstanding tax . For some , this means that that saving or borrowing could be used to avoid having to sell assets to meet these payments . <h> Why target farmers on inheritance ? <p> The changes come as the new Government looks to prevent farmland being used as an inheritance tax-dodging investment opportunity by the very wealthy looking to protect against a hefty tax bill on their estate at death . <p> Sam Dewes , private client partner at HW Fisher , said : ' While there is some sympathy with the aim of preventing very wealthy taxpayers from claiming APR on valuable land without adding to the rural economy , many farmers -- who are often asset-rich but cash-poor - will never actually realise the value from their land whilst they continue to farm it . <p> ' To protect multi-generational farming families , the proposals could be amended to only limit APR on death when the farm is sold afterwards . That way farmers who hope to continue the business are n't forced to sell up to pay for the tax . ' <p> Less than half of farmland sold now goes to farmers , with private and institutional investors now taking a large chunk , Strutt &amp; Parker 's English Estates &amp; Farmland report reveals <p> As sales to farmers have fallen , the price of farmland has risen substantially - massively outstripping farmers ' profits and driving down yields <p> The number of investors purchasing farmland has increased in recent years , with just 31 per cent of land purchases so far this year having been made by farmers , according to data from Strutt &amp; Parker . <p> Previously , farmers and business owners have been fully exempt from inheritance tax thanks to agricultural and business reliefs , which gave 100 per cent relief on these assets . <p> This relief has been in place for 40 years and was specifically designed to stop family farms having to be broken off or have parts sold off to pay death duties . Many farms are passed through the generations to those willing to take them on and land is an essential element for farming but profits tend to be small . <p> Meanwhile , farms are struggling for income due to high costs , the impacts of climate change and the shift away EU subsidies after Brexit . Farmers are angry as promised new payments have not properly materialised . <p> Craig Rickman , personal finance expert at Interactive Investor , told This is Money : ' It 's not going to affect all farms , but for those that it does affect the tax penalties could be could be quite painful . Although some farms have some pretty serious value to them , not all farmers have cash available . ' <h> Share this article <h> HOW THIS IS MONEY CAN HELP <h> How many farms will be affected ? <p> According to the Treasury , these measures could rake in more than ? 230million for the tax man in its first year and ? 520million a year by 2029 . <p> While Treasury figures claim only 500 or so farms will be affected per year , this is almost a third of the 1,800 current claims for agricultural relief . Over the course of a decade , 5,000 farms would be affected , which compares to just over 200,000 farms in total across the country , according to Defra . <p> The Treasury says only 28 per cent of farms will be affected but one of the major controversies around the inheritance tax raid surrounds these figures on its impact . The National Farmers Union says that Defra 's own figures contradict this , stating that around two-thirds of farms are worth more than ? 1million and therefore potentially affected . <p> An Institute for Fiscal Studies report said : ' However defined -- and therefore whatever the proportions -- it is clear that some farms will be able to be passed on tax-free , while others will attract inheritance tax . <p> ' Those farm owners who do not have a ( surviving ) spouse or civil partner , or who face a higher chance of dying within seven years , have less ability to manage their affairs so as not to pay inheritance tax . ' <p> Farms worth ? 3million can be passed on tax-free if all conditions are met and the farmhouse is left to direct descendants <h> Can farmers really pass on farms worth up to ? 3M ? <p> While IHT is now set to be charged on farm assets above ? 1million , some farmers could increase this threshold up to ? 3million in certain circumstances . <p> For a farm jointly owned by two people , they can combine both of their initial ? 1million tax free agricultural property allowances , along with their standard ? 325,000 nil-rate inheritance tax band and ? 175,000 residence nil-rate band . <p> This requires them to pass ? 1million each of farm assets on at their death , while also using the maximum ? 1million combined inheritance tax-free allowance for a married couple or civil partners to pass on their wealth and own home to children or grandchildren . <p> But their individual estate must not be more than ? 2million , otherwise they will start having their residence nil-rate band removed . <p> In total , this means farms worth ? 3million can be passed on tax-free if left to direct descendants . For non-direct descendants the farm would still be tax free up to ? 2.65million , as the residence nil-rate bands would not be available . <p> It is worth noting that some farms wo n't qualify for these extras if they do n't have a home on the farm or one worth enough to benefit , or if they are unmarried or do n't have a surviving spouse or civil partner . <p> Crucially , couples passing on assets worth ? 3million must do so separately , passing the first ? 1million allowance to a descendant when one member of a couple dies , as this allowance can not be used by the surviving spouse . <p> Critics have attacked the complexity of these scenarios when ministers have put forward the ? 3million figure as a reason why most farmers should not be concerned about inheritance tax . <p> They also create a scenario where farms may end up jointly owned for a period of time by different members of a family , who may hold opposing views on how the farm should be run . <p> Family farms are also not always passed to children or grandchildren , sometimes they go to whichever family member is willing to be a farmer . <p> The IFS said : ' A typical couple might expect to be able to use both of their ? 1 million allowances . But people will not inherit any unused part of the ? 1 million allowance from a deceased spouse or civil partner , like they do with the nil-rate band and residence nil-rate band . <p> ' So , to use both partners ' allowances , each must separately bequeath at least ? 1 million of the property to others ( e.g. children ) . <p> ' That means splitting ownership of the property between family members on or before the death of the first partner , rather than bequeathing the whole thing when one of them dies . It will also disadvantage families where one member of the couple has already passed away . <p> ' There is a good case for making unused portions of the ? 1 million allowance inheritable by a spouse or civil partner . ' <p> Protest : Farmers took to the streets of Westminster to demonstrate against the Government 's tax changes <h> What about business relief ? <p> Some farmers have also previously used Business Property Relief on some of their farm 's assets . <p> In order to make use of BPR , a farm must be a working business that has been owned for at least two years before the transfer . <p> The business must not mainly make holding investments or deal in land or buildings . This means that farms purchased for investment purposes do not qualify as trading businesses . <p> However , under the new rules both APR and BPR fall under the same ? 1million allowance from 2026 , meaning that farmers can not benefit from both . <h> How can farmers mitigate their tax bill ? <p> Aside from making use of the available reliefs to the greatest possible extent , there are ways that farmers can plan ahead to cut their inheritance tax bill . <p> Farmers can make use of the seven year gifting rule to pass their farm on long before they die so that it is free from inheritance tax . <p> However , if a farmer still lives and farms on the property , then this may be considered a gift with reservation of benefit , meaning that inheritance tax could still be chargeable . <p> To prevent this , the owner could only pass on some of the farm and then not derive a benefit from that part , although this may seeriously impact their income . <p> If handing over the entire farm and house , they would need to move out of the property or pay a market rent , and not take income from the farm . <p> With the clock starting now on gifts for something that was previously inheritance tax-free , understandably those whose spouses may have already died , or are in ill-health , and are unable to make use of the seven year rule feel put out by the new rules . <p> The IFS , which broadly supports the inheritance tax changes , said that the government should consider changing this . <p> It said : ' If the government wished to give current farm owners the same opportunity to avoid inheritance tax that owners of other assets have , it could do so by transitioning to the new regime more slowly . <p> ' For example , lifetime gifts of agricultural property made before a certain future date could be made inheritance tax free , regardless of the timing of the death of the giver , so that those farm owners who pass away in the next seven years have an opportunity to make tax-avoiding gifts in light of the Budget changes . <p> ' This would reduce the revenue raised from the policy , but this would be one-off , rather than permanent , reduction in the revenue raised . ' <p> Farmers also face a potential capital gains tax if the value of the farm has increased since you acquired it . Typically , the farmhouse , as a main residence , would be exempt from this , benefitting from Principal Private Residence Relief , but other properties , assets and land may not be . <p> The farm could qualify for holdover relief , which means the CGT liability passes to the recipient of the gift to pay on the total gain when they eventually dispose of the property . <h> Share or comment on this article : How badly will Labour 's inheritance tax raid hit family farms - and what can they do ? <p> Some links in this article may be affiliate links .
