" ) <p> The latter approach -- which helped make the Noughties stage ver ? sion of Wicked a $ ? 1 billion hit -- still strikes a chord ( even if your critic was one of only a handful not to be enraptured ) . In the UK , Wicked took ? 13.7 million on its opening weekend , setting a record for the year . <p> Disney 's hairpin turn on this is especially telling , since , in the 2010s , the studio planted itself in the vanguard of progressive blockbusting . ( Judging by the recent trailer , the forthcoming live-action Snow White remake , announced barely a week before the 2016 election but delayed by reshoots and industrial action , already feels like a relic from another age , even though it has n't actually come out yet . ) <p> Look at the iron grip exerted by the studio 's execs on Inside Out 2 , a make-or-break project for the once unstoppable Pixar , which had entered 2024 on its wobbliest footing in 35 years . Lightyear , its post-Covid comeback film , had spectacularly bombed : the likeliest causes were a confusing premise and a gloomy vibe , though certain online reactionaries blamed a brief same-sex kiss between Buzz 's female commanding officer and her wife . <p> Inside Out 2 became the most successful animation ever released this year Credit : Pixar <p> Apparently , studio bosses agreed . Inside Out 2 became not only the biggest film of 2024 by an enormous margin , but the most successful animation ever released . ( Even as an admirer of the sequel and all-out worshipper of the original , I have yet to get my head around this . ) You do n't have to be a marketing guru to work out what lesson the entire industry will learn from that . <p> Though the unwokening of Inside Out 2 reportedly began in September last year , after the Hollywood writers ' strike was resolved , it was n't until the morning after the 2024 US election that the studios ' predicament snapped into relief . No one summed it up better than Richard Rushfield , the author of the trade newsletter The Ankler : " We are talking to people with a Marvel ? Cinematic Universe voice , " he wrote on November 7 , " while we were living in a YouTube world . " <p> In other words , shiny corporate progressivism is out . And auth ? enticity -- or at least a winking ? pantomime of it -- is in . Again , Moana 2 was ahead of the curve here , with its cheerfully meaningless TikTok-ready catchphrase , " Can I get a chee hoo ? Not so long ago , that might have been considered piracy : in 2024 , it 's called engagement . As for the film itself , it was horrendous -- and enormous . Only Inside Out 2 sold more tickets this year . <p> So this was the year Hollywood finally grasped the nature of the battle into which it had previously launched itself . But in the movies themselves , it still took an outsider to capture it properly . In his extraordinary thriller Civil War , Britain 's Alex Garland imagined a near-future US tearing itself apart along partisan lines . Here , the divisions were as intractable as they were inscrutable . An embattled " third-term president " , played by Nick Offerman , clung on to power while his loyalist troops were being pummelled by a breakaway alliance , led by the improbable pairing of California and Texas . <p> The genius of Garland 's film lay in its refusal to set out the aims and ideologies of its two feuding factions , denying its audience the easy comfort of picking a side . Rather , it forced us to reckon with the machinations and temptations of division itself . <p> Appearing at the newly ? resurgent Edinburgh International Film Festival in August , Garland lamented the " idiotic " takes from some quarters that framed Civil War 's refusal to sort the world into goodies and bad ? dies as a dereliction of artistic duty -- when in fact that refusal represented one of the most pressing points that cinema in 2024 could make . <p> Kirsten Dunst and Cailee Spaeny in Civil War <p> Note , however , that " no sides " is a very different position from " both sides " , and since the latter is by far the more commercially advantageous , it 's probably the one we 'll encounter most in the year ahead . Indeed , as the 2025 Oscar season cranks up , the hedging has already begun . Sebastian Stan , who starred in the Donald Trump biopic The Apprentice , was unable to take part in Variety 's annual series of Actors on Actors interviews . Why ? Because no publicists would allow their clients to be paired with him and risk having to talk about the film and its subject . <p> Trump himself described The Apprentice as a " cheap , defamatory , and politically disgusting hatchet job " -- high praise from a master of the form . Yet while the film fared reasonably well in British and French cinemas , it struggled to find much of an audience at home , not helped by a furious cease and desist order from its subject 's legal team , which successfully scared off all the big distributors and streamers . <p> Of course it 's deeply annoying that so much popular cinema is in thrall to another nation 's political conniptions . Again , that 's why Twisters came as such a breath of fresh air , so to speak : it could have almost blown in from the same ? decade that yielded its 28-year-old forerunner , released when " American " still meant an attitude as cool and sweet and covetable as an ice-cold Coke , rather than the pretext for yet another argument .

" <p> Robbie Williams with his wife Ayda Field at the European premiere of Better Man in London Credit : Dave Benett/WireImage <p> As his introduction at the New York screening acknowledged , Williams is significantly less famous in America than in most of the world . " <p> Robbie Williams performing at the Better Man European premiere after party at Lio London on Nov 27 Credit : Dave Benett/Getty Images <p> Listening to the questions Williams faces as he promotes this movie , the general assumption seems to be that Better Man 's existence is the culmination of some hefty strategic planning -- that a day came when he or his people decided that the time was ripe in his life and career to consolidate and amplify his success with a big movie biopic . But , in truth , there 's relatively little Williams has ever done , for better or worse , that has involved such naked strategising . It 's usually a combination of following his instincts and pure happenstance . And Better Man is a perfect example of this . <p> The first seed was sown , by chance , years ago when Williams went with his wife Ayda to a Los Angeles party hosted by the parents of her childhood best friend . Her friend 's father , Robert Wallerstein , is an entertainment lawyer , and Williams was chatting to one of his clients -- an Australian visual effects whizz kid who was looking to direct his first movie . This was Michael Gracey . Gracey started acting out a film he then hoped to make , the tale of the Muppets creator Jim Henson . Williams was captivated . When they 'd meet , Williams would tell -- as he often does -- remarkable , Byzantine stories of his past , and after a while Gracey had a suggestion . " <p> It 's a constant irony of Robbie Williams ' career that , perhaps because he makes pop music for broad audiences , and leans hard into the tropes of entertainment rather than finding them something to disguise , people presume that his most important decisions are calculating and considered . Whether triumphant or otherwise , they rarely are . They are far more likely to reflect the mindset of a man who says " not everything has to be explained , or understood , or make sense " . <p> The trailer for Better Man that audiences see in Britain assumes a certain amount of prior knowledge on the part of those watching it . A realistic presumption . Inevitably , the American trailer needed to explain more . But when Williams was sent the initial draft of his proposed voiceover ... well , he was n't thrilled . <p> I 'm Robbie Williams ! it went . I was one of the biggest pop stars in the world .... <p> He remembers his reaction : " No ! Not past tense , thanks . Fuck off ! " I am in that land , definitely perception-wise , " he says . " The ' are you still doing music ? ' kind of thing . " He relates a conversation he had a few months ago with a British man in Dubai , amiable enough until the man blindsided him with a question . <p> " Do you miss it ? " the man asked . <p> " Miss what ? " Williams countered . <p> " Singing . " <p> There was no easy way forward from there , so Williams just stated the facts <p> " I said , ' Mate , I 'm doing a world tour next year , I 'm in stadiums . I 've just finished a tour . No . And when they come along , the default Robbie Williams strategy tends to be some combination of trying earnestly to understand and analyse them , and to squeeze from the situation every last drop of amusement and absurdity they allow . Which brings us to the story of 22 June 2024 : The Day Robbie Williams Was n't Recognised . <p> On that particular day , he and Ayda were meeting some new friends for lunch . They dressed up smartly , and headed off . On the way there , it turned out that the traffic was all snarled up ( there was a climate change-related protest in central London ) , so Ayda suggested they get out and walk . Her husband reminded her what a bad decision , based on all previous experience , this would be . " I said to her , ' Robbie Williams ? In a pink suit ? In London ? Walking ? You mad ? ' " But after lunch , there was simply no choice at all . If they wanted to get home , they would have to do so on foot . So out they ventured into the Saturday streets , bracing themselves for what would surely follow . <p> Except that things did n't go as expected . <p> After a while , it all seemed so very strange that Ayda got out her phone and started filming what was happening . Or , rather , what was not happening . <p> " So this is very concerning , " Robbie commentated , glancing at the lens as he walked . " I 'm dressed completely in pink . I 've got pink sneaks on . I 've got diamant ? sunglasses . " He got to the point . " Absolutely nobody has recognised me , or bothered me , and I really need them to . " He stood there , in fully visible Robbie Williams mode , as people walked past . " It was n't like this in the ' 90s , " he muttered . <p> ' It was n't like this in the ' 90s ' : Williams fondly recalls the experience of no longer being recognised in the street ... even in a pink suit Credit : Leo Baron <p> In a second video he lay on the grass next to a pathway , to equal indifference . In a third he bought an ice cream at a stand where , absurdly , the radio was playing " Let Me Entertain You " . Nothing . ( To add to the surreality , all of this was taking place in Hyde Park , where two weeks later he would play a sold-out concert to 60,000 people . ) In a fourth video , he was finally approached by a French woman who asked for a selfie . " Back in the game , " he announced , with muted triumph . <p> These videos were posted on Instagram . Then , the next day , he went out again , with Ayda once more filming , this time wearing a shirt with ROBBIE WILLIAMS on the back . " I wanted to see whether that was just a moment in time that was odd or whether that 's my new reality , " he tells me . " Because my reality since 2003 is : it 's not safe out there for me . And maybe now , awkwardly , it is ! " This second experiment was a success . Or , I guess , a failure , depending on which way you look at it . In that he was recognised . In that he was able to confirm , he says , " I 'm still Robbie Williams . " <p> All of this is ridiculous , of course , and in the videos it 's clear that he knows as much . So I guess one could try to argue that he is serving up a brilliant satire of narcissism , self-obsession , and egotism , rather than embodying these qualities . But I 'm not sure it 's quite that straightforward either , or that he would even try to claim or accept that . For on one hand , as he points out : " We 're poking fun at my own ego . We 're letting you in . Because if it really was just egotistical , it would n't be for public consumption . I would n't publish the results . " But on the other hand what he wrote on Instagram at the time showed he was well aware of the irony in finding himself " actively welcoming and seeking the thing that I 've spent the last 30 years desperately hiding from " -- and then , of course , aware of the further irony of immediately sharing the whole experience with his 3.1 million followers . <p> And he 's too honest , and too interested in describing the actual contours of his reality , even when not necessarily flattering , to pretend that the initial experience had n't truly rattled him . <p> " I got to feel what it felt like -- I did n't like it , " he says of his blip of anonymity . " That genuinely affected me . Not a joke ... I was worried . Because I 've got so much wrapped up in Robbie Williams being Robbie Williams . " <p> Williams , far left , pictured with his Take That bandmates in 1992 . He has spoken in interviews about feeling like a ' performing monkey ' Credit : Getty <p> The monkey that is Robbie Williams is created by Weta FX , the New Zealand digital effects house behind The Lord of the Rings and Avatar movies , and is mostly based on motion-capture footage of a young actor , Jonno Davies , though Williams ' body was filmed for some scenes too . Gracey says that the eyes are Williams ' -- " incredibly high-res scans of Rob 's real eyes ' " -- and that much of the monkey 's voice in the finished film is taken from the original audio of his interview with Williams . <p> It 's uncannily effective , but it nonetheless became clear , as the film neared release , that the world might require a more explicit explanation of exactly why Williams was a monkey , beyond it simply making some kind of grand intuitive sense . In service of this , both Williams and Gracey would describe in interviews another part of that initial discussion where Gracey asked Williams what his spirit animal was . Williams ' first answer was that he was a lion ( ' I was trying to find some self-worth for myself , ' he says ) , but when Gracey indicated that this was the wrong answer , Williams immediately hit on the " correct " one : monkey . <p> Gracey says that Williams talked in their interviews about feeling like a performing monkey , and Williams argues that this choice makes sense of how he always felt : " I 'm other . I feel like I 'm something else . " In general terms , Williams also points out that despite " the luxury of centuries of technology and where we find ourselves " , it makes plenty of sense to depict him as not so far removed from who we have all evolved from . " I 'm in a bungalow in the Beverly Hills Hotel , " he reflects , " but let 's not forget , we are cavemen . I 'm just wearing Gucci . " <p> Anyway , once you see the movie , these kinds of questions fade away . As improbable as it may seem , it simply works . You might think that the lead character being a monkey in a world of humans would be never-endingly distracting , but in fact somehow the opposite is true . It beckons you in . Later , trying to figure out why it works so effectively , I realised that often what 's much more distracting in other movies like this is that a part of your brain is forever monitoring how an actor is succeeding or failing to represent a famous figure you think you know . Somehow the monkey takes that off the table . <p> Williams recalls that he did n't ' overthink ' the creative process of the film , during which Gracey recorded 12 hours of stories and memories <p> There is another way , too , as Michael Gracey has pointed out , in which telling the story through a monkey counter-logically -- because of " the empathy we have for animals and watching animals in pain " -- actually makes it easier , not harder , to feel the human story being told . " I think we 're very cinematically numb to seeing human suffering , " Gracey reasons . " But when we see an animal hurting , there is something very uncomfortable about that . " <p> Historically , movies telling stories about musicians with their involvement are obliged to have a heroic sheen . Here again , Better Man , to its credit , may not be what people expect . Hero moments do arrive eventually , but the movie its subject describes as " the greatest hits of my trauma " spends most of its time elsewhere . " I think there may be a heart to this movie that is missing from a lot of biographies because people are scared , " Williams suggests . " I think where other people are sanitising their biographies for the sake of the intellectual property , I do n't have the sense to do that . I 'm not a good guy in this movie . I know people feel for me in this movie , but I 'm egoic and wrong , all the way through , really , till the end . " <p> To tell the story in this way , Gracey plays fast and loose with chronology and various real-world facts -- and interposes some dazzling surreal episodes -- and yet the end result convincingly conveys a really specific , sometimes near-unbearable emotional truth . <p> " All of it felt that way , " explains Williams , noting that it 's important " for the general public to know that , of course , it 's cinematic , and of course , there are tricks , but they 're not being hoodwinked . Like I say : that 's how it felt . " <p> One morning , Robbie Williams awakes in his Beverly Hills Hotel bungalow and heads out on foot , across Sunset Boulevard . He has another full day 's schedule promoting Better Man ahead of him , but before that , he wants to have his photograph taken in a public toilet . To properly explain exactly why ... well , we need to go back a few years , when Jason Williamson , singer with the caustic , rambunctious Nottingham group Sleaford Mods , tweeted about something which was irking him : If I look at Robbie Williams in a photo for too long it sends me into a rage . <p> " Some people can slag me off , " says Williams , " and I get deeply wounded and retaliate . " Truth is , in some circumstances , he 's truly world class at nursing a grudge . Now and then , he will bring up a throwaway condescending comment that some snooty musician made about him in the 1990s as though he 's no less angry about it than on the day it was said . But it very much depends on who 's doing the condescending . With some people , his fury knows no bounds . " Other people , " he points out , " I 'm just really proud they know who I am . " <p> So it was with this Jason Williamson barb . " Because I was really into the Sleaford Mods before -- I was an early adopter , " Williams explains , " I was like ' Wow , Jason from the Sleaford Mods knows who I am ! ' It 's like when Morrissey said , ' I think everything about Robbie Williams is fantastic , except the voice and the songs . ' I was just ' Awww , Morrissey knows who I am ... ! ' " <p> So , in response , Williams simply retweeted Williamson 's original tweet along with the reply Rage ? I can never get past shame . #goals x . <p> That opened a door . He and Williamson subsequently exchanged emails and began to intermittently chat . And it was with Williamson , last year , that the toilet idea first came up . " He was thinking about doing some art while he was on tour , " says Williams , " and I had this idea for him where he just draws all of the toilets that he visits , for no other reason that it 's funny . And I sent him one of me on the toilet in Latvia . " <p> But then , when Williamson did n't seem to embrace the concept , Williams decided to do it himself . <p> In recent years Williams has done about two thousand drawings , mostly on his iPad : typically some kind of image combined with text , veering from scabrous and coarse to wry and witty , from scattershot and surreal to empathic reflective . ( A recent landscape folded into the words : " I want all of the attention and at the same time none at all . " ) He 's quietly serious about it -- most of the images he makes public appear on Instagram , but in the past year he has also had gallery shows in Amsterdam and Barcelona . Sometimes he does a series of related drawings , and that 's what the toilet images have become . <p> Despite his initial reticence to reveal his art publicly , Williams has enjoyed two successful solo shows in Amsterdam and Barcelona this year Credit : Moco Museum Amsterdam <p> He posted the first cache of these images -- Toilets of the Summer 2024 -- in September : it included drawings of himself on a toilet at Heathrow airport , in a rented villa in Provence , in Tahiti , in Amsterdam 's Conservatorium hotel , in LAX airport , and on a plane " somewhere between Monaco and Zurich " . These images are n't salacious or obscene , just rather surreal . Their creation , however , does require a certain weird etiquette issue . As he fashions these images by drawing over photos on an iPad programme called Procreate , each image requires a photograph of him in situ , and so those in his orbit are sometimes requested to help , with understandably varying degrees of discomfort . <p> Staying here at the Beverly Hills Hotel offers a particular opportunity for the ongoing Toilets of the Fall 2024 series , one he feels unable to spurn . Just south of here is Will Rogers State Memorial Park , within which is a toilet that has a highly charged place in pop iconography -- it was here that , in 1998 , George Michael was arrested by an undercover police officer for performing a " lewd act " . That 's where Williams visits this morning -- today with an actual photographer friend in tow for a very brief photo session " and to see the scene of that moment " . But he does n't linger : " I do n't want to be arrested before my film comes out . " <p> Back in his hotel room , a package has arrived with his name on . <p> " Are you expecting anything , Rob ? " he is asked . <p> " No , ' he says . Deadpan pause . " Apart from a knighthood . " <p> Williams says there are ' tricks ' in the events depicted in film , but the public are not being ' hoodwinked ' by the emotional truth it conveys <p> Many of the American interviewers almost seem taken aback by just how much Robbie Williams will share , and how readily . In one interview , he is praised for how he 's managed to open up . But he rebuffs the premise . He points out that , for him , that 's the easy part . <p> " I 'm not closed ! " he retorts . " I 'm open 24 hours a day ! This is n't hard for me . This is n't brave . This is n't any of those things that people are saying . " <p> " This is f -- king breathing for me , " he points out . " This is easy . I do n't know why . And it 's only when it 's pointed out that it 's unusual , I go , ' Oooh , is it ? ' I think it 's braver and dumber to not be so revealing . And more self-harming to not air the dark corners of your life . I suppose if you 're experiencing shame , like I do , you want to release the shame . It 's like a valve . To receive the best experience possible , please make sure any ad blockers are switched off , or add https : **25;1843;TOOLONG to your trusted sites , and refresh the page . <p> Climate scientists agree that severe flooding was probably driven by climate change resulting in record-breaking rainfall . Warmer temperatures increase the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere , especially over warmer oceans , which increases the amount of rainfall . Europe is projected to experience a greater frequency of severe floods , potentially with dire consequences to economies and livelihoods . <p> It 's challenging to reduce flood risk in Europe because of the high density of population and economic activities within flood-prone lands , as well as substantial cultural heritage . Flood risk has increased in Europe largely because people have moved into protected areas that were formerly flood prone , referred to as the " levee effect " . <p> Implementing effective flood management is also difficult because not all floods are the same . Broadly , Europe is impacted by three main types of flood processes : fluvial , pluvial and coastal storm surge . <p> Pluvial flooding occurs when local rainfall is not adequately drained , fields in rural areas become saturated , while flash floods can occur in urban areas . Excessive local rainfall is especially a problem over lowland rivers and deltas during wet winter months , as saturated lands do not permit drainage of additional rainfall and run-off , leading to local flood problems . <p> The most challenging floods to manage are caused by multiple flood processes . Last winter in the lower Rhine basin in Germany and the Netherlands , three flood processes combined to produce flooding ( high water ) , saturating fields and substantially impacting agricultural activities for months . <p> For the first time since its construction in 1997 , the huge Maeslant barrier at the mouth of the Rhine River near Hook of Holland , had to close to manage a storm surge . <h> Three key steps <p> Reducing flood risk in Europe will require massive investment that includes a basin-wide management approach , as recommended in the EU floods directive . In addition to greater focus on nature-based solutions , such as returning agricultural lands to natural vegetation , a unique combination of hard ( structural ) and soft ( policy ) measures are needed to reduce flood risk within a given river basin . <p> While flooding from extreme rainfall in Europe can not be avoided , the risk and devastation can be reduced . In Valencia , Spain , people were not given enough advanced warning of floods . The first step must be to improve public early warning systems and raise awareness so that people take flood alerts seriously . <p> Upper river basin measures may include improved land-use planning , such as afforestation ( planting trees where there were none before ) , to reduce run-off . Reservoirs can be used to either hold back water to reduce downstream transmission of floodwaters or to release reservoir water before arrival of the flood wave . <p> Lower basin approaches should include redesign of hydraulic infrastructure ( such as dykes , groynes , bridges ) downstream to accommodate both higher peak and longer-duration floods . Areas that are allowed to flood can be expanded . This is being done effectively in the Netherlands , as part of the Room for the River programme , which restores the floodplains . <p> The approach was shown to be successful during the devastating European floods of July 2021 . The flooding overwhelmed centuries-old villages along Meuse ( Maas ) River basin headwaters in parts of northern Germany , Belgium , Luxembourg and France , and resulted in more than 200 fatalities . <p> But further downstream in the Netherlands , floodwaters caused much less damage thanks to the Dutch Room for the River scheme . While Maas River floodwaters attained high levels , they were contained and did not overtop the dykes , protecting riverside communities . Enhancing the natural buffering effect of floodplains can reduce the severity of downstream flooding . <p> While long-term strategies to improve flood management are expensive , the personal and financial cost of ineffective flood management is much higher . European nations need to be vigilant , forward-thinking and proactive about implementing effective flood management . <p> Hello . @@118890678 <h> Swing to the right : Is it ' Nazi ' to say Scotland needs babies and less immigration ? <h> Is it ' Nazi ' to say Scotland needs more babies and less immigration ? <p> Leading conservative voices have now entered the fray on the fertility crisis , proposing policies that will both rile and offend progressives -- from encouraging women to have more babies to severely limiting migration <p> Right-wing thinkers have turned their attention to Britain 's declining population . Our Writer at Large talks to them about their controversial beliefs and the policies they back as a fix <p> IF demography is destiny , then Britain -- and Scotland in particular -- is in trouble . The UK is rapidly ageing , and not enough children are being born . Consequently , we depend on cheap migrant workers , especially in the care industry . That 's exploited by the far right , creating division . <p> So what 's the answer ? Well , there are not many ideas from the left . Ground has been ceded to the right . <p> Leading conservative voices have now entered the fray proposing policies that will both rile and offend progressives -- from encouraging women to have more babies to severely limiting migration . It 's a recipe for more culture war . <p> To exacerbate matters , the two big conservative thinkers on the issue are men . Their comments will undoubtedly offend feminists and anti-racist campaigners . <p> Paul Morland is one of Britain 's leading demographers . His latest books -- No-one Left : Why the World Needs More Children , and Tomorrow 's People : the Future of Humanity in Ten Numbers -- chart the demography crisis . He proposes a " pro-natalist " response . <p> That means encouraging women to have more babies . Morland calls himself someone from " the old right " . <p> Britain is n't alone in the population crisis . Most Western nations fare badly . It 's Africa which bucks the trend . " Sub-Saharan Africa will go from about 7% of the world 's population in 1950 to 38% in 2100 . " <p> Morland adds : " Countries that are very poor are seeing life expectancy extend , and infant mortality tumble . " <p> Paul Morland . Photo : Frank Monks <p> In more prosperous nations , including China , the increase in city living has decreased fertility rates . " One of the characteristics of urban humanity is falling fertility rates , " Morland explains . <p> " As people get better educated and richer , they 're more able to control fertility and aspire to more material lifestyles . " <p> South Korea is in dire straits . It has a birth rate where for every 100 people , 33 children are born . If that trend continues , the next generation will see 11 children per every 100 people . <p> Soon , Morland adds , South Korea will " lose 90% of the population . That 's transformational for everything -- the economy , education and welfare . We 're just not used to a world where over the course of 50 years , 90% of people just disappear " . <p> The world is configured around " gentle population growth , but what we 're going to see is rapid population decline " . <p> Burden <p> Britain 's fertility rate hovers around 1.4 . Scotland is worse off at around 1.3 . Those numbers make little sense until you understand that for nations to maintain their population , a fertility rate of 2.1 is required . That 's " the replacement level " . <p> Lower than 2.1 and populations age and decline , placing huge burdens on the young . The average age of new parents in Britain has grown to 33.8 for men and 30.9 for women . <p> In the 1930s , in Catalonia , Spain , the median age was in the mid-20s . Today it 's in the mid-40s . Japan , with a fertility rate of around 1.2 , has about 95,000 people aged over 100 . " We 're getting these very old societies where it 's very difficult for governments to pay pensions and provide healthcare , " says Morland . Japan has among the highest debt-to-GDP ratios in the world at 250% . <p> One way of offsetting ageing populations and low birth rates is using immigrant workers . <p> " But that comes with extremely fast ethnic change " , says Morland . Nations like Britain face a " trilemma " : choosing between " low fertility rates and small families , economic growth , and ethnic continuity -- but you ca n't have all three " . <p> He points to Japan where there are few immigrants , few babies , and it 's " falling off an economic cliff . Britain , which wants to keep the economy growing , is also not committed to large families , and therefore we have rapid immigration " . <p> He states bluntly : " My challenge to indigenous communities which do n't want to see themselves becoming a minority is : you 'd better breed or go the Japanese route . " <p> In terms of Britain , Morland says : " Scotland has more deaths than births . In England , there 's a tiny margin of more births than deaths , but that 's outweighed by Scotland , so Britain now has more deaths than births . " <p> He adds : " We 're going to run out of people . We 're going to go extinct if we all end up like South Korea . <p> " This is n't just a European problem -- it 's gone global . " <p> His answer is that women need to have more children . Morland insists he 's not proposing returning to the 1950s , although he 's aware his proposals will be deemed sexist and extreme by some . <p> He wants to encourage more births with policies like " tax breaks for those with children , which might mean higher taxes for those without children " . <p> Morland says " feminists " will object and " accuse " him of " misogyny " , yet he claims there 's a " good feminist case for pro-natalism . Many women want more children " . He wants to " rebut this idea that anyone pro-natalist is a back-to-the-kitchen , 1950s , right-wing misogynist " . <p> Many progressives , however , see immigration as an alternative solution . " I say no , " Morland replies . " Countries which are the source of immigration from Mexico to India are seeing plunging fertility rates . We should n't plunder them . We should n't be relying on immigrants -- on other people having children , educating them , and then we import their labour . " <p> Struggle <p> THE population crisis " manifests itself in labour shortages and ageing . We 're going from four to three workers per retiree , we can see two looming . In Japan , we see one looming . Societies will struggle when they 've got one or two workers per retiree as opposed to the four or five we had earlier in the 20th century " . <p> In terms of the population crisis , Britain is " in the middle of the pack " . We 're similar to America . Other nations are worse , like Italy , and some " slightly better , like France " . Morland notes that the French government is " pro-natalist " . <p> He adds : " We ca n't reverse what 's happening until we acknowledge the problem and start addressing it culturally , societally and politically . " <p> How bad can it get ? " No-one knows where the bottom is , but the lowest we 've ever seen is two-thirds of a child per woman in South Korea . " <p> These population changes " reverse the demographic pyramid " . Rather than more young people at the bottom and fewer older people at the top , the pyramid flips . That leads to " helter-skelter " population decline . <p> China will " lose 40-50% of its people by the end of the century " . <p> Not only does the pyramid reverse , it also shrinks , leaving fewer young people supporting the elderly . There has never been such an event in history , Morland says . Even during the Black Death -- which killed a third of Europeans -- deaths occurred across generations . It was n't just the young dying , leaving millions of elderly . <p> " If we try to keep our current welfare states , it effectively means enslaving the young , " Morland believes . He thinks that would trigger a youth exodus . <p> " Why would they hang around to be taxed to pay pensions and dragooned into looking after the elderly ? But I think before we get there , our welfare systems will break down and just wo n't be affordable . " <p> He fears this will mean " many old people neglected and impoverished " . Cities could become like " Detroit " where the population leaves and urban centres " rot away . Government debt wo n't be payable . That will have serious economic consequences " . <p> Morland speculates this could have an effect on law and order . The future could be " dystopian . Think of A Clockwork Orange " . <p> Meanwhile , African nations experiencing higher fertility rates of around 4.5 , would become the source of the migrant labour the West requires for its ageing populations . <p> Riots <p> MORLAND says Brexit , the rise of Reform and Donald Trump , and recent far-right riots were " about immigration " . He has " sympathy " for opponents of " root-and-branch ethnic change in their society " . <p> He adds : " But my argument back to them is : bear in mind the demographic and fertility side of the equation . It 's not just about stopping people coming . <p> " If you are n't having children of your own , you either go into obscurity like Japan or inevitably you 'll have mass immigration and ethnic change . A community , society , culture nation that does n't reproduce is consigning itself to the dustbin of history . " <p> He stresses he does n't sympathise with rioters . " Our whole economic model , " Morland says , " is built upon the assumption that populations will steadily grow . That 's not happening any more -- not without mass immigration anyway . " <p> However , would there be such anti-immigrant sentiment in Britain , if politicians discussed the matter rationally ? If governments explained migration 's benefits , and did n't demonise migrants , would n't it be a fix for the population crisis ? <p> Morland replies : " In the long term , no . You ca n't just bring in more and more people . " As immigrant populations arrive , in time their fertility rates also fall . " You just have to bring in the next mass cohort . I do n't think there 's any precedent historically for a nation which , among other characteristics , has at least a myth of common ancestry , becoming a minority within its own homeland , without some people questioning , resisting or opposing it . " <p> Aware that his comments are politically incendiary , Morland says " politicians are working very hard on the bromides and kumbayas . They 've been quite effective so far , but they ca n't go on forever . I think people will resist . Maybe they 're wrong to resist , or think Britain should be predominantly white British to use the category of the census " . <p> He continues : " Some people might believe that it 's perfectly natural and normal to think the majority of the population should remain that ethnicity , and others may say that 's unacceptable or racist , that ethnicity and culture does n't matter . But I think the latter view is one that is n't historically normal . <p> " Maybe we 'll all very rapidly become liberal cosmopolitans but to expect the whole population to buy that within a generation or two is probably unrealistic . I speak as a son of immigrants . I 'm conscious that I 've no ancestor born in these islands . " <p> Both his parents were Jewish refugees from Germany . " I 'm not part of the white British majority , but I do n't expect the white British majority -- all of them unquestioningly , and just because politicians say it 's the right thing -- to say our majority in our own homeland is of no significance to us . " <p> Far right <p> LET 's be frank , however . Many will see this pro-natalist approach as distinctly far right . Wo n't they ? <p> " The first thing is to have some historical perspective , " Morland says . " The Nazis were pro-natalist , but so was Stalin , so was Mao , so was Mitterrand . Macron is pro-natalist . You 've pro-natalists left , right and centre -- so why in the British brain it seems to be associated particularly with the Nazis , I 've no idea . " <p> Morland adds : " The left used to believe in families , in children , in supporting women in childbearing , in child benefit <p> -- all of those things were mainstream for Clement Attlee . If Attlee whose government created the welfare state tried to introduce child benefit today , he 'd be called cisnormative . There 's a madness that 's affected parts of the English-speaking world that if you 're pro-natal you must be far right . It takes no account of what women actually want . " <p> Morland insists surveys show that most women want " two to three children . I just do n't know where all this lunacy comes from , why it all gets associated with Nazi Germany . It 's just ignorance , I 'm afraid " . <p> He adds : " If you say you 're feminist and care about women but you do n't care about this , you 're ignoring what women want . Across Europe and North America , these surveys have been consistent . Women want to have a child more than they 're having today . " <p> Morland 's ideas have already been accused , he says , of having " the whiff of the Brown Shirt " . What he proposes is , he insists , simply " repeating the most fundamental ethics of Judeo-Christian Abrahamic religion " . <p> He makes clear that if women have more children then " men have to step up " , and criticises nations like Greece and Japan which he calls " patriarchal " as women " are n't given equality in the workforce " . <p> Some of the West 's highest fertility rates until recently were in " progressive Scandinavia " , which has strong workplace protections , good childcare , world-class welfare , and shared parental leave . However , even Scandinavia is now seeing falling fertility rates due to Gen Z 's " cultural swing " away from having children . <p> British childcare is " far too expensive " . Government needs to make having children easier , particularly around parents ' workplace rights , access to education for older parents , housing , and subsidised IVF . " We 're a wealthy society , this should n't be beyond our wit . But if we immediately say ' he 's pro-natalist , he 's a Nazi , shut him up and let 's move on ' then we 're going to have tricky days ahead " . <p> He says : " I 'm not talking about us going crazy and having half a dozen children each , I 'm just saying we should go from about one-and-a-half to two-and-a-half , which would make an enormous difference . " <p> Climate <p> SOME Gen Zeders say they 're reluctant to have children due to climate change or the frightening state of the world . But Morland dismisses this . It 's " propaganda " to claim " the world is getting worse " , he believes , as infant mortality , extreme poverty and hunger have all fallen . By the time children born today reach 20 , " we 'll be close to net zero " so a baby should n't be seen as " another emitter " . <p> " Consuming the labour of others " through migration increases emissions , he says , as " you 're merely drawing people from low-emission countries to high-emission countries " . <p> Few mainstream politicians talk of the population crisis . Morland sees it as his duty to " get the discussion going . I have n't got all the answers . I 'm just trying to challenge people who think that we can actually manage society in the long term if we do n't fix our ways " . <p> Scotland needs to pay especial attention to the population crisis . " Scotland has a lower fertility rate than the rest of the UK , and a lower life expectancy , and more deaths than births than the rest of the UK . It 's got immigration largely from English people looking to retire . So Scotland 's demography is very sick . <p> " I do n't want to be the Sassenach preaching to the Scots , but Scotland has serious demographic issues and should think very carefully before imagining that independence would be anything other than at least a demographic problem . If you want to stop English people coming up you 're going to find much of the Scottish countryside rapidly depopulated . " <p> One rich nation which is n't in population decline is Israel . This is probably down to " religion " , Morland says . " The more orthodox , the bigger the family . " <p> Secular American Jews , he notes , " have very low fertility rates " . <p> Morland adds : " There are lessons to learn from Israel , but it 's difficult because it 's a very controversial and not universally beloved country , and if you talk about it some people get very hot under the collar . <p> " Nevertheless , if there 's one highly urban , highly educated , highly successful , technologically advanced country that has a fertility rate of three , we better pay attention . " <p> Care <p> THE care industry is one sector of society dramatically affected by the population crisis . We need lots of young , working people to look after the elderly and fund their care . <p> Another right-wing demographer has ideas around care related to both women 's lives and immigration , which are also likely to infuriate progressives . <p> David Goodhart is head of demography and immigration at the conservative think tank Policy Exchange . He 's already been heavily criticised for his immigration views . His own children " accused " him of " racism " . <p> David Goodhart <p> Now he 's courting controversy regarding the family . His latest book is The Care Dilemma : Caring Enough In The Age Of Sex Equality . <p> The big question facing Britain is : how do we care for all our elderly people ? For Goodhart , the dilemma is " driven by new freedoms , particularly for women -- the movement of women from the home . That hugely increased women 's freedom , but there have been unintended consequences " . <p> Goodhart says there has " been a huge shift away from the family and domestic realm into the public realm of jobs . Much of that 's a good thing , particularly when it comes to the role of women , and women 's abilities not to be defined so much by motherhood and marriage , and to compete equally with men in the labour market " . <p> He adds : " But part of that movement -- and the general relaxation of moral norms , and many adults pursuing their own desires much more -- has seen the diminishment of the domestic role in the family . You can overshoot . We 've got to the point where we undervalue care in the domestic realm . " <p> When Goodhart talks of care , he means both care of the elderly and children . If , as suggested , we have more children , then we need to think about how we care for them too . <p> Currently more than five million people are unpaid carers for mostly elderly relatives . Like childcare , elderly care " remains low status and low paid " . Goodhart says care work is " undervalued " as it 's traditionally considered " women 's work " , and we do n't prize the attributes required like emotional intelligence . <p> " The status of women has increased enormously in the last 50 years which is partly why we have this care dilemma . " He claims much of the " increase in women 's status has been along male default lines , which is why we undervalue things that were traditionally part of the female realm in the home " . <p> Anger <p> LIKE Morland , Goodhart courts anger from women . Many will accuse him of being simply another man telling women how to live their lives . Once traditional " restrictions " on women 's lives were " relaxed , we did n't have an alternative solution " when it came to issues like childcare and elderly care . " <p> Goodhart stresses that he sees the changing role of women as " good , beneficial and liberating " but claims Britain failed to deal with the " negative trends that flowed from this shift " , such as family break-up , " the sharp fall in fertility , and the recruitment crisis in care jobs " . <p> Goodhart wants to " rebalance the diminishment of the family that we 've experienced because of greater freedoms " . He says this can be done " without going back to the 1950s or restricting women 's freedoms " , and claims we should listen to " the majority of women who still value family and traditional feminine virtues " . <p> Goodhart insists " men must step up " , but adds : " Men are stepping up more in the domestic realm than they 're given credit for . This is constantly ignored by the political class . " <p> Most people are much more traditionally minded than politicians , he claims . " Women who are prominent in politics are only the voice of one section of women -- not all women . " <p> But if we want families caring for children and elderly relatives at home , how do we prevent the risk of women bearing the brunt ? <p> Goodhart says we need to balance not setting the clock back with more family-based care . That would require a major shift in attitude from business and government . <p> Goodhart favours " huge childcare subsidies " with money for nurseries going " direct to families " . Parents could choose to stay at home , pay for childcare , or pay grandparents to help . Evidently , plenty of women also earn more than men and it would make no sense for them to stay at home . <p> The " political class " , Goodhart says , is " insulated " from these issues due to wealth and power . For most , parental leave is " miserly " . <p> Feminists <p> GOODHART favours more " Nordic levels of support for reproduction " . @@118891148 <h> FACT CHECK : How does Scotland 's fish farming industry work ? <h> FACT CHECK : How does Scotland 's fish farming work ? <p> SCOTLAND 'S fish farming industry is worth hundreds of millions of pounds and has been lauded for bringing jobs to coastal communities . <p> However , the industry has faced criticism over its welfare standards and environmental impacts . <p> Ferret Fact Service explains the impact of the industry on Scotland , and why it has become a lightning rod for controversy . <h> How does fish farming work ? <p> FISH farms dot the west coast and north-west coast of Scotland , as well as several islands , with more than 200 facilities in operation . The majority are salmon farms . <p> Most salmon begin life onshore , where fish are reared in freshwater until they grow to size . <p> They are then brought to offshore farms where they grow to adult size while kept in netted pens in Scotland 's seas . These pens allow for the constant recycling of seawater . The salmon 's life cycle takes around three years . Once they are fully grown , they are slaughtered and taken to processing plants to be prepared for sale . <p> The high density of salmon in fish farms makes it very easy for parasites like sea lice to transmit disease between fish . <p> Salmon are also regularly killed by chemicals used to treat diseases and kill sea lice , as well as rough handling , algal blooms , jellyfish , seals , poor water quality and oxygen shortages . <p> Animal welfare charities have pointed out that fish are sentient animals that can feel pain , and criticise the conditions in which they have to live , comparing the practice to battery farming . <p> The salmon farming industry says many fish mortalities are linked to climate change , rather than poor conditions . <p> Rises in sea temperature have increased algae and brought large numbers of jellyfish , which sting salmons ' eyes , skin and gills , and can result in death . <p> Phytoplankton algae can reproduce or " bloom " to harmful levels , which can be fatal to farmed fish . <h> Sustainability <p> THE salmon farming industry has been considered a more sustainable way to provide fish for consumption because it avoids overfishing of wild species and fish can be reproduced in a controlled way . <p> The industry body Salmon Scotland argues it is a low-carbon source of protein , compared to meats like chicken , pork and beef . <p> Environmentalists have suggested claims of sustainability from the industry are not accurate , due to the polluting impacts of farms on the seas , as well as the outbreaks of disease . <p> A leading Scottish salmon farming company , Loch Duart , was asked to stop branding its business as " sustainable " by the UK 's advertising watchdog after complaints . <h> Impact on other animals <p> THERE have been concerns that the sea lice which afflict farmed salmon could risk spreading to wild fish . The Scottish Environmental Protection Agency ( Sepa ) , named 19 fish farms that were at high risk of contaminating wild salmon and trout . <p> Wild Atlantic salmon were internationally classified as endangered in 2023 after global populations fell by 23% between 2006 and 2020 . Lice from fish farms has been identified as one of the causes of the decline , along with invasive species , river barriers , and climate change . <p> Seals have also come into contact with fish farms in Scotland . Salmon make up a part of the diets of certain seals living in our seas , so they are naturally attracted to fish farms . <p> Significant numbers of fish are lost each year to seals . It has been reported that 1.4 million fish were lost to seals over a 10-year period . <p> Fish farms have used various methods to deter seals , including controversial acoustic deterrent devices , which transmit loud sounds into the seawater surrounding farms . <p> These can have an impact on other marine species including dolphins , porpoises and whales . <h> Why are you making commenting on The National only available to subscribers ? <p> We know there are thousands of National readers who want to debate , argue and go back and forth in the comments section of our stories . We 've got the most informed readers in Scotland , asking each other the big questions about the future of our country . <p> Unfortunately , though , these important debates are being spoiled by a vocal minority of trolls who are n't really interested in the issues , try to derail the conversations , register under fake names , and post vile abuse . <p> So that 's why we 've decided to make the ability to comment only available to our paying subscribers . That way , all the trolls who post abuse on our website will have to pay if they want to join the debate -- and risk a permanent ban from the account that they subscribe with . <p> The conversation will go back to what it should be about -- people who care passionately about the issues , but disagree constructively on what we should do about them . Let 's get that debate started ! <p> Callum Baird , Editor of The National <h> Comments : Our rules <p> We want our comments to be a lively and valuable part of our community - a place where readers can debate and engage with the most important local issues . The ability to comment on our stories is a privilege , not a right , however , and that privilege may be withdrawn if it is abused or misused. <h> follow us <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . A government that opened the nation 's borders is being replaced by one that favours mass deportations . A government that instinctively regulates is being replaced by one that instinctively deregulates . A president most comfortable in union halls is being replaced by one who iscomfortable on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange . <p> If that ai n't an economic revolution , flawed as most revolutions are , it is hard to tell what is . <p> Start with the revolution in climate policy . Greening is done and dusted . The new government believes that a warmer climate probably has as many positive as negative effects -- that there is no climate crisis and therefore no need to spend billions to avoid it . Relying on the sun and wind for energy is a mistake . Instead , relax restrictions on permitting fuel-transport facilities and " drill , baby , drill " . And give nuclear a nod . <h> Advertisement <p> Remove or relax fuel-economy and emissions standards designed to make it unprofitable to manufacture petrol-driven vehicles , and to drive the market share of electric vehicles from 7.6 per cent to 70 per cent by 2032 . And stop using scarce defence funds to end carbon emissions from military bases by 2035 . <p> Buyers of EVs will no longer receive subsidies of $7,500 , ( ? 6,000 ) , which is scheduled to cost the taxpayer $390 billion by 2031 . A government unfazed by past failures to pick winners is attempting to push about $400 billion in loans out the door before it is slammed shut by a new government that believes private-sector capital markets do a more efficient job of allocating capital . <p> Revolutionary tax and labour market changes are also being considered . The use of tariffs to generate income , while lowering corporate and personal taxes , is a shift from taxing work to taxing consumption -- a long-held objective of conservative economists . The removal of taxes ontips and overtime work would have a similar goal , while increasing the labour supply ... which massive deportations would reduce . Estimates are that 13 and 25 per cent , respectively , of national and Texas construction workers entered the US illegally , making it reasonable to wonder who will build the factories and infrastructure in a booming Trump economy . <p> Perhaps the most revolutionary aspect of Trumpism will be played out in the regulatory field . The chairman of the House of Representatives budget committee reports : " President Biden is on track to impose more regulatory cost on our economy than any president in history , adding $1.4 trillion sincecoming to office ... a staggering 45 times the regulatory costs accumulated under Trump and almost five times the regulatory costs added under President Obama . " <p> Much of this cost results not from legislation but from the rules promulgated by the administrative agencies to implement those laws . " The Great Deregulator " -- get this , President Jimmy Carter , White House resident from 1977-1981 -- deregulated oil prices and the trucking , railroad and communications industries , and set the stage for airline deregulation . Trump as the man in the tradition of Carter 's deregulatory onslaught is a delicious thought . <h> Advertisement <p> Trump is planting an oil-state governor at the interior department , committed deregulators as chairs of the agencies that oversee the financial community , including cryptocurrencies and auditing firms , and competition enforcers who are relaxed about most mergers , with the exception of those in Silicon Valley , which the new team has in its bomb sights . Setting Elon Musk loose on rules-writing , bloated regulatory agencies is the frosting on the cake that the new administration is baking . <p> But for Trump to have his revolution , he will have to overcome forces with a substantial stake in the status quo -- government workers , big business and regulators . The federal government employs more than two million civilians -- many with job insurance recently enhanced by Joe Biden -- and few are likely to roll out the red carpet for sacker-in-chief Musk . Big business does not keep a list of government benefits that it is prepared to surrender . <p> The federal government 's near-300,000 regulators do not see themselves as impediments to economic growth , but as guardians of the economic system . All survived Trump once before and are confident they can hold out during Trump Mark 2 until he is relieved by the voters in 2029 . <p> Trump has the advantage of a rich inheritance : a fully employed , wildly innovative and growing economy , and one where productivity is rising faster than in other countries and the EU . Americans have elected him to make an already Great America Greater still . They are betting the GreatAmerica they have in the hope of winning something Greater . That is no small wager . 
@@118891491 <h> How to make a wildlife pond in your garden <h> In the past century Britain has lost 90 per cent of its wetland habitats , but you can help reverse the trend with a few simple steps <p> Nick Oliver says the garden pond has been pushed aside in favour of decking and leisure space <p> AKIRA SUEMORI FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES <p> Sharon Smith <p> Sunday December 15 2024 , 12.01am , The Sunday Times <p> It may seem odd to say it given the amount of rain we 've had recently , but we all need to do our bit to save our wetlands . Over the past 300 years the UK has lost about 75 per cent of its wetlands due to overdevelopment , farming , pollution and , increasingly , climate change , according to the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust ( WWT ) . In the past century alone , we have lost 90 per cent of our wetland habitats , according to the Environment Agency . <p> This matters because more than 10 per cent of our freshwater and wetland species -- birds , amphibians , insects -- are threatened with extinction and two thirds are in decline . If we create wildlife ponds in our back gardens we can help to reverse the trend . We can also include our drainpipes in the rescue plan by creating a mini-wetlands beneath them . This helps wildlife and slows the rush of rainwater into our drains . If we do both we can help the WWT reach its goal of creating 100,000 hectares of new or restored wetlands by 2050 . <p> Wildlife will use your pond to drink , bathe , rest , feed and breed . If you can attract birds , hedgehogs , newts , frogs and toads , in return they will gobble up garden pests including slugs and snails . Amphibians tend to return to the pond they spawn from , so attracting them could ensure a steady population . Even if they do not hibernate or breed in your pond , they may become a frequent visitor . <p> You should definitely not add fish to your pond , Oliver says <p> AKIRA SUEMORI FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES <p> " If you think how our gardens used to be , a lot of people had ponds so you had a network dotted around and frogs could move around freely , " says Nick Oliver , community action manager at WWT . " However , with people now focusing on decking and leisure space , the garden pond as a feature has been pushed aside . But if you introduce these little staging posts , amphibians on the move will have somewhere they can stop off . " <p> Autumn is a good time to build a wildlife pond because it 's best to fill it with rainwater -- tap water is too nutrient-rich and encourages excessive algae and blanket weed growth . Digging your pond before a forecast for a downpour is a handy way of filling it , Oliver says . <h> Advertisement <p> Ideally , a pond needs a balance of sunlight and shade . Too much sun encourages weed growth , but you need enough to warm up the water for amphibians such as frogs and newts to breed in the spring and for inhabitants such as tadpoles to survive . <p> Avoid locating the pond under a thick band of trees whose dead leaves will clog up the bottom . When you have sorted out your site , how big you make your pond is limited solely by the size of your garden , Oliver says . It does not have to be deep ; one to two feet down is enough . <p> You need just enough sun to warm up the water for frogs to breed in the spring <p> GETTY IMAGES <p> Next , decide on your waterscaping : what do you want the pond to look like ? " You want to create as much diversity as possible for different wildlife and plants , so create different tiers , " Oliver recommends . <p> You will need a shallow end for birds and smaller visitors to be able to get in and out , or to stand on for drinking or bathing . Ponds that sit flush with the ground are easiest for wildlife to negotiate . Raised or sunken ponds will need steps or planks to improve access for critters . " If your pond is level with the land and frogs and newts can get in and out freely , you 'll attract them . At the WWT Wetland Centre in Barnes west London we have three raised ponds , two of which are connected to the bank and it 's in those two that we get our frogs and newts , " Oliver says . <p> When digging out your different levels , remove any sharp objects like tree roots , rocks and man-made materials such as builders ' rubble . Put in a 5cm layer of soft sand for cushioning then install the lining . Butyl , a malleable synthetic rubber , is a popular choice for a liner . For a bigger pond alternatives , the RHS suggests puddled clay or sodium bentonite . Ensure that you have excess liner around the edge to allow for it being pulled downwards when it is filled with water . Dig it in or hold it down with rocks , which will also provide a habitat for creatures . Put sand in the bottom then fill it up . <h> Advertisement <p> Once the pond is made , the only thing you will need to add to it are aquatic plants . Choose species that when fully grown are suitable for your pond depth and size . Avoid over-planting and leave between one third and half of the water surface free from foliage , to allow sunlight to reach oxygenators . Aim for native plants which have evolved with UK wildlife , Oliver says , and avoid non-native invasive species , such as parrot 's feather ( Myriophyllum aquaticum ) and New Zealand pigmyweed ( Crassula helmsii ) . Many are now banned from sale in the UK , but might still be available online . They look exotic but can overwhelm native plants and wildlife . There is a list of prohibited plants on the Royal Horticultural Society 's website . <p> Oliver says that you should definitely not add fish to your wildlife pond . " There 's a big red flag when it comes to wildlife ponds and goldfish because they 're voracious eaters and will snaffle up everything they can . <p> " Once the plants are in , you can sit back and wait for wildlife to populate this new home . An ecosystem will establish itself without your interference . For maintenance , in a prolonged drought you may need to top up the water . Prune your plants when needed . If you scoop out algae and blanket weed , leave it on the side to give invertebrates a chance to climb back into the water . In the winter , if it freezes over , do not break the ice because the shock could kill some inhabitants . Your emergent plants will provide tiny pockets of air , and floating a ball on the surface might keep an air hole open . <p> No wildlife pond is too small , Oliver says . " Even something as simple as sinking a washing-up bowl in the ground in your garden helps . I 've seen some great examples of people repurposing bowls and Belfast sinks as ponds and they 're all flourishing . " <h> And how to plant them <p> Use a container to prevent a plant from becoming too invasive . Aquatic baskets have lattice sides to allow the movement of air , water and gas . Fine mesh is best , otherwise use a hessian lining to keep soil contained . 
@@118891526 <h> Scotland 's idiotic political leaders hate motorists <h> The SNP government seems to want to kill travelling by car despite public transport being unreliable or too expensive <p> Norway is to build the world 's longest and deepest underwater road tunnel . The Rogfast project will link the districts of Randaberg and Bokn , which are separated by a 16-mile-wide waterway more than 1,000 feet deep . The four-lane motorway will cost ? 1.6 billion . We now know it will not be finished until 2035 at the earliest . <p> What kind of government behaves this way ? I found it hard to believe at first , a bit like Boris Johnson 's Irish Sea bridge from Scotland to Northern Ireland . But it is n't . Norway has been building deep roads for a quarter of a century . It is a peculiar form of environmental cretinism that Scandinavians find incomprehensible . This was confirmed by a follow-up study by the Institute of Epidemiology and Community Health . The main impact of 20mph limits , outside sensitive areas like schools , is increased frustration and a bumper crop of speeding fines -- which , a cynic might suggest , is one reason Scottish politicians find them so attractive . <p> The Scottish political classes live in a parallel universe where people are either engaged in " active travel " on bicycles or travelling by public transport . Sixty-eight per cent of commuters travel to work by car in Scotland , 71 per cent if you include passengers . Only 7 per cent travel by bus and , shockingly , given its prominence in government spending and rhetoric , only 4 per cent travel by rail . Public transport use is still way below pre-pandemic levels . This is because buses are largely non-existent outside big cities and because travelling by train is increasingly a pastime for the well-off , given eye-watering fares -- among the highest in Europe . <p> Yet the Scottish government is committed to an arbitrary target of reducing car use by 20 per cent by 2030 . People are fed up with feeling guilty for taking their kids on the school run , trying to get to work or exploring Scotland 's countryside . Eventually , they will crack . So Holyrood , be warned : the rapid growth of populist Reform in Scotland probably has less to do with immigration than with the war on the car .
