@@119141492 <p> Sharon McMahon attends a discussion of her book , " The Small and the Mighty , " at 92NY on September 25 , 2024 , in New York City . <p> Gary Gershoff/Getty Images <p> CNN -- <p> On a cool , breezy Monday afternoon , a crowd of drunken , rowdy men gathering in the nation 's capital stared in astonishment as a striking figure headed toward them . It was a regal young woman riding a magnificent white horse , wearing a gold crown and a flowing white cape . <p> The woman 's name was Inez Milholland , and on that day in March 3 , 1913 , she was about to make history . Dubbed the " poster girl of radicalism , " the 26-year-old was the scion of a wealthy family who had become a lawyer , a labor activist and an advocate for the poor . She was an open advocate of free love -- the belief that government should n't limit how women express their sexuality -- and proposed to the man who would become her husband . <p> But Milholland 's critics called her radical because she believed that all American women were entitled to vote -- and she was willing to defy authorities in dramatic ways to demonstrate her beliefs . On that day , she was leading a procession of some 5,000 women through Washington for the nation'sfirst major suffragist parade . <p> The men 's astonishment , though , soon turned to rage . They attacked Milholland and the marchers with curses , spitting on them and slapping some in the face . Police standing by did nothing . The only group that defended the women was a Boy Scout troop . <p> Milholland 's flair for the dramatic and her public speaking skills helped put the suffragist movement on America 's front pages . Yet she never lived to see the ratification in 1920 of the 19th Amendment , which recognized women 's right to vote . <p> Inez Milholland on a white horse at the National American Woman Suffrage Association parade on March 3 , 1913 , in Washington . <p> HUM Images/Universal Images Group/Getty Images <p> She collapsed while giving a suffragist speech in Los Angeles , " like a wilted white rose " at the podium . She suffered from pernicious anemia and ignored warnings to ease her grueling speaking schedule . Her last public utterance was , " Mr. President , how long must women wait for their liberty ? " She was 30 at the time of her death . <p> Her life sounds like a movie , but Milholland 's crucial role in American history was eventually forgotten . Most historians preferred to focus on men on horseback leading other men into battle . <p> But Sharon McMahon , a former high school government teacher , has resurrected Milholland and others like her in " The Small and The Mighty , " her new book that has topped the New York Times bestseller list . In her book , McMahon highlights the fortitude of citizens who changed America even though they had " the least amount of political , social and economic power . " <p> " The best Americans are not always famous , " she writes . " They are the people who went for broke when everyone else yelled turn back . They are those who know that one becomes great because of who they lift up , not who they put down . " <p> McMahon 's roll call of unsung heroes and heroines include : <p> The teenage girl who rode 40 miles overnight in the rain during the Revolutionary War -- twice as far as Paul Revere two years earlier -- to warn the Connecticut militia that the British were coming . <p> The " gay feminist badass " who wrote the lyrics to " America the Beautiful , " the classic patriotic song . <p> The Black teenager who refused to give up her bus seat to a White woman in Montgomery , Alabama , nine months before Rosa Parks did . <p> The Jewish man who built a fortune in business but found more joy in spending it on erecting schoolsfor poor Black students across the South . <p> McMahon 's book , though , is more than a historical reminder -- it 's a civic sermon that may inspire Americans during this turbulent time for the country . For some Americans , this holiday season brings few tidings of joy . Many have lost faith in American institutions , and a majority believe the country is headed in the wrong direction . <p> McMahon 's book was published in September . <p> Penguin Random House <p> But McMahon 's book evokes the spirit of the Christmas story . The small can turn into the mighty -- whether it 's a child born in a manger to a poor , teenage mom or the unsung people that McMahon chronicles in her book . <p> " My argument is that they 're not the only people that matter , as we 've often been taught , " she tells CNN . " The small can be mighty . It 's not just the mighty who are mighty . " <p> McMahon 's book offers two lessons for how everyday Americans today might move forward with new purpose . <h> Lesson 1 : Do the ' next needed thing ' <p> In an undated black-and-white photograph , an unsmiling , bespectacledVirginia Randolphstares atthe camera with a look that conveys resolve and confidence . She needed every measure of those qualities to do what she did . Randolph , a pioneering educator , is one of the characters that McMahon profiles in her book . <p> Randolph was born to parents who had been enslaved and grew up in the Jim Crow South during an era where lynching was common and millions of Black Americans were stripped of their basic citizenship rights . Despite those obstacles , McMahon says Randolph went on to become one of America 's greatest educators , on par with Booker T. Washington , the civil rights leader who founded Tuskegee University . <p> Virginia Randolph . <p> County of Henrico , Virginia , Historic Preservation and Museum Services <p> Randolph started off teaching Black children in a rural school that was " little more than a shack stuck in a pit of red mud . " She would go on to establish and administer schools in Virginia , North Carolina and Georgia that educated thousands of Black students . <p> She also pioneered teaching methods used throughout America and abroad . Randolph , who never married , adopted at least 14 children ( some estimates said that at least 59 children boarded with her because they could n't afford to pay for housing and attend school ) . <p> What struck McMahon about Randolph was a credo that the educator 's mother used to repeat to her : " Do the next right thing . " <p> It might seem easy now for some Americans to check out and give into despair because problems such as random gun violence and climate change seem insurmountable . But Randolph confronted problems like White supremacy and Jim Crow segregation that also seemed unsolvable . <p> She never felt , though , that she had to fix everything -- and neither should we , McMahon says . <p> " A more helpful posture is to do the next needed thing before us , " she says . " I need to educate the boys and girls in front of me . I need to make soup for a sick relative . " <p> Doing the next needed thing avoids the type of inaction that results from the belief that must rely on charismatic leaders to change America , McMahon says . <p> " We create the kind of progress we want to see far more quickly than waiting for the right leader to be elected , " McMahon says . " Because if we 're waiting , we could be waiting for eight to 12 years . But the power to do the next needed thing is available to each one of us today . " <h> Lesson 2 : Refuse to give up on people <p> In her day , Randolph fought against racial segregation . Today , the country is also confronting another type of segregation : ideological . <p> Racial segregation still exists in schools and communities across America . But Americans also are self-sorting into political enclaves . We live in blue and red states . Some people refuse to date someone of another political party . Even social media is undergoing a schism . Progressives arefleeing Elon Musk 's X , which is increasingly MAGA-friendly , and joining Bluesky , which is seen as more receptive to their views . <p> If that all seems abstract , consider this question : When is the last time you sat down and had a calm , reflective conversation with someone who holds radically different political beliefs ? <p> It 's easy to cancel some Americans when you do n't agree with them , but Septima Clark , one of the characters in McMahon 's book , illustrates the folly of such an approach . Clark , a civil rights activist , was surrounded by enemies . Even her civil rights allies could n't see her worth at times because of her gender . She has been largely lost to history because most historians focus on men like her famous colleague , the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr . <p> Civil rights activist Septima Clark , center , speaks from behind a lectern during a Southern Christian Leadership Conference banquet in Birmingham , Alabama , in August 1965 . Among those also pictured are Dr. Martin Luther King Jr . and his wife Coretta Scott King , at far left , and Rosa Parks , to Clark 's immediate left . <p> Chris McNair/Getty Images <p> Clark , dubbed the " Mother of the Movement , " played a crucial role in securing voting rights for Black people during the Jim Crow era of the mid-20th century . She established citizenship schools and literacy classes throughout the South , teaching Black residents how to fill out voting registration forms . Rosa Parks participated in one of Clark 's workshops just months before she sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott . <p> Clark did n't write off her enemies . She took a magnanimous approach and was willing to engage with White segregationist and civil rights activists who discounted her . Clark explained her philosophy in one passage in McMahon 's book : <p> " Some people slow down their growth after they become adults , " Clark said . " But you never know when a person 's going to leap forward or change around completely -- I 've seen growth like most people do n't think is possible . I can even work with my enemies because I know from experience that they might have a change of heart any minute . " <p> You ca n't change the minds of people you refuse to have contact with . It sounds so simple , but it 's often forgotten by today 's political leaders who believe the best way to win is to turn out your base and ignore or demonize your opposition . <p> Jon Favreau , a former speechwriter for President Obama , alluded to this attitude in a recent essay . He noted Obama was the last Democratic president since Franklin Roosevelt to twice win the majority of the popular vote -- in part because of his background as a community organizer in Chicago . <p> Community organizers spend their time talking to people who are n't like them and do n't think like them , Favreau wrote . Obama tried hard to empathize with people even if they were n't for him , " he made it clear that he was for them , " Favreau wrote . <p> " That 's because organizers are n't looking to perform for the people who already agree with them , " Favreau wrote . " They 're looking to persuade the people who do n't . They do n't just want to be right . They want to win . " <h> ' They knew that hope was a choice ' <p> The victories of the small and mighty are n't always immediately apparent . Some of these historical figures were n't just overlooked ; they were reviled when they were alive . But their impact on America endures , McMahon says . <p> " I love the fact that somebody at her ( Milholland 's ) funeral said no work for liberty is lost , " McMahon says . " It became part of the fabric of the nation . The country changes for the better because of the work of Inez Milholland . " <p> And because of others like her as well . McMahon says Americans can do the same today -- if they remember one final lesson from the small and mighty . <p> It 's about hope . <p> " They were n't waiting for hope to be a feeling that descends upon us from the heavens like a beam of light , " McMahon says . " They knew that hope was a choice that they made . It was a choice to believe that things could be better . 
@@119143470 <h> Get the latest Chronicle Live breaking news on WhatsApp <p> Despite controversy , plans for a ' battery energy storage system ' in South Tyneside are set to proceed , following a decision by a government-appointed planning inspector . The ruling from the national Planning Inspectorate this month ( December , 2024 ) is tied to proposals for a facility aimed at supporting efforts to decarbonise the UK electricity grid . <p> Whirlwind Energy Storage Ltd had sought permission from South Tyneside Council to construct a landscaped compound housing up to 360 energy storage cabinets near the West Boldon Substation , south of the A184 . The facility 's proponents stated it would " import and store electrical power during periods of oversupply from renewable generators " , such as wind turbines , and that this power would " otherwise be wasted " . <p> Planning documents indicated that stored power would subsequently be " exported back to the National Grid during periods of low renewable generation which , in most cases , offsets the use of gas " . However , during a council consultation on the plans , the application sparked over 30 public objections , as well as opposition from some borough councillors and Jarrow 's constituency MP . <p> Concerns included the site 's closeness to the River Don and a local wildlife site , potential pollution impacts , fire safety issues , and the development 's visual impact on the Green Belt . The battery energy storage development was rejected by South Tyneside Council 's Planning Committee at a pivotal meeting in June , 2024 , against the adv . <p> Despite the advice of council planning officers who had recommended the scheme for approval , councillors initially refused the plans , citing them as " inappropriate development " that would harm the Green Belt and alter the character of the landscape . An appeal was subsequently lodged against South Tyneside Council 's decision to reject the proposal , leading to a planning inspector , appointed by the Secretary of State , to adjudicate the issue . <p> The inspector has now upheld the appeal , allowing the development to proceed . <p> The rationale behind the inspector 's decision was detailed in a report made available on the Planning Inspectorate 's website on December 10 , 2024 . The inspector acknowledged that the proposed development would indeed " reduce the openness of the Green Belt , and would conflict with the purposes of including land within it " , and would also cause " moderate harm to the character and appearance of the area " . <p> Nevertheless , the inspector identified " very special circumstances " which " clearly outweigh the harm to the Green Belt and any other harm " . <p> These circumstances included the significant role the BESS ( battery energy storage system ) would play in mitigating climate change and regulating electricity flows within the broader supply network , alongside minor benefits to biodiversity and the economy . The report also highlighted " mitigation and enhancement measures " for the development , such as " green roofing on the compound buildings , removal/thinning of non-native scrub and trees along the riverbank , removal of fencing alongside the river , treatment of invasive species , ... verge enhancement , and bat roost and bird nesting provision " . <p> The riverbank will undergo a transformation with the removal and thinning of non-native scrub and trees , the elimination of fencing along the river , treatment of invasive species , verge enhancement , and provisions for bat roosts and bird nesting . The plan also includes maintaining and enhancing hedgerows and avoiding night time lighting . <p> The planning inspector expressed satisfaction with the proposed biodiversity improvements , stating that " based on the ecology evidence and the size of the overall site , I am satisfied sufficient land is available for additional biodiversity gain to be achieved " . <p> Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service did not raise any objections to the proposal , noting that " fire-fighting water would be held in an on-site underground reservoir , significantly in excess of the guideline amount " . <p> The appeal decision report concluded : " In conclusion therefore , the proposed development would be in some conflict with the development plan , with respect to harm to the Green Belt and to the character and appearance of the area . However other material considerations , including the framework and the very special circumstances cited in this case , indicate that permission should be granted . I therefore allow the appeal . " <p> The applicants initially sought permission for a 50-year operational period for the South Tyneside battery energy storage development , after which the site would be decommissioned and restored . Those behind the appeal previously stated that the development would " enhance the economic development and sustainability of the local area , while also helping to deliver the further decarbonisation of the UK electricity sector " . <p> The further decarbonisation of the UK 's electricity sector could be achieved , along with improvements in biodiversity . It was observed that the " predicted impacts " of the development would be acceptable and could be " adequately controlled " through proposed mitigation measures and planning conditions . <p> The planning inspector 's report stated that battery energy storage developments " allow balancing of demand without resorting to additional generation from fossil fuels , and also reduce the need for further fossil fuel-based grid balancing technologies " . The West Boldon development was noted to potentially " would save between 2,592 and 4,044 tonnes of CO2 per year " . <p> Although it was recognised that " the stored energy would not be ringfenced solely to South Tyneside residents " , it was argued that the proposal would still " contribute to the achievement of national and local ambitions " around Net Zero . The appeal decision was discussed at a meeting of South Tyneside Council 's Planning Committee on Monday ( December 16 , 2024 ) during a standard update on planning appeals . <p> Councillors were informed that no costs were applied for or awarded in the case of the battery energy storage system planning application following the Planning Committee 's refusal decision earlier this year . <p> Councillor Shirley Ford commented at the meeting : " I think that it 's helpful for us to hear and to read in detail the reasoning of the inspectors that make these decisions . They were looking at the same issues , the balance of harms and benefits ... I do n't think there 's any suggestion that we made incorrect decisions that were unreasonable or we have n't weighed things carefully . " <p> Under planning conditions , the development must be brought forward within three years and will be " limited to a period of 50 years from the date of its first beneficial use . " Water drainage , biodiversity , construction , noise and ' risk reduction and mitigation ' issues , including a ' fire emergency response plan ' , will be addressed via planning conditions . <p> For more information on the planning application and appeal , visit South Tyneside Council 's planning portal website and search reference : ST/0486/23/FUL

@@119148056 <h> This is the last article you can read this month <h> You can read more article this month <h> You can read more articles this month <h> Sorry your limit is up for this month <p> MATT WRACK is running for re-election as general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union . First elected in 2005 , when Tony Blair was PM , he 's now on his eighth prime minister and recently completed a year as president of the TUC . But he 's still up for the fight . <p> " There 's still a lot to do , " he tells the Morning Star as ballots begin to land on firefighters ' doormats . " We 've been through some tough times under all those prime ministers , we 've come through it in one piece , and we have plans to try to rebuild the fire service , make Labour deliver on workers ' rights and repeal anti-union legislation . I think I 'm the best person to see that through . " <p> Fourteen years of Tory cuts have hit the fire and rescue service hard . Response times are at their highest in 30 years . There are 12,000 fewer firefighters than in 2010 -- a decline of a fifth . <p> To get back on track , says Wrack , " we need investment in the fire service , investment in all public services . <p> " Labour is saying ' there 's no money , ' and in many ways they intend to continue with the economic approach of the previous government . <p> " But you ca n't deliver a modern fire service , with all the new and emerging risks , with 12,000 fewer firefighters . The most obvious case is perhaps in relation to climate change , the extreme weather events we 've already seen . Within just a couple of weeks we 've had three major storms and major flooding here . <p> " The data shows that a significant number of houses in the UK will face a risk of flooding over the next 10 years . And on top of that we have the increased incidence of moorland and grassland fires . <p> " These major incidents are protracted and require large numbers of people to tackle them . To be resilient , as the buzzword is , we need investment in the fire service . " <p> The political culture Wrack wants to see change goes back further than the 2010 Tory government . He points out that it was Blair 's government , in 2004 , that abolished national standards for fire cover . <p> After years of campaigning , Wrack says the union managed to secure from Labour two significant manifesto pledges : national standards would come back , and a ministerial advisory body would help set them . <p> " That was remarkable because it was Labour that abolished the standards in 2004 , and the advisory structures were also abolished between then and 2010 . <p> " So there has n't been a meeting that would include ministers , fire chiefs , employers and the Fire Brigades Union in more than 20 years : but we won that pledge and the first meeting did indeed take place two weeks ago . <p> " It 's just a start , but it 's an important start and one that shows through careful planning , campaigning and lobbying we have secured a real chance of change . For me , it was the abolition of national standards that drove a race to the bottom , allowed governments to keep cutting forever . " <p> Given his criticisms of Labour 's economic policy , does he see a need to maintain the street campaigning and protest unions helped organise under the Conservative governments ? <p> " I think it 's a mistake to treat this government as exactly like the last one . It 's not , particularly on the issue of workers ' rights . <p> " If you take our rally in October , we decided against holding a protest march on Parliament , opting instead for a mass lobby : putting the demands , but to show MPs , especially new MPs , that we want to work with them . <p> " That does n't mean there is no place for protests . I argued in the TUC we should have had a major rally early on focused on trade union rights , which did n't come off . We do need to put pressure on ministers . <p> " On issues from public services , public-sector pay , we need to be building up pressure . " <p> The FBU has had a rocky relationship with the Labour Party , disaffiliating under Blair because of his government 's attacks on firefighters ' pensions , and reaffiliating when Labour was led from the left by Jeremy Corbyn . The politics of the party have done another about-turn since then ; how are relations ? <p> " Dialogue with ministers and the Prime Minister is part of my job as general secretary . <p> " But I do n't hold back from being firm on the policies of our union , the affiliated unions and workers ' interests . <p> " And challenging Labour over attacks on internal party democracy , the victimisation of particular MPs , the closing down of constituency parties and witch-hunting of socialists is part of standing up for workers ' interests . We will not back down from that approach . <p> " That does n't mean jabbing my finger in Keir Starmer 's chest . It means making a coherent case for different choices when necessary . " <p> One area where the FBU has long campaigned for different choices is the deregulation of the construction industry and fire safety standards , so tragically exposed in the Grenfell Tower fire . Pamphlets produced by the union such as The Grenfell Tower Fire : a Crime Caused by Profit and Deregulation outlined the steps by which safety standards in the building industry were dismantled over the course of the Thatcher , Major and Blair governments . <p> " Grenfell was not just about cuts , but about the way profit-seeking in the construction sector was at the heart of why the fire happened , and the role of central government in allowing self-compliance regimes to replace proper fire certification processes . <p> " I worry that Labour has not grasped that . We did win a battle to include the phrase ' including through regulation ' in the Labour manifesto section on preventing another Grenfell : but it was quite a battle , which tells you something . <p> " I worry the new government will look for what it sees as easy solutions , to deregulate and allow the private sector to fill the gaps in , say , the huge housing need : but a whole host of safety factors are ignored in that , and we know there are thousands of buildings , still , with flammable cladding . <p> " There are many other fire safety failings in residential buildings all across the country . To take just one , some journalists are now researching issues with large panel system building . <p> " To simply allow a free-for-all will not deliver good quality homes and stores up huge risks . " <p> Aside from the direct impact of Labour failing to tackle these issues , the far-right riots of the summer indicate another growing problem : the far right are on the rise , and every Labour failure advances that process . <p> The FBU itself barred a former member ( Grant Mayos resigned just before a disciplinary panel found against him ) this autumn for alleged far-right social media posts and promotion of the extremist Britain First group . <p> " I think the far right is on the rise because of two main factors , " Wrack tells me . <p> " One is that mainstream politicians have allowed a nasty anti-refugee dialogue to develop . <p> " So politics has turned migration into a problem , rather than addressing it in a rational way . <p> " The second reason is something the labour movement has to face up to : our own failure to offer viable alternatives to people . <p> " The far right thrives off the lack of hope . If you look at where those riots took place , they are in very run-down , deindustrialised towns where many people have no decent job prospects . <p> " If mainstream politics does n't offer a solution , if the labour movement does n't offer a working-class solution , they will thrive . <p> " We have to deliver by building council housing , unionising jobs so they are more secure and better paid . This is an international trend , and Labour needs to face up to the fact it faces exactly the same risk as similar parties across Europe unless it changes . " <p> He has a positive vision for what this country needs , but Wrack is frustrated that the FBU leadership election is not focused on such questions . <p> He says his opponent , the union 's vice-president Steve Wright , has refused a debate with him face to face . <p> " That means there 's nowhere members can test two sets of ideas , put their own questions , assess the answers . <p> " No alternative is being presented on how we campaign over pay , or pensions , or win investment , the questions I think members want to hear about . <p> " And that vacuum pushes people to focus on the only thing that can be identified , which is individuals . <p> " The contest has become very personalised as a result . I think I 've seen the worst behaviour I 've ever seen in a leadership election in this contest , particularly through social media abuse . " <p> Wrack says the attacks are hurtful . " But I 'll deal with it . We have to carry on with the campaign -- putting policies and strategy to members , offering a way forward over the next five years for the FBU , the fire service and the wider trade union movement . Thousands of the trees are included in the project ( Louisiana National Guard ) <p> When the trees are deposited in shallow marsh areas -- wetlands filled with grass and other soft-stemmed plants -- slow wave and water movement around the trees trap silt and encourages the growth of marsh grasses , according to the US Fish and Wildlife Service . The agency partners with city offices and the state 's Army National Guard , which uses the drop as a training exercise . <p> Bayou Sauvage National Wildlife Refuge staff retrieve harnesses from the bundles of trees that are dropped . The refuge is the second largest urban wildlife refuge in the country ( USFWS ) <p> " It benefits the city of New Orleans and surrounding coastal environment while also providing valuable training hours for our pilots and crew members of the 1st Assault Helicopter Battalion , 244th Aviation Regiment , " the National Guard 's Chief Warrant Officer 4 Gabriel Ruiz , who is responsible for overseeing aerial operations for the Christmas Tree Drop , explained . <p> Louisiana National Guard members put Christmas trees on harnesses . The trees are bundled together using wire ( Louisiana National Guard ) <p> After the 4,000 to 6,000 trees are collected , they are stored in the refuge until their drop date . Tens of trees are bundled together using wire straps before a crew attaches harnesses . These are then connected to helicopters which are flown to the marsh . The trees are then dropped in shallow areas that are chosen in advance . <p> Following more than 25 years , the project has restored hundreds of acres within the refuge , which is important habitat for fish , crabs , shrimp , crawfish , and other species . It is the second largest urban wildlife refuge in the United States . <p> A Louisiana National Guard helicopter carries Christmas trees over the marshland . The marshland helps to protect Louisiana from storms ( Louisiana National Guard ) <p> " We are very lucky to be able to work with the Louisiana National Guard , and if it was n't for them , we would be manually doing this project , " Shelly Staies , the refuge manager for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service , said last year . " It 's a win-win for both of us because we get these trees put in , and they get to practice dropping sling loads . " 
@@119158258 <p> NEIL Mackay 's Big Read 's on population ( " A swing to the right on fertility " , December 15 ) addressed the issue of falling birth rates from an entirely one-sided point of view , requiring the reader to take for granted the assumption that declining population is a bad thing . However , there is a completely different perspective which takes account of the existential threat to humanity on our planet caused by a multiplicity of environmental crises , and which sees the prospect of declining population as a godsend and a necessity . <p> Scientists have judged that there are nine critical planetary processes with boundaries which define the safe limits for human pressure to maintain a stable and resilient Earth . They have assessed that for six of these , humanity has crossed these boundaries with increasing risk to human life on Earth . Most attention is focused on climate change , but the threats from five other pressures such as species depletion and extinction , diminishing freshwater health and availability , declining land for healthy natural processes , and pollution , are equally stark . <p> There are two major causes of these crises , our economic system based on massive industrialised production and the enormous increase in the human population in the last 100 years ( from two billion in 1928 to eight billion currently and still growing ) . The mindset of our culture remains wedded to unsustainable levels in both these areas as the article very well demonstrates . Such continuing human excess is simply a physical impossibility ; no amount of moaning by the right or the left or any political persuasion can alter the laws of biology , chemistry and physics . We can either manage a decline towards stability at a much-reduced level of production and population , or it will be imposed on us by catastrophe . <p> There is no sign at all that humanity will turn away from its addiction to economic growth , but declining fertility levels across the world are an indication of some hope for population size . As the Earth 's population is projected to grow to at least 10 billion this century , however , and with continuing unchecked economic growth , the decline in fertility rates can not come too quickly . <p> It is obvious that the stabilisation and then decline of population numbers will come with serious social problems , but the planetary disaster of accelerating overshoot of the Earth 's capacity to contain humanity is of an order of magnitude inconceivably greater . <p> If anyone is in doubt about the reality of this planetary crisis , a look at the work of the Stockholm Resilience Centre ( https : **30;54;TOOLONG ) should help . <p> I WAS disappointed to read that some Scottish companies are still exporting products to Russia following its illegal and unprovoked invasion of Ukraine and in spite of sanctions imposed by the West ( " Scotland exports ? 26m of drink to Russia since Ukraine war " , December 15 ) . @@119158606 <p> In one of Brazil 's most deforested Amazonian states , Rond ? nia , an isolated community is thriving . They are experts at hunting with long bows and at protecting their land from unwanted visitors with traps of hidden hardwood spikes so sturdy they can take out a tractor tyre . These spikes that hobbled a vehicle driven by a team from Brazil 's National Indigenous Peoples Foundation ( Funai ) earlier this year -- and ended its mission in the Massaco Indigenous territory . <p> No one knows what they call themselves , the Massaco is the name given to them after the river that runs through their domain near Brazil 's border with Bolivia . The Massaco are one of the 28 isolated communities confirmed to be in Brazil . Another 85 have been reported but have not yet been confirmed through the rigorous evidence-gathering and bureaucratic hurdles required . <p> The spikes have been found with increasing frequency and ever closer to the base from which Funai veteran Altair Algayer oversees the protection of this 421,000-hectare ( 1.04m-acre ) territory . They would seem to send a message : stay out . <p> It was Algayer who placed cameras in the rainforest in an attempt to better quantify the population without risking contact . The images , taken in 2019 and 2024 , and published for the first time by the Guardian and the Brazilian newspaper O Globo , gave Algayer his first look at people he has been protecting for most of his career . It is also vital proof of the Massaco 's existence that will allow Funai to continue its work . <p> This image from February 2019 show a group of young Massaco people collecting tools left by Funai . Photograph : Funai <p> It has become clear from the images and from years of monitoring expeditions led by Algayer that the Massaco river people are becoming more numerous , a trend apparent among many uncontacted communities in the Amazon . For the Massaco , this is a marked change in fortune since the 1980s , when their land was filled with loggers and rubber tappers . At that time , Funai 's mandate was to attempt peaceful contact with Indigenous peoples who stood in the way of highways , new settlements and resource extraction . In 1987 , agents prepared to make contact by luring people along a trail of customary gifts of tools , metal pots , utensils and mirrors . <p> Algayer began working in Massaco in 1992 . Known as Alem ? o ( the German , after his ancestry ) , he has become a legend within Funai for his systematic documentation of the Massaco people and his dogged protection of their land . <p> The territory has become a model . Funai and federal agencies have driven deforestation to zero within its boundaries in a region where forest loss is rampant . <p> Algayer says that in the early 90s he estimated a population of 100 to 120 people . Now , he estimates 50 families , each with four to five members , putting the total number of inhabitants at 200-250 . Tiny bows , toys and small footprints indicate children -- signs that families are growing . <p> Temporary shelters made from babassu palms can be up to five meters tall and are used while the Massaco are hunting and gathering in the forest . Photograph : Funai <p> " On our most recent expeditions and in satellite images , we 've seen more new tapiris thatched huts , so I would n't be surprised if there are 300 individuals , " he says . <p> The new Massaco images were taken at a spot where Funai has periodically left metal tools , machetes and axes . The gifts , once used to lure people into contact , are now employed to avert it <p> Over the years , his team has mapped 174 tapiris , photographed thousands of artefacts , created maps of the Massaco 's trails , and learned about their seasonal movements so that Funai can arrive in a location just weeks after the families have left . They learned that the Massaco burn areas of natural savanna at the beginning of the rainy season and then move there when they are freshly sprouting . <p> " By locating the hotspots recorded in satellite images in July and August , we know in advance ... where they will settle to spend the next rainy season , from December to April , " says Algayer . <p> It is common to find bows and arrows in abandoned shelters . The stout bows are between 2.9 and 3.2 metres in length ; the arrows are nearly as long . The points are made from sharpened bamboo tied using tucum pallm fibres . Photograph : undefined/Funai <p> The bows and arrows found at abandoned Massaco camps can exceed three metres , among the longest ever encountered in the Amazon . <p> " How they shoot the arrow , we have no idea . Other Indigenous people also try to understand , laugh and say it 's impossible . Perhaps lying down , they say , but to this day , we have no answer to this mystery , " Algayer says . <p> Anthropologist Amanda Villa has joined Algayer on expeditions and talked to neighbouring communities . She says the Massaco are distinguished from neighbouring peoples not just by the long bows but also tall tapiris , extensive use of spikes , placement of animal skulls on poles , long hair , moustaches , and lack of piercings or jewellery . One Tupari Indian who knows several of the region 's Indigenous languages overheard a Massaco couple chatting and reported not understanding a word . <p> " That 's why many Funai experts suspect they came from the other side of the Guapor ? River , from Bolivia , " Villa says . The Sirion ? people , in particular , used similar bows , tapiri construction and grooming . " But these are guesses . We ca n't say anything for sure . " <p> Animal skulls are stacked on branches in displays that puzzle Funai experts . They may be trophies or offerings ; no one knows their significance for the Massaco . Photograph : Funai <p> The new images were taken at a spot where Funai has periodically left metal tools , machetes and axes . The gifts , once used to lure people into contact , are now employed to avert it . The practice , employed in other Indigenous territories , dissuades uncontacted people from going to farms or logging camps to acquire tools . <p> Analysing the images , Algayer points to the apparent leader of the group . <p> " The oldest one holding the stick has the spike under his arm . The stick he holds serves as a staff , but it is used more for drilling holes in the ground to place the spikes . He has this leadership posture , helps to place the spikes , and tells where to place them , " says Algayer . <p> Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news , features and pictures , curated by our global development team <p> Enter your email address <p> Privacy Notice : Newsletters may contain info about charities , online ads , and content funded by outside parties . For more information see our Privacy Policy . We use Google reCaptcha to protect our website and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply . <p> after newsletter promotion <p> Machetes left as a gift by Funai are handed out among young Massaco people . Photograph : Funai <p> There are three men aged between 30 and 40 , with moustaches and longer hair , but the others are younger . " They are vigorous , strong . They are not going hungry , " he says . <p> The growth of isolated peoples is wonderful news , but it alerts us to the imminent risk of contact , not only because it could lead to a need for more land , but also because of climate change <p> Altair Algayer , Funai agency <p> Before these images , only one Funai agent had seen the Massaco . In 2014 , Paulo Pereira da Silva , 64 , one of Algayer 's staff , was making coffee at around 2pm when he heard knocking outside . " I went into the office and looked out the window , which has a protective screen , and I saw two people at the foot of the stairs . I froze , " he recalls . <p> Naked and without arrows , the two men were placing spikes in front of the stairs . " An older man was making holes with a stake made of aroeira wood and a young boy was arranging the spikes , " Pereira says . <p> Pereira shouted at the pair . The older one stared at him and the younger one ran , leaving the spikes on the ground . Six other individuals came forward and they planted a trail of spikes for at least two kilometres . <p> Hammocks made from tucum fibres made into thick ropes that are between 1.8 and 2 metres long , found in tapiris . The hammocks are large enough to fit two people . Photograph : Funai <p> Other isolated peoples with sufficiently large , effectively protected forests mirror the Massaco 's population growth . On a July expedition in the Rio Pardo Kawahiva territory in neighbouring Mato Grosso state , Funai experts found evidence of a people they estimate has doubled in size in 25 years . <p> A 2023 report in the science journal Nature analysed satellite images showing that uncontacted people in the western Brazilian state of Acre expanded their crops by 17% each year from 2015-2022 . The same study registered the growth of the uncontacted Moxihat ? t ? a , a subgroup of the larger Yanomami people , in northern Amazon . The Moxihat ? t ? a lean huge rectangular thatch panels in a ring . Each panel shelters a family . In the late 2010s , their new village had an enlarged ring , from 16 to 17 panels . In 2020 , they moved again , this time erecting two rings with a total of 23 panels . <p> Similar growth was seen in the Javari valley after its demarcation as Indigenous land in 2001 . The 8.5m-hectare ( 21m-acre ) wilderness that borders Peru has 16 isolated peoples -- 10 confirmed -- the most of any territory in Brazil . <p> Beto Marubo , a representative of the Union of Indigenous Peoples of the Javari Valley and Brazil 's leading native advocate for isolated tribes , says that before the Javari territory was demarcated , people were dying . " Their longhouses were tiny , there were loggers everywhere , there were drug traffickers , every kind of bad actor , " he says . " The Javari was a no man 's land . " <p> After demarcation and firm enforcement , Indigenous communities started cultivating the land , he says . " They were n't getting malaria any more . Today , you will see a new trend in Javari . There are places we had no clue isolated people might go , and now they are showing up . " <p> In this image it is thought that the man leaning against the tree has a position of prominence and leadership over the group . Photograph : Funai <p> Such successes raise a new problem : their areas may soon not be big enough . <p> " The growth of isolated peoples is undoubtedly wonderful news , but on the other hand , it alerts us to the imminent risk of contact , not only because it could lead to a need for more land , but also because of climate change , " Algayer says . " If the isolated peoples run out of water in their streams , they will go closer to other populations . " <p> Janete Carvalho , Funai 's territorial protection director , echoes these concerns . " We will face this at some point . Nobody knows what this will lead to because , in principle , there 's a real chance that contact will happen , " she says . " Of course , we do n't want that . " <p> This piece is published in conjunction with O Globo . John Reid is the co-author of Ever Green : Saving Big Forests to Save the Planet . Daniel Biasetto is the content editor at the Brazilian daily O Globo . They were supported on this series by a grant from the Ford Foundation .

@@119158966 <h> 52 good news stories you may have missed in 2024 <h> Do n't despair ! There are lots of ways the world got better this year , says Yasmin Choudury <p> It was n't all doom and gloom in 2024 ! This year has welcomed in medical breakthroughs , technology firsts , conservation progress and new laws for a fairer society . So if you want to feel all warm inside this winter , here are 52 ways the world became a better place in the last 12 months . <h> 1 . Amazon deforestation slows <p> AFP <p> Deforestation in Brazil 's Amazon rainforest is at its lowest rate in at least eight years , according to Brazilian government satellite data . In the year to July , 4,300 sq km of rainforest were lost . That is a decrease of almost 46 per cent on the previous year and is the smallest area destroyed in the world 's largest rainforest since this method of data collection began in 2016. <h> 2 . Visionary surgery <p> EVELINA CHILDREN 'S HOSPITAL <p> A three-year-old girl with a rare form of blindness has had her sight restored thanks to pioneering keyhole surgery . Khadijah Chaudhry , from Hull , was born with a genetic condition called Leber congenital amaurosis-4 , which meant she could only see light and dark and was likely to lose all vision by the age of four . Healthy copies of a gene were injected into her eyes at Evelina London Children 's Hospital , part of Guy 's and St Thomas ' in south London . Several months on , her vision is improving . <h> 3 . Live longer and prosper <p> Global life expectancy has increased by 6.2 years since 1990 , according to a study published in The Lancet . Eastern sub-Saharan Africa had the greatest increase of any region , with 10.7 years added over three decades . Ethiopia recorded the biggest increase of any country , at 18.2 years . The rise is largely attributed to a reduction in deaths from diarrhoeal diseases and lower respiratory infections such as tuberculosis . <h> 4 . Manchester 's mossy miracle <p> Greater Manchester 's water quality is improving thanks to volunteers planting sphagnum moss . The scheme began ten years ago at the Dove Stone Reservoir on a hilltop at the edge of Oldham . The reservoir is surrounded by peat bogs that turn rainwater brown and silty ; the moss acts as a natural filter for the rainwater flowing into the reservoir as well as offering flood protection . In March the volunteers planted their millionth moss cutting . <h> Advertisement <h> 5 . Ticked off <p> A pill that kills ticks has shown positive results in a human trial , giving hope it may protect against Lyme disease . The tick-borne disease , for which there is no human vaccine , causes fatigue , fever and , in severe cases , facial paralysis . Up to 3,500 cases are diagnosed every year in the UK . In February the California-based Tarsus Pharmaceuticals found that its drug -- a new formulation of lotilaner , a parasite killer for pets -- can kill ticks on people 24 hours after they take the medication , with the effects lasting for up to 30 days . <h> 6 . Giant redwoods soar in the UK <p> Giant redwoods are thriving in Britain . About half a million giant sequoias and closely related coastal redwoods have put down roots here , according to a study published by the Royal Society in March . Most are the giant sequoia variety , the world 's largest trees by volume , which were introduced by the Victorians as symbols of wealth . In their native Sierra Nevada mountains in California , only 80,000 mature giant sequoias remain . Britain 's are n't yet as massive , but they are growing at a similar rate . In California they can reach 90m and live for up to 2,000 years ; in the UK the tallest has grown to 55m so far . <h> 7 . Equal pay day <p> The UK 's gender pay gap has fallen to 11.6 per cent , the narrowest on record . On average , women now earn 88p for every pound a man makes . That 's still 12p too little -- though seven years ago , when it became mandatory for employers to report the disparity in earnings , the gap was 12.8 per cent , so it 's progress . PwC ( 96p v ? 1 ) and Greggs ( 97p v ? 1 ) are close to closing the gap for good . <h> Advertisement <h> 8 . Return of the giant sei whale <p> Giant sei whales have been spotted off Argentina 's Patagonia coast for the first time in a century . Hunting brought the blue-grey mammals , which can grow to a length of about 20m , to the brink of extinction in the 1920s and 1930s . Commercial whaling bans over the past five decades have allowed the population to recover -- albeit slowly . They breed only once every two to three years and can live for up to seventy years . <h> 9 . Breezy living <p> For the first time over a 12-month period , wind power has overtaken gas to become Britain 's largest source of electricity . In the year leading up to May , wind generated 32 per cent of our electricity . Gas , with 31 per cent , lost the top spot it had held for 28 years . Stronger wind speeds and new offshore wind farms have driven the change to clean , homegrown energy . The shift is important not just to the environment but for our energy security -- the more we generate , the less we need to rely on gas imports . <h> 10 . Tidy job , Wales <p> Wales has been named as the second-best country in the world for recycling . The nation , which recycles 58.6 per cent of its municipal waste , was pipped by Austria ( 59 per cent ) in the global rankings . Northern Ireland made the top 10 , coming in at 9th place . England just missed out at 11 , and Scotland was 15th. <h> 11 . Eco concrete <p> Cambridge University researchers say they have found a " miracle " way of producing eco-friendly concrete . Concrete is the most widely used substance on Earth after water , but producing it emits 7.5 per cent of all human-made carbon dioxide . The Cambridge team learnt to recycle old cement -- the key polluting ingredient of concrete -- in the heat of the steel recycling industry 's electric arc furnaces , slashing the carbon footprint. <h> 12 . The Iberian lynx effect <p> GETTY IMAGES <p> Spain and Portugal 's Iberian lynx population has reached 2,021 , pushing the species away from extinction . In 2000 there were just 94 left , compelling the countries ' governments , the European Union and the World Wildlife Fund to create four breeding centres . So far 372 of the big cats have been reintroduced to the wild and the lynx 's conservation status could reach " favourable " by 2040 . <h> Advertisement <h> 13 . Same-sex Thais to tie the knot <p> Thailand has become the first country in southeast Asia to legalise same-sex marriage . The legislation , passed this month , changes the definition of marriage from " a husband and wife " to " marriage partners " . Couples will have equal rights in areas including healthcare consent , child adoption and inheritance . It comes into effect in January . <h> 14 . Butterflies return <p> ALAMY <p> One of Britain 's most striking butterfly species has been reintroduced into the Welsh countryside decades after local extinction . Hundreds of marsh fritillary butterflies , which have distinctive orange and cream wings , were released on Llantrisant Common in Rhondda Cynon Taf earlier this year by conservationists who had bred them from wild caterpillars . The butterflies have since been observed mating and laying eggs . <h> 15 . Black rhino born <p> A black rhino raised at a North Yorkshire zoo has given birth in Rwanda . Olmoti moved to Akagera National Park in 2019 from Flamingo Land in Malton and has been spotted with a calf . The father , Mandela , was also sent from the zoo . With a population of about 6,500 , black rhinos are critically endangered -- but breeding programmes in Europe have been so successful that some are being returned to their homelands . <h> 16 . Epilepsy implant <p> A teenager from Somerset with severe epilepsy has become the first patient in the world to be fitted with a brain implant to control seizures . Oran Knowlson , 13 , had the device fitted as part of a trial at Great Ormond Street Hospital . Since the age of three he has suffered hundreds of seizures a day . The signals from the implant have reduced these attacks by up to 80 per cent . <h> Advertisement <h> 17 . Sweet success <p> The sugar tax introduced by the Conservative government in 2018 has significantly reduced the amount of sugar eaten and drunk by children in the UK . The levy was for manufacturers of soft drinks with more than 5g of sugar per 100ml . In the year after it was imposed , children consumed 4.8g less sugar a day , of which 3g was attributed to the reduced sugar content of soft drinks . Adults consumed 10.9g less sugar a day overall . <h> 18 . Blood hound <p> A seven-year-old Gordon setter called Sharwood has become the first dog in the UK to make 40 blood donations , saving the lives of an estimated 160 dogs . Canine donors retire aged eight and Sharwood , from Eaton Bray in Bedfordshire , gave his final dose in Northampton in July , at an event held by Pet Blood Bank UK . Sharwood slept through the procedure -- something his owner , Sue Mitchell , puts down to his relaxed nature and cool demeanour as a former show dog . <h> 19 . Grandparent power <p> A new law in Sweden allows parents to transfer some of their paid parental leave to grandparents during their child 's first year . Couples can reallocate 45 days of their joint 480-day allowance ; single parents can pass on 90 days . The move recognises that many grandparents wanting to support their families are still in work too . Sweden pioneered paid parental leave that can be split between parents 50 years ago -- a benefit since replicated around the world . <h> 20 . Elephant freed <p> The last elephant in South Africa 's national zoo has been released back into the wild after 40 years of captivity . After campaigning by animal welfare groups , Charlie is making Shambala Private Game Reserve in Limpopo his new home . <h> Advertisement <h> 21 . Child marriage banned <p> Child marriage has now been banned in Sierra Leone , and Colombia has taken steps to enact a similar law . Sierra Leone had one of the highest rates of child marriage in the world , with about a third of girls affected . Its new Prohibition of Child Marriage Act imposes a minimum jail term of 15 years and/or a fine of about ? 3,200 on any adult involved in the marriage of a girl under 18 , including those attending the ceremony . In Colombia , congress voted in favour of changing a law that allowed minors as young as 14 to get married with parental consent . A new bill makes 18 the minimum age for marriage . <h> 22 . Beaver baby boom <p> Britain is having a beaver baby boom 22 years after the animals were reintroduced following a 400-year extinction . Beavers had been hunted for their fur , meat and the glandular secretion castoreum , which was used in perfume and medicines , but kits ( babies ) have been spotted this summer at wetlands in London , Northumberland , Canterbury and along the River Spey in Scotland . There are now about 1,500 beavers in Scotland and 800 in England . <h> 23 . Plastic fantastic <p> Lego has announced plans to make its bricks entirely from renewable or recycled plastic by 2032 . There were an estimated 98,820 overdose deaths over the year -- under 100,000 for the first time since 2021 . Better access to treatment may be a factor in the drop . <h> 27 . @@119159104 <p> Chocolatiers are facing a Christmas to forget as record prices for cocoa are forcing them into hard choices about the range , size and quality of their products . <p> The price of cocoa -- the key ingredient in quality chocolate -- hit a new high of $12,605 per metric tonne last Wednesday , surpassing peaks reached before Easter and nearly doubling from just two months ago . <p> A combination of climate change , poor harvests and shrinking inventories has created a persistently tight market for the beloved commodity , leaving chocolate makers scrambling for ways to maintain margins and meet demand during the Christmas to Easter season . <p> " This is the new normal , unfortunately , " said Karl Marnane , managing director of Butlers Chocolates , which sources its cocoa months in advance . " Christmas is all about boxed chocolate with fillings , but Easter is about solid chocolate -- there 's no way around that . You 'll see a serious reduction in range and size . " <p> The cocoa market has been on a tear since last January after years of relative stability kept prices generally under the $3,000 mark . Those conditions helped foster a boom in premium chocolate , with producers able to afford the highest quality pods . <h> Advertisement <p> But bad weather and crop diseases in west Africa , where three quarters of the world 's supply originates , sent prices skyrocketing in 2024 . Now mass-market chocolate makers have to pay premium prices while luxury chocolate producers are getting priced out in some cases . <p> " In June , we got a notification that our prices would be going up and all of our price agreements had to be broken , " said Karen Keane , co-founder of Bean and Goose , an artisanal chocolatier in Wexford . " Within six weeks , our raw materials went up 33 per cent . We had to absorb some of it -- there 's only so much you can pass on . " <p> She said corporate gifting had slowed down this year while independent retailers were " hesitant " to stock their chocolate bars at higher price points . Much of the blame , according to Keane , belongs to the big manufacturers who are " still not implementing sustainable practices " in key growing regions . <p> " The price may stabilise , but it will never go back down , " she said . <p> Ironically , one reason behind the cocoa squeeze is the EU anti-deforestation regulation set to take effect in the new year . Under the rules , no cocoa grown on recently deforested land can be sold in the EU . <h> Advertisement <p> While the law is meant to stamp out some of the unsustainable practices derided by Keane , it is putting new costs on growers and wholesalers to establish traceability . It 's also inciting a wave of bulk buying under the old regime in case supply gets even tighter next year , according to Marnane . <p> Forecasters are expecting better production levels next year , which may moderate prices somewhat . But analysts are not ruling out the crop failures and adverse weather that characterised the market this year . <p> " While prospects for the 2024-25 marketing year are looking better , there are still concerns over weather developments in west Africa and what it could mean for output this season , " the Dutch bank ING said in a note for commodities traders .

Operating from a retro-futuristic space station orbiting above the ( newly-formed ) Greater Baltic Ocean , you 're trying to piece together the history of what happened to our poor and abused planet while also communing with some kind of extra-dimensional entity that speaks to you through glitches in a minigolf game . <p> From the little bit I 've played ( and I would n't want to spoil you beyond this point anyhow ) , it 's an audiovisual treat . It 's also sometimes about deep shower thoughts on games , with the developer 's own podcast -- Mini Mini Talk Talk , viewable independently here on YouTube -- being used to deliver ideas and chopped up to provide hints at where the next branch of its non-linear plot lies . @@119161185 <h> The rise in community gardens across Hampshire <h> A look at Hampshire 's community gardens schemes <p> Relaxing in or working in , community gardens offer multi-purpose benefits ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) <p> The greater awareness of the physical and mental health benefits of being in nature and gardening is seeing a rise in community gardens across the country , including here in Hampshire . <p> Community gardens are for everyone , whether just visiting and chatting , getting hands on or using the space therapeutically . <p> Giving back and helping those in pain or distress by sharing your knowledge of gardening , or whatever skills and experience you have , is of real value to the community , as Hampshire Life has covered . <p> Turn an unused patch into a communal space ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) Wellbeing , the relief from loneliness , and connecting with nature became top priorities during lockdown and there was a real surge of interest for home gardeners to cultivate their patch no matter the size , often helped along by existing community gardens and groups who imparted knowledge and advice with enthusiasm . <p> Green social prescribing such as therapeutic community gardening continues to show benefits with over 400 places on offer across England . Add the economic situation , stresses about finances and food poverty , the chance to get into a garden , especially if you do n't have one at home , becomes even more valuable . <p> Sharing the harvest is part of many communal gardens ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) There is no doubt that humans have an innate connection with nature and also the need to socialise and belong to a community of people with similar interests . Studies have shown how your heart rate and blood pressure drops after only three or four minutes in a garden , and that ' green exercise ' from gardening also benefits physical and mental health . Community gardens make gardening accessible , bringing people together from different walks of life with a shared interest in growing and nurturing , creating an enriching experience . For many , community gardening equates to growing food , for others it 's the chance to learn new skills , meet new people , green a local area or conserve wildlife habitats . You are sharing the process and benefits of caring for the environment , while helping others , and there is often the ripple effect to the surrounding area , attracting more wildlife , helping people eat more healthily , and even creating a safer place to live as cleaner , greener streets have been linked to lower crime rates and reduced anti-social behaviour . <p> Hart 's Community Garden is a garden for everyone ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) Hart 's Community Garden , within Edenbrook Country Park in Fleet , is an example of the wonderful work our community gardens do in Hampshire . The creation of the garden is a collaboration between Hart District Council 's Countryside team and Hart Voluntary Action with the aim to offer opportunities for local people to improve their physical and mental health by getting involved in a social , creative and supportive growing space . Everyone is welcome to become a member and join in to help grow a variety of vegetables , fruits and flowers in raised beds and polytunnels . <p> Wide fully accessible paths allow easy access and there is a large pergola ideal for a chat , a piece of cake and a cup of tea , while looking out over this peaceful environment . Members come along for a green , nurturing workout , make new friends and improve their wellbeing . There is also a programme of events through the year to get involved in , including creative workshops and wildlife talks . <p> Connect with the earth and grow food using organic principles ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) Getting the young involved in the joys of nurturing plants together helps build the understanding that they are a part of a community and share custodianship of the planet , and it 's both fun and rewarding . With children in mind , Patrick 's Patch , located opposite Fairweather 's Garden Centre in Beaulieu , has been encouraging little green fingers since opening in 2008 through their abundant productive garden . The garden is used as an educational project for primary school children and young people with additional needs , to give them gardening skills and also understand where their food comes from . An impressive array of fruit , vegetables , herbs and cut flowers are tended by a head gardener and a team of volunteers along with the regular groups of school children , and the garden , open year round , attracts many visitors who take away ideas for their own plot . The key message that is conveyed to the children is that they are part of nature and nature needs to be respected . <p> Communal gardens allow you to garden with other keen gardeners ( Image : Leigh Clapp ) New this year to the community garden landscape is the Garden for Mind at Longstock Park Nursery on the Leckford Estate , which has been created as a sanctuary for mental health and overall wellbeing . This on-going collaborative project , involving volunteers , sponsors and supporters , is transforming a previously unused area on the estate , part of the John Lewis Partnership , into a space that will enable the independent charity , Andover Mind , to hold programmes and activities , such as gardening therapy and mindfulness sessions for service users . Opened in July this initiative is also an asset for the whole community to find peace , tranquillity and connection with the outdoors . Additionally the garden aims to help educate on climate change challenges and biodiversity loss . Features include a sensory garden , nature pond , fruit and vegetables and relaxing patio . As with all community gardens , volunteers are always welcome to help maintain the planting and maintenance . <p> If you fancy creating a community garden or project , it could be that you just need the landowner 's permission and a group of willing volunteers to transform a derelict patch . The RHS can support new groups with resources and training through their communities ' team online at rhs.org.uk . The NGS offers community garden grants via ngs.org.uk and the Hampshire Gardens Trust offers support and advice at hgt.org.uk . <h> Comments : Our rules <p> We want our comments to be a lively and valuable part of our community - a place where readers can debate and engage with the most important local issues . It first reached Cabo Delgado , then travelled further inland to Niassa and Nampula . <p> The country 's INGD said the cyclone impacted the education and health sector . More than 109,793 students were affected , with school infrastructure severely damaged . <p> Some 52 sanitary units were damaged , the INGD said , which further risks access to essential health services . This is exacerbated further in areas where access to healthcare facilities were already limited before the cyclone . <p> Daniel Chapo , leader of Mozambique 's ruling party , told local media the government is mobilising support on " all levels " in response to the cyclone . <p> Speaking during a visit to Cabo Delgado on Sunday , one of the most badly affected areas , Chapo said the government is working alongside the INGD to ensure those affected in the provinces of Mec ? fi , Nampula , Memba and Niassa can rebuild . <p> In Mayotte , Chido was the worst storm to hit the archipelago in 90 years , leaving tens of thousands of people reeling from the catastrophe . <p> The interior ministry in its latest update confirmed 35 people had died . <p> Mayotte 's prefect previously told local media the death toll could rise significantly once the damage was fully assessed , warning it would " definitely be several hundred " and could reach thousands . <p> More than 1,300 officers were deployed to support the local population . <p> One week on , many residents still lack basic necessities , while running water is making a gradual return to the territory 's capital . The ministry has advised people to boil water for three minutes before consuming it . <p> Around 100 tonnes of equipment are being delivered each day , the ministry said , as an air bridge was built between Mayotte , Reunion and mainland France . <p> In a statement on Friday , interior minister Bruno Retailleau said 80 tonnes of food and 50 tonnes of water had been distributed across Mayotte that day . <p> Tropical cyclones are characterised by very high wind speeds , heavy rainfall , and storm surges , which are short-term rises to sea-levels . This often causes widespread damage and flooding . <p> The cyclone , the INGD said , " highlights once again , the vulnerability of social infrastructures to climate change and the need for resilient planning to mitigate future impacts " . <p> Assessing the exact influence of climate change on individual tropical cyclones can be challenging due to the complexity of these storm systems . But rising temperatures do affect these storms in measurable ways . <p> The UN 's climate body , the IPCC , previously said there is " high confidence " that humans have contributed to increases in precipitation associated with tropical cyclones , and " medium confidence " that humans have contributed to the higher probability of a tropical cyclone being more intense .

@@119183551 <p> The Spirit of Queensland rolled out of town slowly , gathering pace as we left the Brisbane River . The city 's glittering highrises and the celebrated Story Bridge drew behind us , chugging through suburbs where glimpses of idyllic childhoods flashed by : sprawling gardens , backyard pools and enormous trampolines . <p> Regular passenger Mark was off to see mates in Townsville .
