@@119424040 <h> Roz Foyer : Scots are losing their jobs as the Just Transition goes backwards <h> Scots are losing their jobs as the Just Transition goes backwards <p> Members of the Unite union march and rally at the Scottish Parliament in protest at Petroineos plans to close Grangemouth oil refinery ( Image : Jane Barlow ) <p> Next year , 2025 , will be the first year since 1882 , that the UK has had no coal generated power . 143 years ago this month , the world 's first coal-fired power station opened at number 57 Holborn Viaduct . The country 's last coal power station , at Ratcliffe-on-Soar , finished operations last September . In Scotland , it is nearly a decade since Longannet Power Station closed . At peak production it was the largest coal-fired power station in Europe producing enough electricity to power over two million homes . <p> Globally however , coal powered electricity reached a new high in 2024 , fuelled by continuing high levels of production in China and growing demand in India . At least we can say that demand for coal is set to level off in coming years . <p> Yet the pace of change in energy appears ironically glacial when considered with the worsening of the environmental catastrophe across the world , and here at home . For all the attention in recent years , peaking around the UN climate summit in Glasgow , it appears the temperature has dropped when it comes to the focus given to global warming at least . <p> A recent YouGov poll showed a falling proportion of people consider the environment as a major issue . When asked , which of the following do you think will be the most important issues facing the country over the next five years ? Just 20% of respondents chose the environment , down from 26% in 2023 . The dismissal of the environment as a key issue in the UK , reflects the huge number of immediate pressures facing people across the country from years of higher prices and lagging pay packets . <p> In another question in the same poll , just half of respondents thought that their individual actions would have an impact on tackling climate change , compared to over three-quarters who said that government and business could make a difference . And they are right . The Scottish Government 's favoured approach , dishing out grants for homeowners for solar panels , encouraging a switch to electric cars , or part-paying the costs for full blown retrofitting are the preserve of a relatively small proportion of the population . <p> But so too is the vast majority of pollution . <p> A recent study found that 50 of the world 's richest billionaires will produce more emissions from luxury yachts in under a year , than the average person in the world would in 860 years . This dynamic plays out in Scotland too , with Future Economy Scotland research showing that the carbon footprint of the average household in the poorest 5% of income is less than a quarter the average household from the richest 5% . <p> The biggest contribution working class people have made to reducing emissions in Scotland has been involuntarily losing their jobs , whether at Longannet , in offshore oil and gas , or manufacturing . It 's not exactly a strong sell . Yet at the same time , the impacts of climate change are already hitting working people 's pockets -- food prices are up , energy prices are up , insurance prices are up . The changing climate is a factor in all three . <p> Grangemouth refinery is set to be axed ( Image : free ) It is in response to this imbalance of responsibility and benefits , that the trade union movement developed the concept of Just Transition . When it comes to the environment , workers and their families have a common interest that is not shared with profit-hungry private companies . Those with the broadest shoulders must contribute , and those living and working in their community should expect security and opportunity , not decline and precarity . <p> The Just Transition Commission , an independent body of experts appointed by the Scottish Government , has warned that Scotland is now " at risk of going backwards on just transition . " They point to a gap between " abstract aspiration " and " the lived realities of people across the country " . <p> As we move into 2025 , there is a toxic combination brewing . People in Scotland , particularly energy workers , have been promised the earth -- in sustainability and economically . Yet all around them is a chasm between their lives and the lives of the wealthiest , and in where expectations fall when it comes to changes to meet climate targets . This combination is a growing reason for the abandonment of traditional political parties and the growth of support for parties of the far right . <p> For all the greenwashing , the disconnect between the expectations currently placed on individual consumers by government and business and the responsibility they place on themselves could not be starker . The two-pronged approach of prioritising profits for multinationals ( spoiler alert : saving the planet might not be a profit-making exercise ) and placing too high a premium on individual behaviour change is a failed strategy which risks further alienating people from the existential threat we collectively face . <p> And yes , that includes our members who work in oil and gas who find it impossible to countenance cuts in oil and gas production when the alternative employment they are being offered is bleak or non-existent . It includes our members across industry who reject car parking levies when there is not an affordable and efficient public transport system they can rely upon . <p> Returning to Ratcliffe-On-Soar , workers and their trade unions report that the closure has been well-managed . With a clear lead-in time and partnership with the unions , plans were made to provide the time and resource to support redeployment and reskilling . <p> Compare this situation to that faced by refinery workers at Grangemouth . Less than 18 months ' notice of closure ( except for the Scottish Government who reportedly had a little longer ) , and no serious role for the trade union on-site in considering alternative and future options . The Scottish and UK Government have thrown money to support PetroIneos plans from 2030 onwards , without any thought to those at the site who are set to be out of a job in 2025 . <p> Just transition remains of short and long-term importance to working people . Failures by government and self-interest of companies does n't change the picture . Climate risks are increasingly hitting people 's pockets , while risks from the energy transition playing out globally are not being managed here in Scotland . <p> Refinery workers at Grangemouth have developed their plan to protect jobs at the refinery and the longer term through green production -- demonstrating once more the instinct of working people to put their jobs , their communities , and the environment first . In the absence of a response from those sitting on the levers of power today to match this , we will continue to support workers to push their answers into reality across the country . <h> Why are you making commenting on The Herald only available to subscribers ? <p> It should have been a safe space for informed debate , somewhere for readers to discuss issues around the biggest stories of the day , but all too often the below the line comments on most websites have become bogged down by off-topic discussions and abuse . <p> heraldscotland.com is tackling this problem by allowing only subscribers to comment . <p> We are doing this to improve the experience for our loyal readers and we believe it will reduce the ability of trolls and troublemakers , who occasionally find their way onto our site , to abuse our journalists and readers . We also hope it will help the comments section fulfil its promise as a part of Scotland 's conversation with itself . <p> We are lucky at The Herald . @@119424469 <p> " Staff members all said they had never seen so many birds before . They suddenly flew in from outside the airport , " an anonymous airport official told the South Korean site , OhmyNews . <p> Between 1990 and 2022 , there were just shy of 300,000 " wildlife strikes " globally , according to a report by the US Federal Aviation Administration and the US Department of Agriculture . <p> With shifting migratory patterns , quieter planes and rising populations of large birds , the problem is only getting worse . <p> Korean footage of the Jeju Air Boeing 737-800 which burst into flames , killing 179 of the 181 passengers on board - AFP via Getty Images <h> Why do bird strikes occur ? <p> With somewhere between 50 billion and 430 billion birds worldwide , and around 115,000 aircraft take-offs and landings per day , bird strikes are inevitable . They are particularly common because birds are drawn to the sort of wide , open areas where airports tend to be built . It is not uncommon for airports to be surrounded by wetlands or open bodies of water , for example , which also serve as nesting and feeding territory for birds . <p> The vast majority of bird strikes ( around 92 per cent ) occur during take-off or landing , below 500ft . They tend to occur during the migratory season , when species go in search of food and warmer climates . However , due to climate change , these migratory patterns are becoming harder to predict . <h> A problem on the rise <p> In the majority of bird strike incidents , pilots are able to land the aircraft safely with little or no damage . Often , a bird strike will go unnoticed until the aircraft is inspected back on the runway and dents or blood are detected . But there are exceptions . Flocks of larger birds can destroy engines ; it is estimated that between 1988 and 2022 , 305 aircraft were destroyed by bird strikes , killing 464 people . <p> One of the highest-profile bird strikes occurred in 2009 , when a US Airways flight departing from New York 's LaGuardia Airport was forced to make an emergency landing into the Hudson River after colliding with a flock of Canada geese . The story of how Captain Chesley " Sully " Sullenberger III safely landed the Airbus A320 near Midtown Manhattan was dramatised in the 2016 film Sully : Miracle on the Hudson . <p> After the incident , authorities in New York took the controversial step of culling hundreds of geese to prevent a repeat event , and wildlife biologists at JFK Airport provoked outrage after they shot two snowy owls to prevent them from colliding with aircraft . But the awareness around bird strikes following the " Miracle on the Hudson " , and resulting debate around bird culling around the world , failed to slow down the number of incidents that occur per year . <p> " Aircraft collisions with birds and other wildlife ( wildlife strikes ) have become a growing concern for aviation safety , " wrote the authors of the Federal Aviation Administration/US Department of Agriculture paper . In 1990 , there were 1,800 incidents in the USA -- in 2019 , there were 17,357 reported incidents , equating to just shy of 47 daily events . Part of this is due to better reporting and the rapid growth of global air traffic , but there are other factors at play . <p> Thanks to successful environmental initiatives , populations of large bird species are growing globally . The population of resident Canada geese in the United States , for example , has increased from 1 million in 1990 to 4.5 million in 2021 . Birds are also adapting to urban environments , creating a greater risk of collisions with aircraft . <p> Another factor is that planes are bigger than ever before , meaning birds have to fly further to avoid a collision . In addition , modern turbofan engines are quieter than in the past , making it more difficult for birds to detect oncoming aircraft . A similar phenomenon is occurring on the roads , where pedestrians are almost twice as likely to be hit by an electric or hybrid vehicle than by a petrol or diesel car , according to the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health . <p> The South Korean Army combs through the site of the lethal plane crash at Muan International Airport , which occurred following a sudden bird strike - Bloomberg <h> How pilots and airlines prepare for bird strikes <p> Brian Smith , a pilot with a British cargo airline who has previously flown with Ryanair , Emirates and Air2000 ( later FirstChoice ) , says that bird strikes can not be replicated on simulators and therefore no specific training takes place . <p> However , certain measures can help to prevent a serious collision , he says . <p> " In flight we rarely fly above 250 knots below 10,000ft and never below 5,000ft . This reduces the energy released if a bird should be struck at these lower altitudes , and therefore the damage they cause . During the approach we switch on all the external lights which birds do see and will invariably try to avoid . <p> " It is impossible to manoeuvre an aircraft away from a bird . Attempting doing so would almost certainly result in putting the aircraft into an undesirable attitude near the ground . In any case if you see a bird at all , it comes into your vision so fleetingly , that you generally only get a startle effect as it hits , or bypasses the aircraft . <p> " I have had a few in my time , mostly with Ryanair , who fly to more isolated and rural airports where it 's more prevalent . None of them were problematic and we were able to continue home to base . <p> " Measures to mitigate the risk are largely ground based , and undertaken by airport authorities . Migration patterns are well studied and can sometimes influence airport schedules but only in a very limited way . Bird scaring is carried out sometimes when birds are congregating . They use flares and sometimes raptors to scare them off , " Brian Smith added . <p> Patrick Smith , a US pilot and author of the book Cockpit Confidential , explains how aircraft are designed to withstand bird strikes . <p> " As you 'd expect , aircraft components are built to tolerate such impacts . You can see web videos of bird carcasses being fired from a sort of chicken-cannon to test the resistance of windshields , intakes , and so forth , " he told Telegraph Travel in 2023 . <p> " Birds do n't clog an engine but can bend or fracture the internal blades , causing power loss . The heavier the bird , the greater the potential for harm . Flying at 250 knots the maximum allowable below 10,000ft , where most birds are found hitting an average-sized goose will subject the plane to an impact force of over 50,000 pounds . @@119424708 <p> The largest escape of Scottish farmed salmon for more than a decade has been uncovered after it was kept from the public for almost two years . <p> The release of about 80,000 farmed salmon threatens the country 's wild population as the genetically different fish can interbreed , leaving the offspring less suited to the wild . <p> Studies have found that the hybrid fish had low survival rates in freshwater rivers and could be less likely to cope with the warmer waters brought by climate change . <p> Farmed salmon can carry high levels of infection <p> TIMES PHOTOGRAPHER JAMES GLOSSOP <p> Under these pressures and after a 23 per cent decline in Atlantic salmon between 2006 and 2020 , wild salmon rose up last year 's red list of endangered species compiled by the International Union for Conservation of Nature . <p> The Green Britain Foundation , a sustainability charity founded by Dale Vince , the energy entrepreneur , discovered that the mass escape had happened in February 2023 . <h> Advertisement <p> The salmon smolts , which were about a year old and weighed about 100g each , were being transported in the tank of a ship from Loch Shin , in Sutherland , to Lochinver on the west coast of Scotland . Human error led to about 80,000 of the farmed fish escaping through an unsecured hatch . <p> The incident has remained unreported to the public until now because government officials say they can publicly record only the escapes that are linked to specific farm sites , leaving transport-related incidents outside their publicly accessible data . <p> Vince , a Labour donor and the founder of Ecotricity , said the mass escape " should be a wake-up call for us all " . <p> ROBERT PERRY FOR THE TIMES <p> He added : " We know fish in these farms carry high levels of infection and disease , which harms local wildlife even when they remain caged , but out in the wild this impact is multiplied many times over . It 's a disaster for the local environment . <p> " The fact that such a significant incident could go unreported for so long shows there are serious failings in the environmental monitoring of salmon factory farms . <h> Advertisement <p> " This incident underscores the urgent need for a complete reassessment of how we monitor and regulate the salmon farming industry . The health of our oceans and the integrity of our endangered wild salmon populations are at stake . " <p> Critics of salmon raised in open net pens in coastal waters have been warning for decades that it comes with an enormous environmental impact . Tens of millions of farmed fish suffer and die annually from sea lice , while escapees spread the lice , breed with wild fish and compromise their genetic fitness . Nutrient pollution from fish faeces wreaks havoc on coastal ecology , and treatments used on nets lead to copper and other materials contaminating local waters . <p> TIMES PHOTOGRAPHER JAMES GLOSSOP <p> The loss of 80,000 farmed fish was mentioned only briefly in the final sentence of the Scottish Fish Farm Production Survey 2023 , which was published on the Scottish government website on October 30 , 2024 . Apart from the number of escaped fish it did not give any details about the causes or date of the escape , nor the company or location involved . <p> The Green Britain Foundation submitted a freedom of information request to the Scottish government to find out more details . The response revealed that the fish belonged to Cooke Scotland , one of the leading producers of Scottish salmon and the largest producer of organic Scottish salmon . It has salmon farming operations in Orkney , Shetland , mainland Scotland and the north of England . <p> The Scottish government said in the FoI response that " the transporter involved in the escape incident has taken remedial action to avoid similar events in future " . <h> Advertisement <p> Escape data is usually updated regularly on a Scottish government website database , but as the escape did not come directly from a farm , the Scottish government said it could not find a way to include it in the usual way . <p> In an email seen by The Times , Lorna Munro , the epidemiology data manager for the Scottish government 's marine directorate , said : " We are currently considering the issue of reporting and transparency further . " <p> The Green Britain Foundation said the fact that officials were only considering changes to reporting requirements nearly two years after such a significant escape had occurred was " deeply concerning " . It said the mass escape starkly contradicted recent salmon industry assertions . <p> In October , Ben Hadfield , the chief operating officer of Mowi Scotland , the UK 's largest supplier of farm-raised salmon , told a Scottish government inquiry that " escape levels have dropped massively -- to one fish , out of all the fish held in Scotland " . <h> Advertisement <p> In 2022 there were two incidents in which a total of 52,463 farmed salmon escaped into the ocean . The previous year 19,686 escaped in a single incident . <p> Addressing these concerns in a recent House of Lords debate , Lord Forsyth of Drumlean , a Tory peer , said : " Escapees bring diseases to the wild population and whole rivers have been cleaned out of wild fish . " He said that salmon farming had " resulted in environmental damage to wild fish populations and threatened other species " . <p> The Green Britain Foundation said it wanted the implementation of stricter regulations for fish transport and containment , and " comprehensive environmental impact assessments of all aspects of salmon farming operations " . <p> A spokesman for Salmon Scotland , the industry trade body , said that Scottish salmon farmers " meet the highest animal health and welfare standards anywhere in the world and work incredibly hard to achieve zero escapes " . <h> Advertisement <p> He said : " It is inaccurate to suggest that these fish might be diseased , cause environmental damage , or pose any significant risk to wild breeding populations . @@119424729 <h> In a troubled world , Sir Keir Starmer 's right to roam <h> Faced with possibly the most challenging foreign policy agenda since the Cold War ended , the PM ca n't turn inwards <p> Tom Baldwin <p> Monday December 30 2024 , 9.00pm , The Times <p> A rare Westminster consensus has formed between jet-lagged political journalists and Downing Street 's even wearier political advisers about Sir Keir Starmer 's foreign travel . <p> Most seem to agree that , notwithstanding the prime minister 's much-needed family break this week , he has been spending too much time abroad . This latest piece of conventional wisdom holds that he should be focusing a lot more on fulfilling voters ' desire for down-to-earth change , which gave him such a stonkingly large parliamentary majority six months ago . <p> It 's why Starmer will start 2025 in " sleeves rolled-up " mode . Proposals for him to make a big foreign policy speech next month have been shelved and his new year video message to the nation tomorrow apparently contains no overt reference to the rest of the world . This will be followed by fresh announcements on cutting NHS waiting lists , one of the six " measurable milestones " unveiled this month on which he now wishes his " five missions " be judged -- all of which are determinedly domestic . <p> Certainly , Starmer 's globe-trotting since he entered Downing Street has been relentless , with tens of thousands of miles travelled across dozens of time zones to attend no fewer than eight summits , as well as seemingly endless bilateral meetings with leaders from nations big and small . At least one pollster has warned that the impression Starmer is always flying somewhere else has been mentioned , unfavourably , by some of Labour 's key voters in focus groups . <p> But no self-respecting prime minister can afford to ignore a turbulent and dangerous world right now . Israel 's brutal conflict in Gaza is having far-reaching consequences across the Middle East . Russia continues to grind deeper into Ukraine and America has elected a president who appears ready to take Europe 's security blanket away . Those wars have distracted from a terrible humanitarian crisis in Sudan and undermined efforts to reduce the impact of climate change , even as the prospect of a US-China trade war threatens the European economy and much else besides . <h> Advertisement <p> And while Starmer can not be expected to solve any of these problems by himself , he will neither retreat inwards and away from global challenges as the populist right would do , nor revert to the kind of posturing from the sidelines where the far left habitually resides . The best way to address the UK 's lack of influence around the world is surely to build it back up , piece by piece , with those who have it already . <p> In any case , the sheer scale of the world 's crises means that Starmer 's international itinerary is n't going to get less demanding any time soon . I 'm told that plans are being finalised for a trip to Washington for a formal White House meeting in January either around , or immediately after , Donald Trump 's second presidential inauguration , where they will doubtless have much to talk about . <p> That will be followed at the start of February by a European summit on Ukraine where Starmer may be asked to commit British troops in a peacekeeping mission alongside a " coalition of the willing " -- from which , the presumption is , the US would be a notable absentee . In spring there will be another summit in Brussels on structural changes to the Brexit deal where he hopes to deepen the security relationship with the EU , ease some trade and travel restrictions , as well as make it easier to sell billions of pounds worth of clean energy . <p> As ever , domestic political pressures will intrude . For instance , Britain may be willing to commit troops to Ukraine but whether it will be able to do so depends on both the strategic defence review being published over the next few months and the Treasury finding money for increased military spending at the cost of more tax rises or cuts elsewhere . At the same time , Labour 's post-Brexit neuralgia means there will be no return to the single market or the customs union , while even the EU 's desire for a " youth mobility scheme " appears to be beyond the government 's pale . <h> Advertisement <p> But Starmer has always insisted that delivery at home depends on progress abroad . For instance , if you 're worried about unsustainable levels of migration , you really should be bothered about wars in the Middle East or the climate change that have driven it . And , for all the talk of the budget squeezing out growth , that 's nothing compared to what a combination of Brexit , the pandemic and an energy crisis triggered by Russia 's invasion of Ukraine have done to the UK economy . <p> On the plus side , seasoned diplomats travelling with Starmer or David Lammy , the foreign secretary , say they are struck by the warmth and relief with which they have been greeted . If the PM is not the world 's most charismatic leader , he 's at least recognised as one who is serious and properly engaged , which elevates him above most of his immediate predecessors in Downing Street . <p> But for all the feelings of goodwill towards Britain , tangible results from this new global outreach are limited . The most notable achievement so far seems to be a deal to hand over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands that 's still generating more controversy than it probably deserves . While Downing Street points out that efforts to tackle people-trafficking gangs will be helped by a new agreement with Germany to target warehouses where boats are stored or the European co -- operation that resulted in the arrest of a smuggling kingpin in the Netherlands , aides privately acknowledge this is not going to be transformative . <p> Here a familiar criticism of Starmer looms back into view . After six months in charge there are complaints that we still do n't know the answer to basic questions . Will he lean towards closer alignment with the EU or with the US ? Does his lifelong commitment to human rights and international law find realpolitik limits when it comes to China and Israel ? How far will he really go to defend Ukraine ? This is not , say critics , like the big vision of Margaret Thatcher in the Cold War or of Tony Blair when he was preaching his doctrine of liberal interventionism . <h> Advertisement <p> To which the best answer is that there is no simple narrative that can explain this turbulent world . As Starmer said earlier this month , he does not intend to make a dangerous choice between America and Europe when " the national interest demands that we work with both " . Indeed , maybe this is an era in which ambiguity can provide the shade we need from ideas that glitter rather than shine . <p> Instead of being presented with a leader who 's obsessed with delivering his domestic " milestones " , we should perhaps accept Starmer for what he is -- and as he has , largely , been seen abroad . The prime minister can yet come to embody the good sense , moderation and decency that were once associated with our country , an internationalist Britain that has been sorely missed on the world stage in recent years . <p> Who knows , voters back at home might then even feel a flicker of patriotic pride the next time they see him stepping into an aeroplane .

@@119425029 <p> If you are in search of your next show to watch , La Palma is the perfect bite-sized series . It recently dropped on Netflix and is brilliantly binge-able , but also makes for great watches in several sittings . WARNING : Some spoilers ahead . <p> Centred around a Norwegian family who are holidaying in Spain , the series is just four episodes long and tells the fictional story of how volcanic eruptions result in a piece of mountain " the size of Manhattan " slipping into the ocean and causing a massive tsunami . Like any natural disaster story , it 's grim and gripping at the same time . <p> But what I loved most was how the island itself becomes almost as much of a character as the people in the story . The relationship between the location and scientists and researchers was depicted beautifully , and felt like it really highlighted a combined sense of grit lots of environmentalists are forced to embody , along with the struggle and turmoil felt around conversations which involve climate change . <p> The divisions in how people would respond in such a scenario in the series is stark , and due to the nature of the climate crisis worsening , the narrative feels uncomfortably close to home . Recently , the WMO State of the Climate 2024 Update once again issued a Red Alert at the sheer pace of climate change , and seeing the flaws in governmental responses as well as the human emotions brought to light in La Palma feels equally timely and pointed . <p> The narrative also plays on the importance of strong communication and quick thinking - and the need for people to be able to make their own decisions about how best to prepare for such a horrific event . It also seems to reflect the possibility that there are many theories buried in research that are statistically unlikely to happen which officials are hesitant to raise the alarm on for fear of " causing panic . " <p> But , as we see in La Palma , where one key character goes against the grain , putting his career on the line by sharing the co-ordinates of a " safe spot " where the tsunami may not reach , despite not having complete confidence in the concept - the risk pays off . <p> There 's also a much quieter theme running through the show that gets viewers thinking about how we relate to nature ( and how often we are failing to listen to it ) . At the heart of the series is the idea that nature does n't just act randomly . It reacts and communicates , and if we take a moment to truly pay attention , it can tell us exactly what it needs . <p> The issue at the root of climate change remains not the environment , but with our own responses . What struck me ( another large spoiler alert here ) is that even when you get to the end of the last episode and realise that , somehow , the whole family who are the main focal point of the series all survive , there 's still a really cold sense of despair that hits you that is connected with the climate crisis . <p> For me , I was hit with the same feeling which the characters seem to be going through during the episodes , as the large scale events force them to confront things they 've taken for granted , and it 's only in that confrontation that you can begin to comprehend what an incident like this would really mean . <p> According to scientists , the world could reach a tipping point for irreversible climate change in as little as 12 years if we do n't take dramatic action to reduce carbon dioxide emissions . This is a topic which needs to be dominating discussions in every corner of the world this year , and every year , and at the moment it feels like a drastic sense of urgency has been lost . <p> But what La Palma subtly suggests is that nature is constantly speaking , even when we are n't listening to what it has to say . And sometimes it does take watching a fictional , worst case scenario play out in front of you to internalise what is going on and create more space for thinking about this aspect of life going forwards . <p> Story Saved <p> You can find this story in My Bookmarks.Or by navigating to the user icon in the top right . 
@@119425201 <p> Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council , the author of the award-winning " Goodbye Globalization " and a regular columnist for POLITICO . <p> We are in a maritime mess . Unknown perpetrators are sabotaging undersea cables , the Kremlin has grown its shadow fleet to encompass a chunk of the world 's commercial vessel fleet , and the Houthis are intensifying attacks on Western shipping to the point that Western carriers are avoiding the Red Sea altogether . <p> But all this is n't just a headache for shipping companies or undersea cable operators -- it threatens coastal states , the environment and most countries ' economies . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> That 's why we need a " Protect the Oceans " coalition . <p> In November , the bulk-carrier Yi Peng 3 allegedly sabotaged two undersea cables in Sweden 's exclusive economic zone ( EEZ ) . A month later , the Chinese-flagged vessel was still taunting Swedish authorities , anchored in Denmark 's EEZ , adjacent to Swedish waters , biding its time . And the two countries could n't get to the bottom of what had happened : Chinese authorities were simply not responding to Sweden 's request for cooperation . On Dec. 21 , having refused the Swedish prosecutor permission to board , the Yi Peng 3 sailed off . <p> Nearby , a steady stream of suspected Russian shadow tankers was passing through Danish and Swedish waters on their way from Russia 's Baltic Sea ports to international destinations . Shadow tankers violate a host of international maritime rules , including the requirement to have insurance and undertake regular maintenance . These rickety vessels thus pose considerable risks to other ships , coastal countries and the marine environment but , again , there 's little nations can legally do to stop them since all vessels have the right to travel through any country 's waters under the U.N . ' s Convention on the Law of the Sea . <p> To be sure , coastal countries can demand proof of insurance and seaworthiness in their territorial waters , but in their EEZs -- where shadow vessels primarily sail -- they have fewer rights . <p> For example , on Dec. 16 , the U.K. , Poland , Sweden , Finland , Denmark and Estonia announced they 'd start requesting proof of insurance from suspected shadow vessels passing through the English Channel , the Danish Straits , the Sound between Denmark and Sweden as well as the Gulf of Finland . But these are not EEZs , which are shadow vessels ' favorite waters , precisely because coastal states have fewer rights there . Meanwhile , Malaysia , Singapore and Indonesia have seen a string of near-disasters involving shadow vessels , with one such ship even exploding off the coast of Malaysia in 2023 . <p> Then , there 's the Red Sea , where the Houthi rebels continue their vicious attacks on Western-linked shipping . Although the U.S. Navy , the Royal Navy and an EU task force are trying to protect merchant vessels in this strategic waterway , the Yemeni militia has kept going , deterred not even by the risk of environmental disaster . In August , they came close to causing an oil spill even worse than that of the Exxon Valdez . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> In the South China Sea , meanwhile , Beijing continues a campaign of maritime harassment against civilian vessels from neighboring nations , including Vietnam and the Philippines . <p> Yes , our oceans are under threat . And lest we forget , climate change is contributing even further harm . The shipping industry is a significant carbon emitter , and in the past decade , its grown by 20 percent . Now , ambitious countries ' green policies are being derailed by geopolitics . <p> But paradoxically , the fact that the oceans face so many adversaries may be a positive thing . Considering how indispensable they are to modern economies -- not to mention life on Planet Earth -- an extraordinary range of people , organizations and nations ought to be interested in a better future . <p> In other words , we need a coalition to protect our oceans . <p> Imagine if governments as different from each other as those of Indonesia and the U.S. , organizations as varied as Greenpeace and shipping lines , and celebrities as wide-ranging as , say , actor Tom Hanks ( who endured the horror of ocean disorder in his role as Captain Phillips ) and activist Greta Thunberg teamed up to speak about the threats to our oceans -- those posed by governments , by shady operators , by the climate crisis . Imagine if they spoke about what would happen to our oceans if those harming it were to prevail , and how profoundly that would affect not just the world 's economies but the health of our oceans too . <p> Thunberg and the Pentagon may have diametrically different perspectives on the world , but protecting our oceans is a cause they can both agree on . In fact , the only parties one could imagine standing against protecting our oceans would be those actively harming them : an unpalatable coalition including the Houthis , its main backer Iran and the countries that do nothing to stop or even criticize their attacks ; countries that conduct trade using the shadow fleet despite knowing it can cause oil spills ; China , which engages in dangerous maritime harassment in the South China Sea ; Russia , which appears linked to recent attacks on undersea cables ; shady operators that sell scrapheap-ready ships into the shadow fleet ; the elusive entrepreneurs who buy these ships ; and pirates and fishermen who overfish or illegally catch . <p> But this group is n't so enormous . It 's certainly not so big that the oceans ca n't be protected . And if such a campaign were to exist , which country , company or person would openly announce : " No , I support harming our oceans " ? <p> Of course , such a campaign would n't save our oceans straight away . And some members of the ocean-harming coalition may brazenly continue harmful activities . But an ocean-protection coalition could help bring attention , name and shame some of the shady characters and outfits involved , and demonstrate to the world that a massive majority of nations and people still support order on the high seas . 
@@119425202 <p> LONDON -- The U.K. , along with the rest of the world , may be on the brink of climate disaster . <p> If the worst happens , Whitehall is going to want a little bit of warning . <p> So it is turning to scientific experts for help -- and to a government-backed center for innovative research which also happens to be the legacy left by one of the most controversial figures in recent U.K. political history . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Scientists , assisted with millions in government funding , are about to embark on a mission to set up an " early warning system " for two so-called climate change ' tipping points ' : critical thresholds which , if breached , could plunge Britain and much of the world into a new reality of extreme weather and food insecurity . <p> The ? 81 million , multi-year scheme could deploy robots -- dubbed WALL-E by some experts , in honor of Pixar 's robotic environmental hero -- to monitor the impact of climate change in the Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic . The cash would also be used for supercomputer models of historic climate data . <p> It will all be led by the Advanced Research and Invention Agency ( ARIA ) , an independent body funded by the government and founded at the instigation of former Downing Street adviser Dominic Cummings , Boris Johnson 's top aide until he was forced out of Downing Street in a swirl of ignominy in 2020 . <p> ARIA has a remit to carry out research considered " too speculative , too hard , or too interdisciplinary to pursue elsewhere , " according to its own mission statement . <p> This includes work on prospective climate disasters . " It is incumbent on governments to think the unthinkable about what might happen , " said Laurie Laybourn , a researcher on climate and security at the Institute for Public Policy Research , a think tank . <h> Climate monitor <p> Full details of the project will be announced in early 2025 . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> But the aim is to monitor for changes in ocean circulation , temperature , and ice melt -- driven by global warming -- that could herald the collapse of the subpolar gyre ( SPG . ) <p> The U.K. , along with the rest of the world , may be on the brink of climate disaster . Benjamin Cremel/Getty Images <p> That system of marine currents plays a critical role in maintaining northern Europe 's temperate climate . The project will also assess the linked risk of the Greenland ice sheet collapsing . <p> If there are signs the SPG is about to collapse , it would tell anyone paying attention that potentially existential changes to global conditions could be on on their way . <p> There is still significant scientific uncertainty , but some climate models anticipate that SPG collapse could happen as soon as 2040 , resulting in colder , snowier winters and hotter summers in the U.K. and Europe , while potentially disrupting monsoon rains that are vital for food security in west Africa . <p> Ultimately , the goal is to create a permanent monitoring system that would alert policymakers if a tipping point was coming -- buying governments and their populations vital time to prepare . <p> Sarah Bohndiek , one of the two scientists leading the climate change program at ARIA , warned the world was less prepared for climate tipping points than it had been for COVID-19 . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> " We saw the devastating societal and economic consequences of the coronavirus , but also the speed with which we were able to respond and start delivering vaccination and delivering medical care , " Bohndiek told POLITICO . <p> " What would happen if we cross one of these climate tipping points ? Well , actually , we do n't have the same level of preparedness that we had for the pandemic . " <h> ' Catastrophic losses ' <p> But warning signs over the SPG could be just the first stage of a still bigger tipping point : the breakdown of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation ( AMOC ) ocean current . <p> A recent IPPR report , written by Laybourn , the climate and security specialist , concluded that AMOC collapse would lead to such extreme cold that it " would effectively wipe out crop-growing in the U.K. " Its wider effects could cause " catastrophic losses to key crops globally , " the report said . <p> The paper criticized the government for failing to take account of climate tipping points when assessing national security risks and strategy . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Laybourn welcomed the idea of an early warning system . If a tipping point is approaching " we need as much warning as we can , " he said . <p> A government spokesperson said : " We continue to support fundamental research into climate risks , such as the work being conducted by both the Met Office and ARIA , as part of our record-breaking ? 20.4 billion backing for U.K. research and development . " <p> There is still significant scientific uncertainty , but some climate models anticipate that SPG collapse could happen as soon as 2040 . Carl Court/Getty Images <p> Gemma Bale , Bohndiek 's co-director on the early warning system project , described the research as " edge-of-the-possible stuff . " <p> " What we want to do over the five years of our program is to demonstrate that it could be possible , " said Bale . " Maybe we 'll have something that looks like an early warning system at the end of five years . But maybe we 'll have just changed the conversation so people are thinking : ' This is what we need to do to actually build that system -- and take these risks really seriously . ' " <p> The challenges are technical as well as scientific , said Bohndiek . Robotic measuring instruments -- the ones she likens to WALL-E -- would have to operate for years in the depths of the ocean or out on the wastes of the Greenland ice sheet in the middle of an Arctic winter . <p> Bohndiek and Bale , both founding directors at ARIA , have a background in medical physics , not climate science . They have asked top climate scientists already working on the problem for proposals to design the early warning system , as well as specialists in sensor technology . The agency also wants to work with social scientists who can then help convert the findings into policy recommendations . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <h> Be prepared <p> The chosen " creators " -- ARIA speak for researchers -- will take the project forward early next year . <p> Tim Lenton , professor of climate change at the University of Exeter , is one of those who has submitted a proposal . An SPG collapse , if it happened , could unfold " quite quickly ... in the space of a decade , " he said . <p> The costs of government investing in an early warning system now is " trivial compared to what you can save in terms of damages , " he added . <p> But if the unthinkable happened , and the SPG early-warning system was triggered , what could Whitehall actually do ? <p> " You 'd start with the basics , " said Lenton . <p> " So , snowier , harsher winters -- let 's get some more salt . Let 's think more like British Columbia and how they cope with their winters . How do we make the rail network more resilient ? How do we cope with more heating demand ? " <p> Advertisement <p> The ? 81 million , multi-year scheme could deploy robots to monitor the impact of climate change in the Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic . Drew Angerer/Getty Images <p> In more extreme scenarios , ministers would have to ask , " What kind of agriculture we can credibly maintain and how do we support farmers to keep doing it ? " Lenton said . " Forewarned is forearmed . " <p> In the more unlikely scenario of a full-scale AMOC collapse , those early warnings would demand even more drastic action from governments around the world . <p> Laybourn describes AMOC collapse -- and its knock-on effects on agriculture and society -- as a " planetary-scale cataclysm . " <p> " Hyperbole is a feature of our age -- but these are appropriate words for this , " he said .

@@119426695 <p> Kenya continues to lead in diaspora inflows across the eastern Africa region , receiving $4.8 billion in 2024 . The figures tower over Somalia 's $1.73 billion and Uganda 's $1.49 billion , according to newly-published World Bank statistics . <p> The Democratic Republic of Congo and South Sudan recorded declines in inflows on a year-on-year basis , to $1.35 billion and $1.14 billion respectively , while the remaining three EAC States Tanzania , Rwanda and Burundi are still stuck below the $1 billion ceiling . <p> The latest figures were published along with World Bank estimates that diaspora remittances have significantly overtaken other types of external financial flows to low and middle-income countries across the world , including Foreign Direct Investments ( FDIs ) , within the past decade . <p> In EAC , South Sudan and Somalia have become increasingly dependent on remittances to prop up their economies , contributing 17.5 percent and 13.6 percent of GDP respectively this year . <p> Kenya 's remittances-to-GDP ratio currently stand at 4.6 percent after inflows climbed steadily from $51 million in 2001 . Rwanda 's ratio is now up to 3.9 percent following a further improvement in inflows from $518 million in 2023 to $537 billion in 2024 . Uganda 's ratio is 2.6 percent . <p> Remittance inputs to economies of the remaining three EAC member States are stunted at below two percent . For DR Congo it has dropped to 1.8 percent of GDP in tandem with a sharp decline in inflows from record levels of $3.26 billion in 2022 and $3.3 billion in 2023 . <p> Burundi 's figure is 1.6 percent of GDP on average inflows of just below $50 million since 2018 while Tanzania continues to trail far behind its EAC counterparts with diaspora remittances of $757 million contributing just one percent of its GDP in 2024 . <p> In a blog published on December 18 to mark the annual International Migrants Day , World Bank economists Dilip Ratha , Sonia Plaza and Eung Ju Kim said the whole of sub-Saharan Africa had recorded an estimated 2.4 percent growth in remittance flows in the past year . <p> Officially recorded remittances to low and middle-income countries across the globe were expected to reach $685 billion in 2024 , larger than FDIs and Official Development Assistance ( ODA ) combined and excluding flows through informal channels . " During the past decade , remittances increased by 57 percent while FDI declined by 41 percent . Remittances will likely continue to increase because of enormous migration pressures driven by demographic trends , income gaps , and climate change . " <p> The top five recipient countries for remittances in 2024 were India with an estimated inflow of $129 billion , Mexico ( $68 billion ) , China ( $48 billion ) , the Philippines ( $40 billion ) and Pakistan ( $33 billion ) . " Therefore , countries need to take note of the size and resilience of remittances and find ways to leverage these flows for poverty reduction , financing health and education , financial inclusion of households , and improving access to capital markets for state and non-state enterprises , " the blog authors said . <p> In Africa , Egypt topped the list with $22.65 billion in 2024 , followed by Nigeria ( $19.84 billion ) and Morocco ( $12.05 billion ) . <p> The World Bank report covers remittance inflows to low and middle-income countries since 2000 with Uganda maintaining the healthiest stream of inflows among EAC countries throughout the period under review , starting off with $238 million in 2000 . <p> Tanzania 's slowness in encouraging more diaspora remittances to bolster its economy , in the face of a snail 's pace growth in figures from $8 million in 2000 to $757 million in 2024 , has been attributed primarily to a reluctance to introduce laws allowing its diaspora to adopt dual citizenship . <p> In May this year the government said it was planning to table a bill granting Tanzanian nationals who have taken up permanent residence abroad with a " special status " in lieu of dual citizenship , giving them specific rights and privileges in terms of property ownership and investment tax favours . Earlier this year , the company announced the signing of a firm and binding agreement with the leading Norwegian crop nutrition company Yara for the supply of green ammonia on a long-term basis from the Oman project . @@119426709 <p> Doha , Qatar : The momentum around environmental , social and governance ( ESG ) is growing in Qatar driven by various government initiatives , efforts to diversify the economy , and increasing requirements for sustainable activity disclosures and reporting . <p> Sustainable finance in Qatar holds significant potential on both the supply and demand sides . In 2024 , Qatar 's sustainable finance reached new heights with the issuance of green bonds totaling $2.5bn , the first of its kind in the region to fund environmentally friendly projects , noted Invest Qatar in a report entitled ' Sustainable Growth in Qatar -- Road to ESG investing . ' <p> The Qatar Central Bank ( QCB ) unveiled in 2024 its ESG and sustainable strategy , with the goal of establishing Qatar as a primary hub for sustainable finance . Sustainable finance is an emerging area that is rapidly gaining traction around the world . It is most succinctly defined as the process of taking environmental , social and governance ( ESG ) considerations into account when making financial investment decisions . <p> This initiative allows investors to engage in Qatar 's efforts to combat climate change while advancing the sustainable finance sector , following the successful launch of a $600m green bond by Qatar National Bank ( QNB ) in 2020 . <p> The Qatar Financial Centre ( QFC ) also became the first in the Gulf Cooperation Council ( GCC ) to introduce a sustainable framework for Sukuk and bonds in 2022 . Sustainable FDI is vital for achieving ESG goals , as it directs capital toward projects that support renewable energy , environmental conservation and social equity . By attracting sustainable FDI , countries can drive economic growth while integrating social and environmental considerations into business practices . <p> This investment not only creates jobs and facilitates transfers technology but also helps countries meet their ESG targets and build resilience against climate change impacts . Together , these goals and the various measures launched by the government and the private sector in Qatar present an investment opportunity of at least $75bn by 2030 , the report noted further . <p> Qatar 's actions have been following its stated ambition and vision , and it has taken several initiatives . In particular , key milestones have been achieved in the path to sustainable development in the ecosystem development , buildings and transportation and energy sector . <p> The country is playing an active role in transforming its building standards towards higher sustainability levels by adopting the Global Sustainability Assessment System ( GSAS ) standards . The number of projects registered for GSAS certifications has been rapidly increasing thereby facilitating the transition towards green buildings . <p> In 2022 , Qatar successfully hosted the ? rst carbon-free FIFA World Cup Championship . This was the first FIFA World Cup to feature a dedicated programme to manage stadium energy , water and waste impacts through design , construction and operations . All eight tournament stadiums achieved Global Sustainability Assessment System building certification . The stadiums were designed to be reused and repurposed , with all but one of the arenas featuring demountable components . All the venues were accessible via public transport . <p> Qatar has set itself on the path of sustainability with the release of its historic Qatar National Vision 2030 ( QNV 2030 ) . The vision anchors the developmental activities along four pillars , the two being social and environmental development which lay the foundation of Qatar 's path towards ESG-guided development . <p> To materialise QNV 2030 , Qatar has released a series of National Development Strategy ( NDS ) , with the latest being the Third National Development Strategy ( NDS3 ) for 2024-2030 . NDS3 has specific targets for the promotion of sustainable development . It aims to conserve natural resources , protect ecosystems , reduce greenhouse gas emissions and build resilience against future environmental threats . <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider . @@119426722 <p> DUBAI - The General Civil Aviation Authority ( GCAA ) has launched the region 's first digital platform dedicated to implementing the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation ( CORSIA ) . <p> CORSIA , a global scheme adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organisation ( ICAO ) under its General Assembly resolution in 2016 , was implemented starting in 2019 . <p> This digital platform plays a pivotal role in implementing CORSIA by streamlining the calculation of offset and reduction values for carbon units used by national carriers . CORSIA provides a structured framework to minimise international aviation emissions while accounting for the unique circumstances and capabilities of each country . <p> It requires national carriers and operators to offset any unavoidable carbon dioxide emissions -- those not reducible through technological advancements , operational improvements , or the use of sustainable aviation fuel -- using carbon market emission units . <p> Saif Mohammed Al Suwaidi , Director-General of the GCAA , stated , " The UAE is fully committed to adhering to all global and international requirements to reduce the negative impact of international aviation emissions . Since ICAO 's first climate change resolution for the aviation sector in 2010 , the UAE has supported ICAO 's efforts in this vital area and has continuously collaborated with ICAO member states to achieve all targets aimed at reducing international aviation emissions . <p> " A prime example is the recent adoption of the ' Dubai Framework for Aviation Fuel ' in November 2023 , with an ambitious goal of reducing international aviation emissions by 5% by 2030 . " <p> He added that CORSIA is the only globally approved system for implementation . All fuel standards and future fuel developments fall under its framework . <p> The launch of this digital platform marks a significant shift from traditional data submission processes that have been in place for the past four years . Previously , national carriers submitted data manually to GCAA representatives , consuming considerable time and effort . Now automated , the platform ensures data confidentiality and ease of use for UAE carriers . It also significantly reduces review times and minimises human error . <p> Moreover , the digital platform serves as an important archival system and provides a comprehensive digital record of international emissions data . This will facilitate the development of future applications related to offsetting and reducing carbon emissions in aviation . <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider . @@119426724 <p> A robust global price on carbon is the holy grail of climate change . If emitting activities were artificially made more expensive , proceeds from richer citizens ' carbon usage could help poorer states adapt to already existing signs of global warming . In 2025 a quasi-carbon price will become increasingly apparent -- but in a much more regressive way . <p> With the world looking increasingly unlikely to restrict temperature rises to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial times , climate change is ceasing to be a hypothetical risk . Take the insurance sector . On average natural catastrophe insured losses were $63 billion a year between 1993 and 2022 , according to Swiss Re . But in the years since 2020 they have topped $100 billion . Hurricane Milton and European floods mean 2024 losses may exceed that level again . <p> This is not as bad as it might sound for the insurers themselves . After years in which they faced low returns due partly to low central bank rates , they can now demand higher premiums to cover losses . An index compiled by broker Guy Carpenter of global property catastrophe rates for reinsurance , where insurers farm out the risk of extreme losses , has risen by over 75 per cent since 2017 . US property and casualty insurers like Chubb or Allstate have returned over 140 per cent including dividends in the five years until November 2024 , according to LSEG data . <p> Higher insurance costs could conceivably incentivise homeowners and builders to make houses that are less prone to flood , fire or other risks . Yet in Britain 8 per cent of new homes are built in flood zones , even though new houses are not eligible for support from the Flood Re programme , a kind of mutual insurance for vulnerable properties . More importantly as insurance costs rise , fewer people will be able to shoulder the burden . A recent paper estimated that the most disaster-prone houses in the US could face annual increases in homeowner insurance of $700 , by 2053 . <p> Elevated rates are unlikely to subside . Reinsurers used to fret over large , one-off catastrophes once every decade or so . They are now having to cope with much more frequent mid-size losses of $1 billion or more due to climate change , dubbed secondary events . That can be seen in the record number of US tornadoes due to convective storms , or floods across many countries in eastern and central Europe . <p> At such high rates , more and more properties will be uninsured , and more insurers may leave markets . In Florida , the largest property insurer is state-backed Citizens Property Insurance . With the world also way off the finance needed to help affected countries adapt to climate change , the best realistic outcome is that the taxpayer foots the bill . The worst is that poorer citizens endure a disproportionate amount of the costs . <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider . @@119426754 <p> ( The views expressed here are those of the author , a columnist for Reuters . ) <p> LAUNCESTON , Australia - It may pay to be a contrarian in 2025 , as the upcoming year has the potential to be one of the most volatile in recent memory , particularly in commodities . <p> There is the return of U.S. President-elect Donald Trump , who is threatening to disrupt global trade flows with a wall of tariffs on imports into the United States . <p> With an incoming Republican-led Congress , he will have little to restrain him this time around . <p> There is also still considerable uncertainty over the economic trajectory of China , the world 's second-biggest economy and largest buyer of commodities . <p> And the future of the global energy transition has become much hazier because of Trump 's climate change scepticism , the increasing influence of right-wing political parties in Europe , and increasing public wariness of the costs they may be forced to shoulder as the world shifts away from carbon-based energy . <p> All of the above could create an environment in which contrarian ideas turn into realities . Below I outline five such scenarios . To be clear , these are not my base case expectations for 2025 . Rather they are possibilities worth keeping an eye on . <p> 1 . Trump is way better than expected <p> In this scenario , virtually everything goes right for the incoming Trump administration . The threat of tariffs is enough to force concessions from major trading partners , resulting in the implementation of only a few small trade barriers . <p> The United States remains the global economic standout , and the rest of the world essentially rides on its coattails . <p> In turn , commodity prices are pushed upward , apart from crude oil , which would probably struggle from too much supply , especially if U.S. producers increase output significantly as Trump is demanding . <p> There may also be a peace dividend if Trump helps to broker ceasefires in Ukraine and the Middle East , even if the former requires giving into some of Russian President Vladimir Putin 's demands . <p> This would be bullish for commodities exposed to global growth , such as copper , but potentially bearish for crude and natural gas if Russian supplies return to the market . <p> 2 . Trump is way worse than feared <p> The new Trump administration follows through on his most extreme threats , erecting massive trade barriers and withdrawing from , or undermining , international pacts and treaties , including the Paris climate deal and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation . <p> If this happens , expect the global economy to suffer as countries battle to re-order trade flows and supply chains . Inflation would probably rise globally , and monetary policy may be tightened in many major economies as a result . <p> Commodities exposed to global growth , such as copper and iron ore , would weaken , as would crude oil and LNG as demand softens . <p> A preview of this is copper 's reaction to Trump 's election victory , with London contracts dropping 7.7% in the following week . <p> It is also likely that bond vigilantes would punish Treasuries in response to Trump 's policies , especially if he combines huge tariffs with deficit-boosting tax cuts . <p> And U.S. equities may ultimately turn bearish if Wall Street realises that the sugar high from tax cuts will not outweigh the economic damage from tariffs . <p> 3 . China comes roaring back <p> Many Western analysts now hold the view that China is the sick man of Asia , meaning a rebound in its economy would come as a big surprise . <p> But it is possible that 2024 will be remembered not as a moment of decline but as the year Beijing cleaned up the troubled parts of its economy , such as the poor financial state of housing developers and local governments . <p> These efforts could start to bear fruit in 2025 , allowing Beijing to focus more on boosting consumer sentiment and spending . <p> If China is also able to successfully navigate the new Trump administration 's policies , it could change tack to engage more constructively with Europe and build better partnerships with the global south , finding new markets to exploit its leadership in energy transition technologies and products . <p> A revitalised China would be a boon for commodities such as copper , iron ore , liquefied natural gas and coal , but perhaps not as much for crude oil , given its ongoing and rapid switch to electric vehicles . <p> 4 . OPEC+ starts to fracture <p> The remarkable cohesion of OPEC and its allies , the group known as OPEC+ , has been a defining feature of crude oil markets in recent years . <p> This collective export body has used output cuts to anchor crude prices in a range around $75 a barrel for the past two years . That may not be as strong as some members would like , but is still considerably higher than would likely have been the case without the production discipline . <p> However , the ongoing demand softness and the new Trump administration 's aims to further boost U.S. output may place more pressure on the bloc 's unity . <p> Some members , such as the United Arab Emirates , may take the view that it is best to monetise reserves sooner rather than later , especially if they start to believe that the China-led switch to electric vehicles ( EVs ) has become a juggernaut that could upend global energy markets . <p> 5 . The energy transition accelerates , but the United States is left behind <p> One way China can counteract any U.S. trade barriers is to boost its engagement with the rest of the world , and one of the best ways of doing this is by expanding trade in manufactured goods such as EVs , solar panels , batteries and wind turbines . <p> The energy transition could accelerate on the back of cost-competitive Chinese goods , coupled with a willingness among buyers outside the United States to move away from expensive fossil fuels . <p> In this scenario , the United States gets further left behind as Trump 's " America First " policy effectively becomes America alone . <p> If the energy transition does accelerate , it will be positive for copper , lithium and a host of minor metals . Silver may also benefit , given its use in making solar panels . <p> Overall , the first part of 2025 is likely to be defined by a period of uncertainty , followed by markets adapting to whatever new realities unfold . Past experience suggests that initial price and volume volatility does not last and commodity markets are remarkably adept at adjusting . <p> The views expressed here are those of the author , a columnist for Reuters . <p> ( Editing by Anna Syzmanski and Clarence Fernandez ) <p> Reuters <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider .
