@@119443228 <h> Mushy ice and lost kit : The scientists studying Antarctica as it melts <p> Getty Images <p> ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> With Antarctica 's climate warming at an unprecedented rate , scientists are battling with dangerously thin ice and equipment falling through into the sea beneath . <p> For 20 years , Simon Morley has been cutting holes in Antarctic sea ice and diving into the frigid waters below to study strange and colourful sea life -- including sea squirts and sponges . But climate change is thinning out this ice , meaning it is often no longer safe enough to travel over . <p> " ' We 'd get 100 or more dives through the sea ice in the winter period in the past , " says Morley , a marine biologist with the British Antarctic Survey ( BAS ) . " Last year , I think my colleagues managed maybe five to ten dives through the sea ice . " <p> The ice is creating a Catch-22 situation . " It 's too thick for them to get the boats out but it 's not thick enough to cut holes in with the chainsaw and actually do the diving , " he explains . A helpful way around this , however , is to keep boats ready and standing by during the winter , so that they can launch immediately when a window opens to use them , he says . <p> The scientists who study Antarctica and the organisms that live there have noticed these changes . Not least because their jobs are getting more difficult . <p> " The glacier that I learnt to ski on in South Georgia is no longer a glacier , it 's not there anymore , " says Morley , who has worked in Antarctica since 2005 . Instead the island , which lies northeast of the Antarctic Peninsula , has gained areas of bare ground and patches of invasive meadow grass have appeared there . Now that it is no longer possible to carry out so many dives throughout the year to study life in the seas , he and his colleagues are trying to carry out those dives in clusters during the summer and winter , which allows them to make seasonal comparisons instead of performing continual monitoring . <p> What 's the hurry ? <p> One reason scientists are interested in Antarctic ice is to study past patterns of climate change . Research activities such as taking ice cores , which are composed of layers of ice laid down millennia ago , can reveal what global temperatures were like at the time . And trapped pockets of gas in those cores can be analysed to help us understand how the makeup of the atmosphere has changed . However , these precious records are threatened by the retreat of glaciers and the warming of polar regions . The pressure is on to collect as much data as possible before it 's too late . You can read more about the ancient memories trapped in the world 's ice in this article by Lou Del Bello . <p> Morley enthuses about the extraordinary species that he has seen on his trips : " Amazing sponge , anemone and sea squirt gardens -- they 're absolutely incredible . " However , these underwater wonderlands are at risk . <p> Now that there is less ice covering the cold waters where these animals live , algae that blooms with the increasing levels of light from above is spreading and threatening to smother the sponges and similar lifeforms , says Morley . In May , he and colleagues published a paper noting that these creatures face an additional climate change-related problem : there 's a rising risk of huge , moving chunks of ice ploughing into the seafloor where they live . <p> Another researcher at the BAS , sea-ice physicist Jeremy Wilkinson , says that he has had to adjust some of the experiments he carries out in the other polar region , the Arctic . This is because sea ice there is far less reliable than before . When the climate was cooler , he and colleagues used to place waterproof suitcases on the ice with instruments able to track things such as wind speed and temperature over the course of a year . <p> " Now , with the ice retreating so fast , we ca n't do that because the ice melts and your instruments drop into the ocean , " says Wilkinson . " All our systems are now designed to float . " <p> Getty Images <p> At McMurdo Sound , sea ice is getting thinner and forming later than it did historically ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Back in Antarctica , the lack of sea ice in the southern hemisphere winter has startled Natalie Robinson , a marine physicist with New Zealand 's National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research ( NIWA ) . <p> She and colleagues use satellite imagery to keep an eye on ice formation in McMurdo Sound , a body of water on the Antarctic coast directly south of New Zealand . " In 2022 , we had a winter growth season the period in which ice cover is usually expanding that no one had ever seen anything like before , " says Robinson . " As late as the end of August we still had open water . " <p> While sea ice did form in McMurdo Sound in the following weeks , it never got thick enough to allow Robinson and her colleagues to carry out their planned experiments in certain locations . In some areas of McMurdo Sound , other researchers were able to transport scientific equipment over the ice on foot . With ice that was only around 1.1m ( 3.6ft ) thick -- roughly half as thick as usual -- it was judged too dangerous to drive . It was the first time the team of New Zealand scientists have had to transport their equipment on foot . <p> " We describe that season as unprecedented , but pretty much exactly the same thing has happened two years later , " says Robinson , of the situation in 2024 . <p> Getty Images <p> Storms are becoming more prevalent across Antarctica , making research more difficult ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> For seven years , Robinson has been hoping to use an ice-coring system to study platelet ice -- a fuzzy-looking mass of ice crystals full of seawater-filled cavities -- which forms on the underside of sea ice . She and her colleagues have designed an ice-coring system that would allow the scientists to retrieve this delicate kind of ice intact , so that they can study its structure and also observe how lifeforms may dwell within it . <p> Robinson 's intention had been to take such samples from sea ice near to the Ross Ice Shelf , a giant ice shelf with an area of more than half a million square kilometres ( 200,000sq miles ) . However , the unfavourable weather conditions meant that they could n't get out to the desired location , and instead had to sample ice much closer to Scott Base , New Zealand 's Antarctic research station . " It was effectively a whole different part of the ocean we were studying , " she says . " Not at all what we were planning . " <p> Getty Images <p> With temperatures increasing , Antarctica is losing its ice and grasses are thriving -- including invasive meadow grass ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> The problem is not just that warmer temperatures are hampering ice formation , it 's also that storminess appears to be increasing in the Southern Ocean , which churns up ice and prevents it attaching securely to land , says Robinson . This storminess has other implications , too : " If we 're looking at a windier general setup , it 's definitely going to make any of the fieldwork that we do much more challenging , " she says . <p> Robinson explains that her experiences in Antarctica during the past 22 years revealed to her what a dramatic impact climate change is having on the continent . She describes what she has seen as " sobering " . <p> That said , in her career , Robinson has noticed public attitudes to climate change evolving . Climate change denial seems to her less widespread than it once was , for instance , she says : " That , certainly , is hopeful for me . " <p> However , time is running out to perform certain scientific experiments in Antarctica , meaning the next few years will be crucial . Potentially , some fieldwork will no longer be possible if huge swathes of sea ice disappear entirely . <p> " We 're racing to gather all the data we can , " adds Robinson , " Before those major shifts happen " . 
@@119443245 <h> Inside the exquisite Tibetan monasteries salvaged from climate change <p> Tashi Gurung says the restoration work has provided him with a stable income and allowed him to stay in Lo Manthang ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> Extreme weather is threatening these intricate 15th Century Tibetan monasteries , but local people are rising to the challenge to preserve them . <p> Tashi Kunga stands before the Kag Choede monastery , built into the Dhaulagiri mountain range on the Tibet-Nepal border . The monk 's carmine robes glint in the rain , as he recounts the ancient legend of Guru Rinpoche 's battle with a demon . <p> The legend goes that centuries ago , a demon wreaked havoc on a monastery in Tibet . Guru Rinpoche chased it south to Upper Mustang in Nepal and defeated the demon following a ferocious battle , burying the demon 's remains across the mountain range . The people of Mustang honoured the sacred grounds by building monasteries atop the demon 's body parts . <p> Climate Guardians <p> This article in the Climate Guardians series was supported by funding from the European Journalism Centre , through the Solutions Journalism Accelerator . This fund is supported by the Bill &amp; Melinda Gates Foundation . <p> " And right on the demon 's heart , the capital of Lo Manthang was built in 1380 , " says Kunga , pointing towards the narrow alleys , ancient monasteries , and flat roofs adorned with prayer flags of one of the last medieval walled cities in the world . <p> For centuries , Lobas , the indigenous people residing here , have thrived in this remote region situated on top of the Tibetan Plateau . One thing that has remained constant is the monasteries , locally known as " Gonpas " , the most treasured heritage of the region . But almost two decades ago , many of these monasteries , which date back to the 15th Century , started crumbling . <p> Tulsi Rauniyar <p> The ancient monasteries of Mustang , Nepal , have started crumbling due to climate impacts ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> Experts sounded the alarm , attributing the collapse to the severe impacts of climate change . Data indicates a significant increase in the intensity of storms and rainfall across the region . Increased rainfall saturates the rammed-earth buildings , as moisture in the soil is drawn upward into the walls , leading to issues such as leaking roofs and rising damp . <p> " For us , Buddhists , the paintings and the artifacts in the monasteries are embodiments of the gods themselves , and we ca n't worship a half-damaged idol , " says Kanga . " There was no one to repair it . Our heritage was slowly decaying away . We thought the deities were angry . " <p> Buddhist monasteries have long been revered as the foundation of Tibetan culture , serving as a vital hub for the creation and safeguarding of both tangible artifacts and profound intellectual traditions . But as unprecedented weather patterns pose a threat to their cultural heritage , local community members have stepped up to restore them . Local people have gained diverse skills , from reinforcing walls to crafting metal statues and restoring paintings . <p> Over the past 20 years , a team of local Lobas trained by Western art conservationists have replaced the old , leaky roofs of the temples with round timbers , river stones , and local clay for waterproofing , and have restored the wall paintings , statues , sculpted pillars and the ceiling decorations , giving these centuries-old monuments a new life . <p> Luigi Fieni , the lead art conservator at Lo Manthang , has spearheaded the restoration project . Transforming a community of farmers into conservators has been challenging , he says . Most of the Lobas had never held a pen or a paint brush before , and undertook extensive training before they began restoring the 15th Century paintings . <p> " But it all worked out , " says Fieni . " Tourists visiting Mustang were keenly interested in religion . So we felt these sacred artifacts needed preservation not only for their historical significance but also for sustaining livelihoods here . " <p> Tulsi Rauniyar <p> The Lobas have given the damaged monasteries a new life ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> The team , initially made up of 10 members , has grown to 45 conservators , mostly women , although there was initial reluctance to accept any women in the group . According to local tradition , women are prohibited from touching sacred objects . However , women did eventually take part in the Lo Manthang restoration project . <p> " It took years of discussion and negotiation with the local clergy and community , but we succeeded in including local women in the wall-painting conservation team , " says Fieni . <p> Married Tibetan women are typically responsible for cooking , cleaning , milking the animals , churning the butter and collecting yak dung for fuel . Tashi Wangmo , 40 , used to spend her time herding yak , collecting and selling herbs , and doing various odd jobs , but it never provided much income . When she received the opportunity to pursue new training and earn a daily wage in the restoration project , she jumped at it . <p> " It enabled many of us women to break free from the limits of our homes , expand our skillsets , and find new opportunities , " she says . " Otherwise , life remains stagnant for us , confined to the corners with little purpose or prospects . " <p> Another female restorer Dolma Tsering , 42 , was n't there just to learn art or refine her painting skills . She believed that by participating in the monastery 's restoration , she would earn spiritual merit and contribute to the promotion of Tibetan Buddhism through her work . <p> " Once you compare the faded , scraped-off outlines of deities and the vibrant expressions of revived figures , you will recognise the incredible scale of everyone 's efforts . It has increased the cultural value of Lo Manthang , " says Tsering . " And as women , we were able to play a role in it . " <p> Tulsi Rauniyar <p> Tashi Wangmo says the restoration project has given women a sense of purpose and freedom ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> But the community continues to face challenges amid the onslaught of climate change . The Himalayas are particularly vulnerable to rising temperatures and climate impacts . When rainfall comes , it pours in abundance , but prolonged drought is also common . In 2023 , heavy rainfall flooded many small rivers and brooks in Mustang , leading to widespread flood damage in neighbouring villages . <p> The roads facilitating easy transport in the region have also contributed to rapid population decline , with many Lobas moving to cities in search of economic opportunities , says Gurung . <p> Tulsi Rauniyar <p> When the monasteries started crumbling , the local community believed it was because the gods were angry , says monk Tashi Kunga ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> Tashi Gurung stands out as a prime example of a farmer-turned-restorer who chose to remain in the region . He was n't exposed to Tibetan Buddhist art as a child , but today he owns an art gallery in Lo Manthang . <p> His gallery showcases a remarkable array of thangkas , portraying the Buddha , his teachings , and various deities and other spiritual beings such as the bodhisattvas . His art sales not only sustain himself but also enable him to send his children to school . <p> Reflecting on his decision to stay , Gurung acknowledges the profound impact of monasteries on his life . " If it were n't for the monasteries , I might have followed my friends who left Mustang for better opportunities abroad , " he says . <p> Tulsi Rauniyar <p> Lo Manthang 's climate-ravaged monasteries have been meticulously restored by the local community ( Credit : Tulsi Rauniyar ) <p> The restoration efforts have sparked a cultural renaissance , according to Fieni . Numerous women and young people have received training in traditional craftsmanship , long-forgotten festivals have been revived , magnificent wall paintings restored for religious purposes , and monasteries and nunneries are thriving once again , he says . <p> " Om mani padme hum , " the students at the Lo Monastic School chant the mantra that Tibetans use to invoke the bodhisattva of compassion , who is also Tibet 's patron saint . Today , Kunga says , the danger imperilling the walled city of Lo Manthang and its age-old monasteries does n't stem from mythological demons , but rather from the impacts of climate change . <p> " If we want to save our culture , we all need to join hands and save the monasteries because everything here spins around religion , " says Tsering. 
@@119444710 <h> Get the latest Chronicle Live breaking news on WhatsApp <p> A doctor has issued a stark warning about the potential for Disease X to become the next major pandemic , stating that the world is ill-prepared for a sudden surge in cases . Disease X , a term used to describe an as-yet-unknown infection , was listed among 11 other diseases that have raised significant concern for the coming year . <p> These include measles , cholera , scabies , bird flu , and even another Covid outbreak . The World Health Organization ( WHO ) had previously identified unknown pathogens as Disease X , including it on its priority list of diseases requiring urgent research . <p> Recently , at least 31 people , primarily children , died from this disease in the Panzi region of the Democratic Republic of Congo ( DRC ) . Between October 24 and December 5 , the WHO recorded over 400 cases of an undiagnosed disease in the DRC , with symptoms ranging from fever and headache to body aches and severe cough . <p> Severe malnutrition was often associated with the most serious cases . According to Dr Michael Head , Senior Research Fellow in Global Health at the University of Southampton , Disease X is one of the infections most likely to cause severe outbreaks or even a pandemic . <p> He warned that if an outbreak were to occur immediately , the world would likely be as unprepared as it was for the shock of the coronavirus , reports the Mirror . <h> Disease X <p> Disease X is n't an actual infection but rather a placeholder name for any unidentified disease that could emerge . However , the threat of an unknown virus or bacterial infection is very real , and scientists are calling on governments to be ready for whatever challenges may arise from nature . <p> " Disease X is the name given to an as-yet-unknown bug , that has the potential to cause large outbreaks or even a pandemic , " Dr Head explained to the Mirror . " This bug would have the potential to spread quickly and have a high mortality rate ; for example like COVID-19 . " <p> He also highlighted the world 's lack of preparedness for the recent pandemic , noting that despite technological advances such as mRNA vaccines , we might still struggle if Disease X were to appear imminently . <h> Dengue fever <p> Dengue fever , known as the most prevalent mosquito-transmitted virus globally , results in tens of millions of cases each year , with up to 25,000 fatalities . While it 's predominantly found in South America and Southeast Asia , climate change is driving more cases into southern Europe . <p> Countries like France , Italy , and Spain are increasingly at risk of dengue outbreaks , often referred to as the ' bone breaker ' disease due to its severe symptoms . <p> The mosquito carrying the virus is anticipated to establish itself in the UK , though it remains uncertain when this will occur . Paul Hunter , a professor of medicine at the University of East Anglia , predicts an increase in dengue fever cases by 2025 , particularly in southern Europe . <h> Chikungunya <p> Chikungunya , another mosquito-borne viral infection similar to the Mayaro and Ross River viruses , had only one confirmed case in Europe in 2024 , but Professor Hunter warns that it could be on the rise next year . The majority of these cases are found in South America , especially Brazil , which reported over 400,000 cases between August and October 2024 . <p> However , as European climates become more hospitable for mosquitoes , scientists fear an increase in Chikungunya . " I think we will likely see more mosquito-borne diseases in southern Europe ; mainly dengue but also probably chikungunya . I also worry about West Nile fever , " said Professor Hunter . <h> West Nile fever <p> West Nile fever , caused by the West Nile virus , goes unnoticed in approximately 80% of human patients . However , for the remaining 20% , it can lead to deadly West Nile fever . <p> The virus is transmitted via mosquito bites , but can also spread through blood transfusions and organ transplants . While there have been no reports of local transmission in the UK , there have been instances of travellers returning with the infection . <p> Reports indicate that human infections of West Nile virus have increased in Spain , France , Italy , Greece , and Germany from November 2024 . At its most severe , the disease can progress to West Nile neuroinvasive disease ( WNND ) , which has dire effects on the nervous system , potentially leading to meningitis , encephalitis , or acute flaccid myelitis . <h> Measles <p> Meanwhile , measles , a serious airborne infection , continues to pose a significant risk , particularly to young children . In 2023 , over 107,000 global fatalities were attributed to measles , predominantly in children under five . <p> Highly contagious , the virus spreads through coughing and sneezing , remains viable on surfaces , and infects roughly 90% of all non-immune individuals upon exposure . Recent years have seen an uptick in measles cases in the western world , correlated with declining vaccination rates -- the first dose coverage dropped from 86% in 2019 to 83% by 2023 . <p> According to Dr Head , " Measles is vaccine-preventable . With two doses of the MMR vaccine , that stops measles in its tracks . With a high uptake , we could literally eradicate it from the planet , like smallpox . A lower uptake , partly due to too much covid interrupting health service delivery in the pandemic , means children in the UK and globally are being affected . It is a nasty infection in unvaccinated children , and it can and does kill . " <h> Covid <p> The current state of COVID underscores these health concerns . <p> Coronavirus has persisted , quietly evolving in the background , with new variants emerging that could potentially be more infectious and resistant to vaccines . In October , the UK Health Security Agency identified a new variant , XEC -- a combination of KS.1.1 and KP . 3.3 strains -- which led to a significant increase in Covid cases across the country . <p> Hospital admissions for those testing positive for Covid jumped from 3.7 per 100,000 to 4.5 per 100,000 within a week . <p> Dr Head commented : " The vaccines , along with use of medicines and diagnostics etc. , have massively blunted the public health impact of COVID-19 . But , it 's still here , very much has n't gone away , and will continue to pose a problem to health services and populations everywhere around the world . Do get vaccinated if another dose if offered to you ! " <h> Cholera <p> Cholera remains a serious global health concern , as highlighted by the WHO . This acute diarrhoeal disease , caused by ingesting food or water tainted with Vibrio cholerae bacteria , can escalate rapidly , potentially leading to death within hours without prompt treatment . <p> Cholera claims up to 143,000 lives annually worldwide . <p> There have been seven cholera pandemics since the 19th century , with the most recent one in 1961 primarily affecting south Asia . However , Professor Hunter has warned that forced migration due to climate change could lead to a significant increase in cholera cases by 2025 . <p> Despite this , cholera remains extremely rare in Europe , with the majority of confirmed cases found in Africa and Asia . For instance , in 2022 , nine EU countries reported a total of 29 cases , all of which involved travel history to a cholera hotspot . <h> Bird flu <p> Avian flu , also known as bird flu , is widely recognised as the most probable cause of the next pandemic . This type of flu virus typically spreads among birds but can also infect humans . <p> Although the virus does not easily transmit to humans , it can mutate rapidly , causing concern for a potential mass outbreak . Currently , almost all reported cases of H5N1 - the most common bird flu strain in humans - are among those who work closely with animals . <p> Dr Head stated : " A permanent member of any ' possible infectious disease threat ' list , avian influenza evolves its shape and style a little like the Covid variants , and has the potential to cause a pandemic , " adding , " We have n't yet seen widespread human-to-human transmission - but we could do . " <p> Bird flu can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals , their droppings or bedding , or during the preparation of infected poultry for cooking . Dr Head remarked that while there is no specific seasonal vaccine for bird flu , a universal jab that could protect against all types of flu , including avian flu , would be the " holy grail " . <h> Antimicrobial-resistant bacteria <p> The UK Health Security Agency ( UKHSA ) has issued warnings about the rise in antibiotic-resistant infections within the UK , and the World Health Organization ( WHO ) has identified antimicrobial resistance as one of the top global health threats . Antimicrobials , which include antibiotics , antivirals , and antifungals , are essential for treating infectious diseases . <p> However , scientists have raised concerns that these infections are becoming more difficult to treat as they evolve to resist medications . . <p> According to the UKHSA , individuals with bacterial infections that are resistant to antibiotics have an increased risk of death within 30 days . Professor Hunter expressed that antimicrobial-resistant bacteria are a " significant concern " as we approach 2025 . <h> E.coli <p> E.coli , which often leads to diarrhoea , vomiting , and urinary tract infections , is the most prevalent type of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the UK . By mid-2024 , the UK had reported over 600 cases of this bacteria , a significant increase from previous years . <p> In a stark warning issued last November , UKHSA Chief Executive , Professor Dame Jenny Harries highlighted the growing challenge posed by antibiotic resistance : " Increasingly the first antibiotics that patients receive are n't effective at tackling their infections . That 's not just an inconvenience -- it means they are at greater risk of developing a severe infection and sepsis . Our declining ability to treat and prevent infections is having an increasing impact , particularly on our poorest communities . " <p> She emphasised the importance of responsible antibiotic use , stating , " Only take antibiotics if you have been told to do so by a healthcare professional . Do not save some for later or share them with friends and family . This is n't just for your own health - it 's about protecting everyone in our communities and future generations . " <h> Whooping cough <p> Pertussis , commonly known as whooping cough , is a serious bacterial lung infection , posing a particular threat to young children and babies , though individuals of any age can present with symptoms upon infection . The illness draws its name from the ' whoop ' sound young babies make after a bout of coughs while gasping for breath ; however , this sound may not be present in all cases , potentially delaying treatment . <p> A significant surge in whooping cough infection has ruffled the UK , with figures exceeding 10,000 confirmed cases by August , and the second quarter witnessing more cases than any since the last major outbreak in 2012 . <p> Professor Hunter has expressed concerns about the trajectory of whooping cough cases , stating it 's unclear if 2025 will see more instances than 2024 , but the situation remains a " big concern " . The UK has witnessed at least 10 infant fatalities since the outbreak began in November 2023 . <p> Dr Mary Ramsay , UKHSA 's Director of Immunisation , emphasised earlier this year : " Vaccination is the best defence against whooping cough and it is vital that pregnant women and young infants receive their vaccines at the right time . Pregnant women are offered a whooping cough vaccine in every pregnancy , ideally between 20 and 32 weeks . " <p> She added , " This passes protection to their baby in the womb so that they are protected from birth in the first months of their life when they are most vulnerable and before they can receive their own vaccines . " <h> Scabies <p> In a separate health alert , doctors are warning not to overlook symptoms of scabies , following a surge in cases . The skin condition , caused by mites burrowing to lay eggs , results in a highly uncomfortable itchy rash . <p> While scabies is n't typically fatal , Dr Head points out that it can significantly impact quality of life . It 's especially prevalent in the UK , often occurring in communal environments such as schools , care homes , and prisons . <p> Scabies cases in England have seen a significant 58% spike in the first six months of 2024 when compared to the previous year . With diagnoses by GPs surging past the five-year average , the north of England appears to be the most affected region . <p> Dr Head highlights the cause and method of transmission , explaining : " The mites burrow under the skin , causing an immune response that triggers inflammation and itching , " and adds , " You can catch it by prolonged skin-to-skin contact , or via clothes , furniture or bedding that an infected person may have used previously . "

The watchdog is expected to get a new chair and several new board members after Donald Trump takes office as US president on January 20 . <p> BlackRock and the FDIC declined to comment . State Street has not been affected by the battle because it is a bank and therefore already more tightly regulated . 
@@119448398 <p> Even at the moment of his death , Jimmy Carter provided his treasured Democratic Party with one final service . Taking his final breath on Sunday at the age of 100 , America 's 39th President unwittingly ensured that Joe Biden , the country 's 46th leader , will preside over arrangements for his state funeral , not America 's president-elect , Donald Trump . <p> The relationship between Biden and Carter stretches back over half a century . When the peanut farmer and the one-term governor of Georgia , little known outside his home state , decided to launch a pugnacious run for the White House , one of his earliest supporters was the newly elected junior senator from Delaware by the name of Biden . <p> In 1976 , Biden became the first elected figure on Capitol Hill publicly to endorse the upstart seeking the presidency . Ten presidential elections later , Carter would return the favour and endorse Biden 's run to become the Democratic Party 's nominee . In February 2023 , shortly after their final private meeting , Biden disclosed that Carter had invited him to deliver the eulogy at his funeral , whenever the moment came . <p> President Jimmy Carter and first lady Rosalynn Carter walk down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington after Carter was sworn in as the nation 's 39th president in 1977 ( Photo : AP ) <p> It took a while . Jimmy Carter spent almost two years in hospice care , and last month his family disclosed that he was determined to live long enough to vote for Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election . <p> Carter 's state funeral , preceded by his lying-in-state in Washington , is likely to be the final set-piece event of Biden 's presidency . Democrats , and possibly the Carter family , will be relieved not to have to navigate memorials and remembrances in the early stages of president-elect Donald Trump 's second White House term . <p> President Jimmy Carter at the White House , in Washington in 1977 ( Photo : Marion S. Trikosko/Reuters ) <p> The passing of Jimmy Carter represents not only the loss of a former president but the symbolic end of an era rooted in democratic ideals and moral leadership . Carter 's life was a testament to the belief that public service could be grounded in humility , compassion , and an unwavering commitment to human rights . <p> During Trump 's first term , in a mark of the civility rapidly evaporating from American discourse , Trump rarely found the capacity to honour the death of Americans with whom he politically disagreed . <p> On Sunday , a brief first statement published on the president-elect 's social media platform , claimed Carter " did everything in his power to improve the lives of all Americans . For that , we all owe him a debt of gratitude . " <p> Hours later , for undisclosed reasons , Trump felt moved to explain his earlier comments . In a follow-up posting , he wrote that " while I strongly disagreed " with Carter " both philosophically and politically , I also realised that he truly loved and respected our Country .... He was a truly good man , and of course will be greatly missed " . <p> As his fellow Democrats come together to revere Carter 's memory , the word " decency " is the one that appears most often in their statements . Former President Barack Obama expounded on the theme : " Jimmy Carter " , he wrote , " promised voters that he would always tell the truth . And he did -- advocating for the public good , consequences be damned . He believed some things were more important than re-election -- things like integrity , respect and compassion . " <p> Former President of South Africa Nelson Mandela shakes hands with former US President Jimmy Carter during a ceremony marking Mandela 's 89th birthday in Johannesburg , South Africa in 2007 ( Photo : Siphiwe Sibeko/Reuters ) <p> It is easy to forget that in office and during his post-presidency , Carter often challenged even the Democratic party to rethink its core principles , " consequences be damned " . In a 1977 televised address from the White House , dressed in a beige wool cardigan , Carter dared Americans to combat the country 's energy crisis by emulating his example , and pulling on a sweater while turning their central heating down . Many Democrats quietly recoiled from the messaging , knowing how badly it would sit with American voters determined to continue using their large , gas-guzzling cars . <p> Former President Jimmy Carter , right , and former first lady Rosalynn Carter raise a wall as they help build a Habitat for Humanity house in 2007 . The pair were working on the 1,000th Habitat for Humanity house in the Gulf Coast region since hurricane Katrina and Rita ( Photo : Alex Brandon/AP ) <p> He urged Democrats to focus on climate change and its impact on the environment , long before the notion was commonly accepted . Early solar panels were installed on the White House roof during Carter 's presidency , only to be vigorously torn down the moment Reagan rode into town . <p> Carter 's life of public service , rooted in respect for human and civil rights , faith-based compassion and personal humility , came from a time in America that is now largely past . <p> His death serves as a sobering reflection on how far we have drifted from those principles . <p> Jimmy Carter when he was the Democratic presidential hopeful in 1976 ( Photo : AP ) <p> As Americans confront a political future increasingly dominated by authoritarian rhetoric , polarisation , and the erosion of democratic norms , Carter 's legacy stands as both a beacon and a warning . His steadfast belief in diplomacy over division and integrity over self-interest feels like an anachronism in a world where these values are increasingly derided or dismissed . <p> Carter 's passing challenges us to ask , are we witnessing the closing chapters of a democracy rooted in decency , or will we find the resolve to carry forward his legacy against the tide ? <p> This is not merely the end of one man 's journey but a pivotal moment to determine whether his life 's work will serve as an epitaph for democracy or a rallying cry to save it .

Bitcoin has also inspired more than 10,000 other cryptocurrencies and spawned an entire industry of crypto exchanges , digital wallets and trading apps . <p> So as bitcoin celebrates its Sweet 16 , how did it get here , and where might cryptocurrency be heading ? <h> The birth of bitcoin and cryptocurrency <p> Bitcoin came as a reaction to the 2008 financial crisis , with the first ever block of bitcoins containing a headline from that day 's edition of The Times : " Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks " . <p> Nakamoto 's creation offered an alternative to traditional finance -- one that did not rely on banks or governments to control its supply . A white paper detailing bitcoin described it as a " peer-to-peer electronic cash system " that uses a network of computers to support an online ledger known as a blockchain . <p> This blockchain , which publicly tracks bitcoin 's supply , provides an incorruptible record of transactions of the digital currency that no single individual or institution can ever control or alter . It also forms the fundamental basis for all other cryptocurrencies . <p> Bitcoin 's decentralised design meant that it was also borderless , requiring only an internet connection to send or spend it anywhere on Earth . While the idea was to democratise finance , its semi-anonymous nature meant that many of the early adopters were people using it to buy and sell drugs and other nefarious items on the dark web . <h> Making its way into the mainstream <p> Despite bitcoin 's rebellious beginnings , its popularity has inevitably attracted the interest of the same traditional institutions that it once set itself apart from . <p> The latest bull market , which has taken bitcoin from below $20,000 to above $100,000 in the space of 18 months , has been fuelled by institutional demand . <p> The landmark decision by the US Securities and Exchange Commission ( SEC ) was hailed as a " historic " moment for the crypto space , and pushed bitcoin to new record price highs . It also prompted speculation that the SEC would approve spot ETFs for other major cryptocurrencies , which finally occurred in July this year for Ethereum -- the world 's second most valuable cryptocurrency . <p> That same month , Donald Trump made history by becoming the first US presidential candidate to actively court the crypto industry . The Republican 's appearance at the Bitcoin 2024 conference in Nashville prompted a price surge that continued to accelerate following his victory in November . <p> Trump has promised to make America the " bitcoin superpower of the world " when he comes into office in January , and has already nominated a pro-crypto candidate to lead the SEC . The incoming president has also pledged to form a crypto advisory council and create a bitcoin strategic reserve from the stockpile amassed from government seizures from cyber criminals . <p> The backing of leading politicians and traditional financial institutions has helped legitimise bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies , while also significantly boosting their price . <h> What is cryptocurrency used for ? And why are there so many ? <p> Bitcoin 's continued price volatility -- it regularly experiences swings of 10% or more each month -- makes it impractical as an everyday form of payment . Investors have instead likened it to a form of " digital gold " due to its limited supply and tendency to appreciate in value over the long term , making it a popular store of value . In December , the world 's largest asset manager , BlackRock , laid out recommendations for investors to allocate 2% of their portfolio to bitcoin . <p> Other cryptocurrencies have emerged that are more suitable for transactions , either due to lower transaction fees , less price volatility , or an active user base . The memecoin dogecoin , which launched in 2013 , has emerged as an unlikely currency accepted by major retailers , including Microsoft , Tesla and Twitch . Its popularity , utility and low fees have even led tech billionaire Elon Musk to suggest it could one day become the " currency of the internet " . <p> The majority of the 10,000 cryptocurrencies currently in circulation were created in an attempt to offer something unique . Some provide increased privacy , making it impossible to track transactions or users , while others leverage blockchain technology to create a platform for things like smart contracts and non-fungible tokens ( NFTs ) . <p> The amount of money in the crypto space has also inevitably attracted scammers and other cyber criminals , who have been aided by a regulatory landscape that is still catching up to such a nascent technology . But with the latest interest from the incoming US administration , as well as the world 's biggest financial institutions , the remarkable rise of cryptocurrency looks set to continue . <p> When investing , your capital is at risk and you may get back less than invested . Past performance does n't guarantee future results .

@@119461934 <p> What is dark matter made of ? Does every subatomic particle have a mysterious twin ? What are the missing pieces in the jigsaw that will help us understand how the universe fits together ? <p> The remarkable discovery of the Higgs boson by the Large Hadron Collider ( LHC ) -- one of the most important breakthroughs in modern science -- may only be the " tip of the iceberg " compared with the revelations that lie ahead in particle physics , according to the British scientist set to take charge of Cern . <p> Professor Mark Thomson 's life-long love affair with subatomic physics was kindled when he read a book as a teenager in the 1970s that featured the work of the world 's largest particle physics laboratory , the European Organisation for Nuclear Research , or Cern from its French name . <p> Almost half a century later he will take charge of that very laboratory . He will shepherd Cern 's efforts to answer the " very , very big questions " that are still plaguing physics -- and champion plans to build a new ? 15 billion collider in a huge tunnel that will dwarf its predecessor in size and power . <p> Just as Nasa uses telescopes to peer ever further into the cosmos to answer questions on the giant scale of stars and galaxies , Cern is peering ever deeper into the world of subatomic particles to answer questions on the minuscule scale of bosons and fermions : the smallest building blocks that make up all known matter in the universe . <h> Advertisement <p> " It 's a bit like looking out into space with a better telescope , " said Thomson , 58 , an expert in neutrinos who is currently the head of the UK 's Science and Technology Facilities Council , which funds research and innovation . " We can see finer detail and have the opportunities to discover something new . We know there is a lot more out there beyond our current understanding . " <p> A discovery made at the LHC in 2012 was big enough to ignite the whole world 's interest in particle physics . Protons were smashed together in the 17-mile circular tunnel beneath the Franco-Swiss border , creating a splash of new particles . This splash included the elusive Higgs boson , which had been predicted in 1964 by scientists including Peter Higgs but had never been detected . <p> The discovery proved there is an invisible force field that permeates the universe . When fundamental particles such as electrons and quarks interact with this Higgs field it creates a " drag " , like they are wading through a field of sticky mud , Thomson explains . This is what gives them their mass . Without this field , all particles would race about the universe at the speed of light . Atoms could not form and nor could larger structures like stars or planets . Or human beings . <p> The LHC is now set to have its brightness cranked up in a new " high luminosity " phase from 2030 which will increase the number of proton collisions and could yield a host of new knowledge about the Higgs boson -- churning them out like a sort of " Higgs factory " , said Thomson , who has a year of lead-in time before starting a five-year term as director-general of Cern in January 2026 . <p> He is also championing a project to build the Future Circular Collider ( FCC ) , which will be almost eight times more powerful than its predecessor , set in a vast circular tunnel that will be more than three times longer than the LHC -- and almost twice the length of the Channel tunnel -- at 56.5 miles . <h> Advertisement <p> The LHC smashes protons together at 13 trillion electronvolts ( or 13 TeV ) -- a unit of energy tiny on the macro scale but colossal for two subatomic particles . The FCC will smash electron and positrons together at 100TeV . Unlike protons , which are made up of quarks , electrons are fundamental particles with no smaller constituent parts inside and will create a much less " messy " set of results when they collide , Thomson said . <p> He said there are " known unknowns " that scientists will be looking for , but added : " We might actually see something completely unpredicted . That 's really exciting . " <p> Thomson will be moving to Geneva with his wife , Sophie , from January . Luckily for someone moving to Switzerland , he counts hiking and skiing among his hobbies . <p> His two children , a daughter aged 21 and son aged 24 , are in the UK studying medicine and computing . " We have n't quite figured out what the family arrangements are going to be , " he concedes . <p> ANNA-TIA BUSS FOR THE TIMES <p> Thomson 's father ran and later owned a curtain shop in Worthing , West Sussex , where his mother also worked . He was the first in his family to go to university . <h> Advertisement <p> He later ended up working down a mine , but was not digging for coal . Instead , this was the best place to work with protons and , later , neutrinos , shielded from the interference of cosmic rays that bombard the Earth 's surface . <p> " We know that most of the universe we can see -- the stuff we can see with light -- does n't make up most of the universe , only about 5 per cent . Another 20-plus per cent is the thing we call dark matter . We know it 's there but do n't really know what it is , " he said . One candidate for being dark matter is Wimps , or weakly interactive massive particles . <p> " We have some theories , and some of these are things we could see at the collider . We 're smashing things together very , very hard and if we have enough mass we can make something new ... We 're seeing the tip of the iceberg at the moment . " <p> " We might be able to see supersymmetric particles , " he added , pointing to a theory that all particles have a twin particle with different properties . This could address stubborn gaps in the standard model -- the current best theory for how the basic building blocks of matter and fundamental forces of the universe work together . It could even help scientists towards the holy grail of physics , creating a " unified field theory " that marries them all together . <p> The LHC is set to reach the end of its life in 2041 . " Today we 've probably only analysed 7 per cent of the total data that will come out , so we 're right at the beginning , " Thomson said . <h> Advertisement <p> Sir David King , the UK government 's former chief scientific adviser , has described plans to spend ? 12 billion on a giant new collider as " reckless " , asking if it would not be " wiser " to spend that money tackling climate change . Dr Sabine Hossenfelder from the Munich Centre for Mathematical Philosophy has called it a " high-risk " project with only a low chance of making major breakthroughs . <p> Building the FCC , which would start operations in the mid-2040s , is " incredibly ambitious " , Thomson conceded . However , he said : " We 've got to be ambitious to continue to push back the frontiers of knowledge . Humanity is exploring the universe that we 're living in and we 're asking questions that are almost impossible to answer . " <p> Asked why such a big tunnel is needed , he said : " Imagine you 're driving a Ferrari and you 're going round a corner . The faster you go , the harder it is to go around a sharp bend . If we want the particles to collide with more energy , we need to steer them around a ring more gently . " <p> The UK government backed Thomson 's application to lead Cern , touting him as the man who can " set the direction for Cern at a critical time " through his " outstanding record of service to the scientific community " . <p> While it is important to expand " knowledge for knowledge 's sake " , particle physics experiments have led to the development of useful technology , such as accelerators used in cancer treatment , Thomson said . " We have to develop new technology ... and that will at some point filter down into everyday life . "

Further records are expected next year as a vast new wind farm at Dogger Bank comes on stream . And in other parts of the world , new renewable energy sources are rapidly growing with solar energy proving to be the cheapest energy in many countries . <p> In transport , there were more than 1,300,000 fully electric cars in the UK this year , about 3.94 per cent of the approximately 34 million cars on the country 's roads . Worldwide , the number of electric vehicles is growing quickly , led by China , although rates of uptake vary widely between countries . <p> There are also increasing efforts to clean up excess CO2 in the atmosphere . Nearly 21,000 hectares of newly created woodland were planted in the UK over 2023-24 , helping to absorb and store CO2 in the trees . Boglands are even more important for locking away CO2 and storing it for millennia in peat deposits , and this year the sale of peat for gardeners was banned in the UK , to be followed by a phased ban on peat for commercial horticulture . Some 250,000 hectares of degraded peatland have also been restored over the past 30 years . <p> In Brazil , the annual deforestation of the Amazon fell to a nine-year low , a decrease of more than 30 per cent in the 12 months to July 2024 , despite a nearly 18-fold increase in fires in the Brazilian Amazon . <h> Advertisement <p> But fossil fuel use still remains stubbornly high and technology is being developed to suck CO2 straight out of the atmosphere . The University of California , Berkeley , developed a type of porous material that captures and stores CO2 from the air , which is cheap , efficient , uses low energy and now needs to be tested on a large scale . 
@@119462328 <p> BRUSSELS ? In 2024 , you 'd be forgiven for feeling a distinct sense of d ? j ? vu . <p> Syria was back in the news , European leaders had to focus again on migration and , across the Atlantic , Donald Trump is preparing for his return to the White House , sending more shock waves through the political establishment in an unprecedented year of elections . <p> And , as our charts show , even all that could be overshadowed by the threat posed by a world getting hotter , which looms over humanity 's future . Despite a plethora of warnings from scientists and international organizations , countries are still failing to contain global warming -- and , if his rhetoric is to be believed , Trump 's second term could further weaken the international effort . <p> So this holiday season may not feel as jolly as it should . But as we hope for cheerier news in 2025 , POLITICO 's data journalism team is here to illustrate how the old year played out . <h> War , war and another war <p> With over 44,500 Palestinians dead and a further 105,000 estimated to be wounded , according to the Hamas-controlled Ministry of Health , the humanitarian cost of the Israel-Hamas war continues to rise . <p> Geospatial analysts estimate that almost 60 percent of buildings in the Gaza Strip had likely been damaged by November 2024 , meaning many of the 1.9 million internally displaced people there will have no home to return to . <p> The Israel-Hamas war increased hostilities across the region , with assassinations , bombings and missilebarrages spilling the Iran-Israel proxy conflict into the open . After almost a year of exchanging missile strikes , conflict between Israel and Hezbollah peaked in October , with Israel 's ground invasion in southern Lebanon , although attacks reduced significantly following a cease-fire agreement . <p> In neighboring Syria , the dramatic overthrow of Bashar Assad 's regime , swiftly followed by Israeli airstrikes on the country 's weapon stocks and the arrival of ground forces via the demilitarized zone , increased uncertainty in the region . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> At the other end of Europe , Russia 's war in Ukraine continues . Ukrainians chalked up some successes in 2024 , becoming a dominant force in the Black Sea despite the country 's tiny navy , and mounting a counteroffensive into Russia 's Kursk region in August . But they are ending this year on the back foot , having lost many of their territorial gains and having seen many of their soldiers killed . <p> But Russia 's constant pressing comes at a huge cost for its troops too , with the past few months being extraordinarily brutal . The Institute for the Study of War , a U.S. think tank , estimated there were 53 Russian casualties for every square kilometer of Ukrainian territory gained between September and November of 2024 . <h> Blockbuster election year <p> With votes in more than 60 countries including France , the U.K. , Bulgaria , India , Japan and the U.S. , as well as for the European Parliament , 2024 was a huge election year . As right-wing forces broadly consolidated their position firmly in the political mainstream , the polls themselves saw social media platforms like TikTok have ever greater influence and even shape campaigns . <p> Europe 's lurch to the right was on display in many of this year 's votes . In some countries , far-right parties rose to power ; in others , they gained a position to exert significant pressure on governments . <p> Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni 's right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists became EU power brokers after the June European Parliament election . French President Emmanuel Macron 's shock decision to call a snap election in the aftermath of the EU vote plunged the country into political chaos . <p> What was interesting is that the far right 's success in many of the votes called for an update to the stereotypical image of their voters being angry old men . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Instead , elections , exit polls and surveys in different parts of the bloc suggested young voters were increasingly throwing their support behind far-right parties . <p> A German youth survey showed the growing popularity of the Alternative for Germany party among the country 's youngest voters . <p> In December , Romania 's top court annulled a presidential election after ultranationalist underdog Calin Georgescu won the first round , citing evidence of widespread interference and a TikTok influence operation -- allegedly orchestrated from Russia . <p> And while TikTok did not give Europe 's far-right forces an outright victory in June 's European Parliament election , it did provide them with a huge platform to reach new voters . <h> Panic about migration like it 's 2015 <p> Wars and political instability in the EU 's neighborhood , coupled with a marked rightward shift in the political landscape , put migration firmly back on European leaders ' agenda . A surge in support for hard-right , anti-immigration parties in several European countries led governments to adopt increasingly restrictive policies . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Gone are the days of Europe 's open-door policy for Syrian refugees , epitomized by then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel 's slogan " We can do it ! " Securing Europe 's borders has become the No. 1 priority , and in some places the political debate has even started to include removing migrants from the EU 's territory entirely . <p> Brussels has been no exception to this reality . The European Commission , reconstituted on Dec. 1 under President Ursula von der Leyen ( who was confirmed by a right-leaning majority in the European Parliament ) , has already promised to get tough on migration . Policies once considered fringe and extreme , such as setting up " return hubs " and " hot spots " in third countries to hold asylum-seekers waiting for their claims to be processed , as well as forced deportations , are now firmly in the political mainstream . <p> Schengen -- the world 's largest free-travel area and a crown jewel of European integration -- is also falling victim to anti-immigration sentiment . Several countries including Germany have reintroduced temporary border controls within the zone , citing security risks , terrorism and migration as reasons for the renewed checks . These restrictions are supposed to be temporary , but some have been extended so many times that they have become nearly permanent . <h> And Europe 's problems do n't stop there ... <p> The EU has other concerns going into 2025 . With disappointing economic growth , issues with competitiveness and a struggling industrial sector , the last thing Europe needs right now is a trade war . <p> But that might be exactly what it gets . Trump 's threat of 10 percent tariffs on all goods and a whopping 60 percent on Chinese goods has Europeans scared of possible knock-on effects . It will be a struggle for the bloc to juggle a conflict between the U.S. , the EU 's largest trading partner , and China , its second-largest trading partner and largest source of imports . <h> ... or there <p> Putting tariff terror into perspective is the fact that 2024 is on course to be the hottest year on record . It will also be the first year that is 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than pre-industrial levels . The inability to contain warming to 1.5 degrees -- a commitment countries made at the 2015 Paris Climate Conference -- is symptomatic of international climate cooperation 's failure . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> The latest U.N . assessment confirmed that global climate action is woefully insufficient . Current plans and policies will lead to 2.6 to 3.1 degrees Celsius of global warming this century , with no prospect of limiting the temperature increase to the 1.5C target . The Paris Agreement 's upper limit of 2C is also at grave risk . <p> The severity and frequency of dangerous heat waves , destructive storms and other disasters rises with every fraction of warming . Scientists say that with warming of 3C the world could pass several points of no return that would dramatically alter the planet 's climate and increase sea levels , including through the collapse of polar ice caps . <p> This year 's COP29 climate conference in Baku , Azerbaijan , was once again marked by controversies and contradictions . While negotiators reached a deal that would see wealthier countries provide a minimum of $300 billion per year by 2035 to aid poorer nations in their battle against climate change , several analyses found that this amount falls far short of the trillions of dollars needed to help vulnerable countries that will have to withstand droughts and floods , rising seas and worsening storms .

@@119477675 <h> Climate progress screeched to a halt this year . One country had its foot on the brake . <p> By Laura Paddison , CNN <p> 6 minute read <p> Published 6:00 AM EST , Tue December 31 , 2024 <p> Link Copied ! <p> An oil refinery in Shubaytah is seen in Saudi Arabia on January 12 . <p> Patrick Hertzog/AFP/Getty Images <p> CNN -- <p> In a year in which global efforts to tackle some of the planet 's most pressing crises -- from climate change to plastic pollution -- have ended in failure or bitter disappointment , there is one country whose name comes up again and again : Saudi Arabia . <p> For years , the oil-rich kingdom has been accused of using its vast resources and savvy negotiating tactics topush against and delayclimate progress , but multiple experts say this year it has been bolder than ever . <p> Over the past few months , United Nations-backed talks on climate change , the biodiversity crisis , plastic pollution and desertification -- the last of which was held in the Saudi capital Riyadh -- all collapsed or resulted in agreements criticized as vastly insufficient . <p> This pattern of failure is not due to Saudi Arabia alone , experts say , but the country has been among those pushing hardest against ambitious action . " They 're the most brazen , the most outspoken , " said Alden Meyer , a senior associate at E3G , a climate think tank . <p> Saudi Arabia 's increased boldness may be due to a number of factors experts say , including the imminent arrival of climate-denier Donald Trump in the US White House . <p> But , it could also be a response to a growing global consensus around the need to stop burning fossil fuels . " They 're emboldened because they are now seeing writing on the wall , " Singh said . <h> A kingdom built on oil <p> Modern Saudi Arabia was built on fossil fuels . The discovery of oil reserves in the late 1930s took it from a nomadic , desert country to a prosperous kingdom within a handful of decades . <p> Oil is so fundamental to Saudi Arabia 's identity , it applied for some of its infrastructure including a pipeline and refinery to receive UNESCO World Heritage status . <p> Today , it boasts the world 's second largest oil reserves . Saudi government revenues depend on fossil fuels to the tune of around 70% -- a reliance experts say helps explain its approach to climate action . <p> The country has " been obstructionist " since the beginning of the UN 's climate process three decades ago , Meyer told CNN . Not only has it consistently cast doubt on and undermined the scientific consensus on climate change -- that it is caused by fossil fuel pollution -- it also managed to bake in its own influence , he said . <p> In the 1990s , Saudi Arabia pushed for global climate decisions to be made on a consensus basis , rather than majority vote , meaning a handful of countries could block decisions , Meyer said . " They gamed the system at the very beginning . " <p> This consensus approach helped create " a world where the rules were set by the big and powerful , " said Juan Carlos Monterrey G ? mez , Panama 's special representative for climate change . <p> While Monterrey G ? mez did not single out any countries , he said the reliance on consensus " has turned into a weapon against the most vulnerable , " used by wealthy nations to block progress . <p> The system also helps explain why , for nearly three decades , fossil fuels werenot explicitly named in global climate agreements . <p> This changed last year at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai , when nearly 200 countries , Saudi Arabia among them , agreed to an unprecedented call for the world to transition away from fossil fuels . <p> Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman , Saudi Arabia 's Minister of Energy , speaks with colleagues at the COP29 climate conference in Baku , Azerbaijan , on November 24 . <p> Sean Gallup/Getty Images <p> But almost immediately after the agreement was struck , Saudi Arabia tried to walk it back . Saudi officials were saying " it 's voluntary , nothing to see here , just move along , " Meyer said . " Clearly they are on a warpath to prevent anything from building on that decision . <p> At the COP29 talks in Baku , Azerbaijan , last month , Saudi negotiators explicitly rejected any mention of fossil fuels in the final agreement . They got their way : The summit ended with a $300 billion finance deal for developing countries , heavily criticized as insufficient , and no recommitment to move away from oil , coal and gas . <p> " What we saw in Baku was very brazen , " Meyer said . Saudi Arabia acted like a " climate wrecking ball . " <p> " We have adopted a pragmatic , practical , problem-solving approach -- non-emotional , non-political , " he said . " We are not about grandstanding , we are about tackling this challenge . " <p> But it 's not just the climate negotiations where experts have criticized Saudi 's role . <p> " What we 're seeing ( Saudi Arabia ) do in the climate space is entirely mirrored in the plastic space , " said David Azoulay , director of environmental health at the non-profitCenter for International Environmental Law , or CIEL . <p> At the failed global plastic treaty talks in Busan , South Korea , which ended this month , Saudi Arabia was among those rejecting any limits on the production of plastic -- almost all of which is made from fossil fuels . <p> Plastics are increasingly seen as a backup plan as demand for fossil fuel energy slowly recedes , Azoulay added . " We 've seen the whole fossil fuel industry , not just the Saudis , reorient their businesses towards plastic and petrochemicals in general . " <h> A global problem <p> Saudi Arabia is far from alone , said said Nikki Reisch , director of the climate and energy program at CIEL . " It 's all too easy to just say , ' oh , one single country is holding the world hostage on climate , ' " she told CNN , but the picture is more complicated . <p> For decades , wealthy countries with fossil fuel interests -- including the United States -- have " hidden behind ( Saudi Arabia ) , really benefiting from the tactics that they 've masterfully used to dilute and delay progress " on climate and environmental issues , Reisch said . <p> These other countries may even shoulder more of the moral blame for the slow pace of action , saidSingh , the climate advocate . Unlike Saudi Arabia , whose economyhinges on fossil fuels , " it is far easier for those ( other ) countries to move away from fossil fuel extraction . " <p> A senior US official said claims the country has hidden behind Saudi actions were " completely inaccurate . " It was " openly at odds with Saudi Arabia " on plans for keeping global warming below internationally agreed limits , the official told CNN , " and clearly disappointed when consensus outcomes fell short . @@119478479 <h> The English wine that 's rivalling Champagne <p> Alamy <p> ( Credit : Alamy ) <p> As a result of climate change , English wine producers are now able to grow grapes traditionally associated with Champagne and producing top-quality sparkling wine . <p> For more than 300 years , Champagne has been the de facto drink of celebration : used to toast weddings , sprayed by winning motor racing drivers and bathed in by Marilyn Monroe . Since this " bubbly " was first produced in 1668 by monk Dom P ? rignon in the French region that gave it its name , its reputation has been unsurpassed in the sparkling wine market , despite plenty of competition from other fizzes . <p> But there 's a new contender in the premium sparkling wine industry , and it 's produced in a region which may surprise global imbibers : the south of England . Global warming means the notoriously cold , wet UK is slowly getting warmer and sunnier , and southern England now has a climate very similar to that of the Champagne region some 50 years ago . <p> " As a result of this change in climate , English wine producers have been able to grow grapes traditionally associated with Champagne , and produce high quality sparkling wines that exhibit characteristics reminiscent of traditional Champagne , " says Sam Linter , head of wine production at Plumpton Agricultural College , located at the foot of the South Downs ( a 100-mile chalk escarpment stretching across south-east England ) . <p> " Climate change means we are now able to ripen top quality grapes like Pinot Noir , Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay , suited to sparkling wine production , " says Chris Boiling , editor of the International Wine Challenge 's online magazine , Canopy . " Talent also plays a key role . We have a new generation of wonderful winemakers who are producing consistently good wines . Twenty years ago , the wines were regarded as imitations of Champagne . Now , the wine producers have more confidence in their own abilities , grapes and terroir -- and English sparkling wine is developing its own distinctive identity , with prominent fruit and toasty , elegant notes , " Boiling says . <p> Alamy <p> Due to climate change , winemakers in southern England are now able to grow grapes traditionally associated with Champagne ( Credit : Alamy ) <p> Thirty years ago at Plumpton , the curriculum revolved around arable and animal farming . Now it centres on viticulture , oenology and winemaking . The surrounding land , where sheep once grazed and apple orchards blossomed , is now covered with rows of vines . <p> " The growth of English winemaking has had a transformative impact on traditional agriculture , " says Linter . " It has altered the landscape and also created new economic opportunities for agricultural communities , including hospitality and tourism . " <p> World 's Table <p> BBC.com 's World 's Table " smashes the kitchen ceiling " by changing the way the world thinks about food , through the past , present and future . <p> Fifteen miles south-east from Plumpton , Rathfinny Vineyard is nestled on the southern slopes of the South Downs in the historic county of Sussex . It 's a 600-acre site , producing 300,00 to 400,000 bottles annually and exports as far afield as the US , Japan , South Korea and Norway . <p> Before husband-and-wife team Mark and Sarah Driver decided to diversify and embrace wine production in 2010 , the vineyard was a working farm employing two people . Now , 90 employees are split between wine production and running the onsite accommodation and restaurant . <p> Alamy <p> Sussex 's unique chalky soil holds water and is well suited for winemaking ( Credit : Alamy ) <p> " We are close to Gatwick Airport and London and in a perfect position to capitalise on both wine growing and tourism , " Sarah says . " Our vines are planted on sunny , south-facing slopes . This protects them from frost and the grapes are kept clean and mould-free by a sea breeze , which also adds a lick of salinity to the wine . " <p> Another key factor in the success of Sussex wines lies in the surrounding landscape and its soil . A short walk from Rathfinny takes you to the mysterious Long Man of Wilmington , a vast chalk figure carved into the side of the hill . A ramble from here , beside the meanders of the Cuckmere River brings you to another mysterious chalk figure -- this one of a white horse -- and then the iconic Seven Sisters cliffs , whose dramatic crags feature in the films Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire , Robin Hood Prince of Thieves and on Rathfinny 's bottles . <p> " The soil we are on is chalk , which is perfect for vines as it holds water and allows vines to flourish without irrigation , " says Sarah , as she runs her fingers over the chalky textured , cut-out cliffs depicted on a bottle of Rathfinny Blanc de Blanc . " It 's exactly the same in Champagne . " <p> This downland has long provided inspiration for artists and writers . Eric Ravilious evoked the area 's gentle curves and flint-walled buildings in numerous paintings . Writer Virginia Woolf lived at Monk 's House in the village of Rodmell . Her sister , Vanessa Bell , and her lover Duncan Grant ( both painters ) were close to Rathfinny at Charleston Farmhouse . The old Saxon church in the village of Berwick is decorated with murals the pair painted during World War Two . It includes scenes from the grain and fruit harvest . <p> Alamy <p> Ridgeview , in Sussex , has been named one of the world 's top vineyards ( Credit : Alamy ) <p> At the time , though , there were no grapes . <p> It was the Romans who first brought grape vines to Britain 2,000 years ago . The Normans also successfully established viticulture 1,000 years later , but viticulture declined in the Middle Ages . And despite a flurry of interest sparked by 18th-Century adventurers , it was not until the 1970s that an English winemaking renaissance truly began . <p> " The Bolney Wine Estate , established in 1972 by Rodney and Jean Pratt in West Sussex , has been at the forefront of the English wine movement and played a significant role in shaping the country 's winemaking landscape , " says Linter , who was previously Bolney 's chief winemaker . " In the 1970s , the production of English wine faced inherent risks and challenges due to unpredictable weather patterns , limited knowledge about suitable grape varieties for the climate and a lack of established winemaking traditions . " <p> Bolney , along with a few other pioneering producers , took on these challenges and paved the way for the modern English wine industry by demonstrating that it was possible to produce exceptional wines . <p> There are now nearly 1,000 vineyards in England and Wales , with 500 in Sussex alone . Perched on the site of a former Neanderthal encampment overlooking Chanctonbury Ring 's Iron-Age fort sits Redfold Vineyard . Its owners , Charles and Wendy Outhwaite , are part of a new generation of winemakers getting international recognition . Redfold 's Ambriel Classic Cuv ? e was nominated by Decanter Magazine as one of their Wines of the Year in 2020 . In fact , all the wines from their first harvest won international medals , and they are not alone . <p> Guy Bell <p> Half of England 's vineyards , like Ambriel , are located in Sussex ( Credit : Guy Bell ) <p> English wines have garnered significant recognition and acclaim on the national and international stage and have been featured at prestigious state dinners and royal events . Plus , in blind tastings against Champagne , they have held their own -- so much so that Champagne producers have started buying large swathes of land in the UK . <p> Sussex sparkling wines retail on average from about ? 20 to ? 40 a bottle and names of South Downs ' vineyards , such as Bolney , Ridgeview , Nyetimber and Rathfinney are becoming synonymous with premium sparkling wines among bubbly connoisseurs . Alongside other vineyards , they are regular winners of English Sparkling Wine accolades awarded by Decanter Magazine , the International Wine Challenge and Wine of Great Britian ( Wine GB ) . <p> " Our wines are now recongised as being of consistentely high quality , " says Sarah . " So our hope is that , one day , people will celebrate with a glass of Sussex rather than Champagne . " <p> -- <p> This story was first published in September 2024 and was one of our most-read Travel stories of the past year .
